articles.title: Microsoft continue de faire le tri dans Windows 11, de nouvelles commandes Copilot passent à la trappe
articles.text:
Microsoft poursuit le nettoyage des intégrations de Copilot dans Windows 11. Huit commandes d’intelligence artificielle vont disparaître de l’Explorateur de fichiers, sans que les fonctionnalités associées soient abandonnées.
En mars dernier, Microsoft promettait de simplifier Windows 11 et de se débarrasser des accès à Copilot jugés superflus. Après avoir supprimé ou rebaptisé plusieurs boutons dédiés à son assistant dans les applications natives du système, l’entreprise s’attaque désormais à l’Explorateur de fichiers. Dans une communication publiée le 19 octobre dans son centre d’administration Microsoft 365, elle annonce le retrait de huit commandes d’intelligence artificielle accessibles depuis le menu contextuel des fichiers OneDrive. Un coup de balai qui ne remet toutefois pas en cause les ambitions de Redmond en matière d’IA dans Windows.
Des raccourcis au rebut, des fonctionnalités toujours disponibles
Dans le détail, les huit commandes concernées se trouvent dans le sous-menu OneDrive, accessible d’un clic droit sur les fichiers compatibles pour les utilisateurs et utilisatrices disposant des accès Copilot nécessaires. Elles permettent de résumer un document, de générer une FAQ, de comparer plusieurs fichiers ou de poser des questions sur leur contenu. Pour les images, elles proposent également d’en analyser une ou plusieurs, de les comparer et d’en extraire le texte.
Leur suppression débutera à la mi-novembre et se poursuivra progressivement jusqu’au début du mois de décembre 2026. Seuls ces raccourcis sont concernés, puisque les fonctionnalités associées demeureront disponibles depuis le centre d’activité OneDrive.
Dans l’Explorateur de fichiers, il sera également toujours possible d’utiliser l’option « Demander à Copilot » du menu contextuel pour interroger l’assistant sur un fichier sélectionné, ou de passer par l’icône Copilot affichée au survol des fichiers dans la page d’accueil.
Moins de boutons Copilot, mais toujours plus d’intelligence artificielle
Cette décision prolonge les changements engagés au printemps dernier. Depuis, Microsoft a fait marche arrière sur le bouton Copilot flottant imposé dans Word, Excel et PowerPoint, tandis que le Bloc-notes a remplacé son bouton Copilot par une entrée « Outils d’écriture », plus explicite.
Mais comme nous l’expliquions déjà début septembre, ces ajustements ne traduisent aucun désengagement de Microsoft en matière d’intelligence artificielle. Le 7 octobre, le groupe présentait encore sa stratégie d’« intelligence hybride », destinée à faire travailler ensemble des modèles locaux et des services cloud. Parmi les nouveautés annoncées, Copilot pourra, avec autorisation, exploiter le contexte du PC pour réaliser des actions à la demande. Redmond prépare également une intégration facultative de son assistant dans la nouvelle recherche Windows, pour obtenir des réponses directement depuis la barre des tâches.

articles.title: Chip Design AI Benchmarks: Beyond Functional Correctness - EE Times
articles.text:
Demand for custom silicon is rising as physical AI, data centers, automotive systems, and edge devices require architectures optimized for specific workloads, memory bandwidth, latency, and energy efficiency. Delivering these designs requires teams to coordinate heterogeneous compute blocks, complex interconnects, and multiple domains while closing increasingly demanding power, performance, and area (PPA) targets.
AI offers a way to expand engineering capacity and accelerate chip design cycles. Design and verification engineers already use AI to generate test cases, assist debugging, and implement portions of RTL. The next question is whether these capabilities can extend across an entire design flow, where decisions made during RTL implementation must hold up through verification, synthesis, and physical design.
To help answer that question, ChipAgents developed Build-A-Chip-Bench with NVIDIA to evaluate AI agents across the end-to-end digital IC design flow, from specification through physical implementation and verified Graphic Design System (GDS). The benchmark evaluates AI agents on realistic, demanding tasks that connect individual design steps to a measurable engineering outcome.
How Build-A-Chip-Bench differs from existing benchmarks
Benchmarks such as CVDP and ChipBench have helped advance AI for chip design by providing common tasks for evaluating and comparing systems. As frontier models improve, however, we need more demanding evaluations to distinguish progress on individual tasks from the ability to execute a complete design flow.
Build-A-Chip Bench raises the bar in two ways: task difficulty and end-to-end scope. It challenges agents to carry a design from workload specification through final GDS, connecting stages that narrower benchmarks evaluate in isolation. Success requires more than generating correct RTL. An agent must preserve functional correctness, satisfy PPA constraints, and resolve problems that emerge during synthesis and physical implementation.
Testing a representative design flow
The tasks exercise a representative specification-to-GDS flow and the dependencies across architecture, RTL, verification, and physical implementation at moderately large scale (designs of 100K-5M standard cells). In industry, these activities typically involve teams of architects, RTL designers, design verification (DV) engineers, physical design (PD) engineers, EDA engineers, and more. The benchmark requires an agent to manage the technical dependencies across these disciplines.
Each task supplies a workload specification, a fixed interface, and an open-source EDA environment. The agent is responsible for architecture, microarchitecture, RTL, verification, and physical implementation. Reference designs establish achievable constraints. Hidden verification IP evaluates functional behavior against held-out tests, and a separate grader evaluates the final submission.
One example task requires an INT4 inference accelerator for Qwen3-0.6B using Verilator, OpenSTA, OpenROAD, and Nangate45 PDK. The implementation must meet a 400 MHz timing target, fit within 6 mm², and deliver at least 15 decode tokens per second at less than 10 W. Memory bandwidth is pinned at 12.8 GB/s. The agent selects the datapath architecture, buffering, and scheduling. Beyond RTL, it also writes testbenches, creates EDA flow scripts, and does manual floorplanning and placement as needed.
Evaluating correctness and PPA
All models were evaluated using fixed open-weight harnesses. Designs must pass functional verification against the hidden VIP and a physical gate requiring a routed GDS layout with no hold-time or design-rule violations. Designs passing both gates are scored on PPA relative to task constraints; failures receive zero. The overall score averages all tasks.
Claude Fable 5.1 achieved the highest overall score at 16.6%, with functional and GDS pass rates of 65% and 75%, respectively. GPT-6 Astra led both pass rates at 85%, but its lower PPA score yielded an 8.7% overall score. These preliminary results do not establish production signoff or silicon validation. Learn more about the findings from our research. [URL]
Where end-to-end design agents still struggle
The evaluation reveals useful engineering judgment alongside inconsistent completion. In one run, an agent applied a post-route engineering change order (ECO), resizing one instance to eliminate a remaining slew violation, then passed final-netlist equivalence checks. Attempts to improve PPA, however, can introduce functional regressions and consume the remaining time budget in debugging.
Agents can also delay architectural corrections while adjusting physical-design parameters. In one run, an agent documented a storage change that would reduce SRAM macros from 51 to 27, deferred it, and spent roughly six hours trying routing configurations before implementing it. Effective closure requires tracing physical failures back to the design decisions that produced them.
Tool runtime further limits iteration. A single place-and-route run can exceed four hours, requiring agents to prioritize changes and reserve sufficient time for final verification and implementation.
The score plateaus in these sample runs reflect the same failure modes: functional regressions during optimization, delayed architectural corrections, and slow tool loops that stall further improvement (Figure 3).
For engineering teams, evaluation should therefore measure whether agents preserve verified behavior during optimization, identify architectural causes of physical failures, and allocate runtime effectively. Work performed at any stage must remain valid in subsequent stages.
Although the benchmark spans the design flow, it captures only part of the complexity of a production silicon program. Under the tested toolchain and resource budgets, frontier agents demonstrated the ability to execute the specification-to-GDS flow, but still struggled to preserve correctness and converge on strong PPA. The demonstrated capabilities point to substantial potential for AI-assisted silicon design, with engineers guiding design decisions and validating the resulting implementations.
Call for partnerships
We are working with industry partners to launch a live leaderboard with broader model coverage and an expanded set of tasks. We welcome collaboration with semiconductor teams, model developers, and researchers advancing AI-assisted silicon design.
To explore a partnership on building Build-A-Chip-Bench together, or discuss how we can help evaluate your models and agents on Build-A-Chip-Bench, contact research@chipagents.ai.

Melhor TV Semp em 2026: qual modelo comprar?
Encontre a melhor TV Semp para o dia a dia; lista reúne modelos com Google TV ou Roku TV, 4K ou Full HD em diversos tamanhos
TVs Semp são ideais para quem quer um aparelho simples para sala de estar ou quarto, já que focam na boa relação custo-benefício e praticidade de uso.
Modelos como S62 oferecem tamanhos de tela maiores e chegam com Google TV. Já televisores como a Semp S42R operam sob o sistema Roku OS e entregam experiência básica, sem recursos adicionais para otimização de imagem.
A seguir, o Tecnoblog lista quatro opções de TV Semp que podem se enquadrar no seu perfil de uso e orçamento disponível. Confira vantagens e desvantagens de cada modelo.
A Semp S62 é uma boa opção de TV 4K barata para sala, com tamanhos de 43″, 50″, 55″ e 65″. O aparelho tem tela LCD com retroiluminação por LEDs convencionais e usa tecnologia HVA, que oferece mais contraste e maior eficiência energética do que telas IPS.
O suporte à tecnologia HDR10+ ajusta contrastes de uma cena para outra automaticamente. E ainda existem outros quatro recursos de otimização com IA para melhorias de cores, contraste, nitidez e conteúdos HDR.
No entanto, o painel HVA também limita os ângulos de visão, resultando em perda de contraste e saturação ao olhar pelas laterais (ângulos oblíquos), e tem menor clareza de movimento do que painéis IPS e OLED (sendo, portanto, menos recomendado para jogadores competitivos).
A smart TV opera sob o sistema Google TV, baseado no Android TV. Com ele, você pode acessar a diversos apps disponíveis no Google Play e espelhar a tela de smartphones ou PCs, por meio do Google Cast embutido.
A Semp S62R também é uma smart TV indicada para sala de estar, com direito a resolução 4K UHD. Contudo, ela é mais simples que o modelo S62 e está disponível somente em tamanhos de 55 ou 65 polegadas.
O televisor é compatível com o HDR10: uma versão antecessora do HDR10+ que usa metadados fixos de brilho e contraste, sem ajustes automáticos para cada cena. Ela não conta com os recursos de otimização de imagem vistos na Semp S62. Logo, as configurações são limitadas a modos de imagem e ajustes básicos de cor.
Outra grande diferença é que a Semp S62R chega com o Roku OS de fábrica, que não é compatível todos apps disponíveis na Play Store. São três saídas HDMI e uma porta USB, mas a TV não possui Bluetooth integrado para conexões sem fio.
A Semp S42 é uma TV básica com boa relação custo-benefício disponível em versões com 32, 43 e 50 polegadas. O modelo maior oferece a melhor experiência devido à resolução 4K UHD. No entanto, as versões com 43″ e 32″ têm resolução Full HD (1920 x 1080 pixels) e HD (1280 × 720 pixels), respectivamente, entregando menos detalhes por conta da taxa de pixels mais baixa.
O suporte ao HDR10 traz melhorias de contraste e brilho das cenas, mas a TV não oferece outras otimizações de imagem. Ao menos, o sistema de som Dolby Audio consegue entregar diálogos e sons mais nítidos.
O sistema Google TV comanda a interface do televisor, organizando os principais apps de streaming e fornecendo recomendações de conteúdo. O aparelho também inclui Wi-Fi e Bluetooth integrados, com duas portas HDMI e uma porta USB.
A Semp S42R é uma TV de entrada voltada para usos menos exigentes, com versões de 32, 43 ou 50 polegadas. Todos os modelos são limitados à resolução Full HD, ou seja, vão exibir menos detalhes e contornos do que modelos 4K.
O televisor não conta com ferramentas de otimização de imagem e nem oferece suporte a tecnologias como HDR10 ou HDR10+. Em compensação, o sistema Dolby Audio traz equilíbrio para os sons e entrega uma experiência mais imersiva.
A TV Semp S42R chega com o sistema operacional Roku OS para facilitar a navegação de streaming. Há Wi-Fi integrado, mas o aparelho não tem Bluetooth nativo para conexões com caixas de som, fones, entre outros dispositivos.

articles.title: The $15 billion ad-powered AI startup your doctor may already be using
articles.text:
Nearly two-thirds of US doctors are turning to an AI-powered search engine to make patient decisions, propelling a little-known tech startup to a $15 billion valuation while prompting a debate over the future of patient care.
Miami-based OpenEvidence, founded by serial entrepreneur Daniel Nadler in 2022, said that many of America’s 1 million physicians processed more than 42 million prompts last month. Doctors are using the company’s chatbot to scour medical journals and clinical guidelines to help diagnose and treat patients.
The ads-powered platform has grown largely by word of mouth, penetrating a sector where few tools have seen similar traction. “We’re the first viral consumer internet app in healthcare,” Nadler told the FT in an interview.
OpenEvidence has won praise from medical professionals who have found it helped ease workloads, according to interviews with eight senior physicians.
But it faces a nascent threat from large AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, who are making a push into the space. Its growing influence has also prompted scrutiny from researchers concerned over the accuracy of its results, as doctors grow more dependent on an AI tool shaping the course of treatments.
The company’s rapid ascent has attracted nearly $1 billion in investment in the past 18 months, from backers including Andreessen Horowitz, Blackstone, Thrive Capital, and Sequoia. The group raised $250 million in its latest funding round in September at a $15 billion valuation.
OpenEvidence booked $100 million in “ad buys”—a metric that covers current and future advertising commitments—for this year at the end of 2025, according to a person close to the company. The startup is on track to generate between $400 million and $500 million through ads by the end of 2026, the person added.
Nadler’s company has penetrated an established market for medical software that was sluggish to incorporate generative AI models. Dutch IT group Wolters Kluwer released an AI version of its leading subscription-based UpToDate medical software tool in October 2025, nearly two years after OpenEvidence entered the market.

articles.title: Blacksmith hits unicorn valuation after Sequoia leads Series C | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Blacksmith, a platform that helps companies more efficiently build and test software, including code written by AI, announced Wednesday a $66 million Series C funding round led by Sequoia that values the company at $1 billion.
In announcing the round, Blacksmith co-founder and CEO Aditya Jayaprakash said the company was founded to make continuous integration (CI) — the process of building, testing, merging, and validating code changes — “less painful.” In a blog post, he said that “most companies are struggling to keep up with the volume of CI they need to run,” especially in an era where so much code is written by AI.
“As agents write more of the world’s software, the question that matters is whether it can be trusted,” he added.
The company also announced that its annual recurring revenue has grown 17x and that it has run over 90 million CI jobs, or individual automated code checks. Customers include Mercury and Granola.
The Series C comes just two months after its $45 million Series B, which valued the company at $550 million. A year ago, Blacksmith was valued at $60 million after raising a $10 million Series A. It has raised $125 million to date.

articles.title: Rogers will soon charge a 1.6% credit card processing fee on bills
articles.text:
Rogers is taking a page from Telus’ playbook and will soon hit customers with a credit card processing fee if they use one to pay their phone or internet bill.
Per a notice on its support site and a warning spotted by some customers already, Rogers will start charging a 1.6 per cent credit card processing fee on January 17, 2027. This will only apply to those who pay their bills via a credit card, with other payment options being exempt. These include:
- Direct debit from your bank account
- Online banking payments
- Cheques
- Rogers gift cards
- Prepaid cards
- Debit Mastercard
- Visa Debit
In the notice, Rogers says the charge “reflects the fees we are charged by credit card companies.”
However, there are some exemptions. For one, customers in Quebec won’t be subject to the credit card processing charge, nor will customers on “select specialized plans.” These include Connected for Success customers and former Shaw Mobile customers on migrated plans.
Quebec residents are exempt because the province’s Consumer Protection Act prohibits charging those kinds of fees.
The CRTC can’t save you
Notably, this comes after Telus pulled a similar stunt in 2022. The carrier filed a request with the CRTC in August of 2022 seeking permission to add a credit card processing fee of 1.5 per cent. But while the CRTC expressed concern over the practice, it also admitted that carriers didn’t need permission to charge such a fee.
The commission did say it would “explore all available regulatory options” if the process continued, but frankly that hasn’t amounted to much more than former CRTC chair Ian Scott saying the telecom industry should “treat Canadians with respect and do better.”
Ultimately, Telus reversed the decision roughly a year later, telling CBC News it heard customer concerns about the fee.
Back when Telus added its credit card fee, Rogers told MobileSyrup that it had “no plans to move ahead with a fee like this at this time.” Frankly, I’m shocked Rogers waited as long as it did to add the fee. So far, Bell has not added a credit card fee.
But perhaps the most frustrating part of this is that carriers have spent the last several years pushing customers into using credit cards for automatic payments. Carriers incentivized auto pay by bundling discounts with it.
Telus, meanwhile, requires customers to sign up for pre-authorized bank payments to get an auto pay discount, but that brings a host of other issues with it. For example, if a carrier overcharges customers and takes the money right from their bank account — which happens more than you think! — it can be extremely difficult to get the money back. The horrible state of telecom customer service makes this problem even worse. One of the few resources available to Canadians, the CCTS, is facing a rising tide of complaints, causing slower resolution times.
And don’t even get me started on the rampant fraud plaguing the telecom industry right now.
All this is to say, Canadians are being squeezed from all sides by telecom companies. And as much as a credit card fee sucks, I would be very hesitant to give any of these companies pre-authorized bank access. But, hopefully Rogers takes another page from Telus’ playbook and reverses course on the credit card processing fee.

articles.title: AMD brings official Ryzen overclocking to Linux with AOD driver support — no official app, but third-party options should arrive soon
articles.text:
AMD brings official Ryzen overclocking to Linux with AOD driver support — no official app, but third-party options should arrive soon
This is a major milestone for improving the DIY tuning experience on Linux.
While Windows overclockers have spent years lazily sliding UI controls to adjust frequency curves and tweak voltages inside Ryzen Master, Linux users have largely had to treat their CPU tuning like an archaeological dig into the opaque veil of UEFI/BIOS firmware. Well, rejoice, Linux users, as AMD has officially published a fresh set of patches for the Linux kernel introducing AOD (AMD Overclocking Driver) support for Ryzen processors, Phoronix reports.
Instead of forcing developers to reverse-engineer closed-source firmware hooks or rely on messy, machine-specific ACPI workarounds, this new kernel driver is a direct pipeline to AMD's platform adjustments. By exposing core tuning capabilities straight through the standard sysfs interface, AMD is laying down an official, upstreamed foundation for software-level CPU management.
Right out of the gate, the driver handles platform-level SMT toggling, memory clock visibility, and power tunables. That's right: you can now toggle Simultaneous Multithreading (SMT) dynamically through this driver interface. That works through the CPU hotplugging mechanism and acts as a clean alternative to passing the old 'nosmt' boot parameter to the kernel. The new driver also allows real-time monitoring of memory clocks, and initial power controls are being wired up, too.
Now, if you're expecting a polished, one-click official AMD application equivalent to Ryzen Master for Linux, just pump the brakes. AMD is following its open-source amdgpu graphics driver playbook here, building the kernel plumbing and then leaving the user-space presentation layer entirely up to the community. That means you're going to have to wait for utilities like CoreCtrl to build out interfaces for this new driver, but it shouldn't be long now before that work gets underway in earnest.
This approach is arguably a better fit for the Linux philosophy anyway. Because the controls are being exposed via clean kernel sysfs nodes, it won't be long before independent developers integrate these knobs into powerhouse open-source monitoring and tuning suites, or even write dedicated desktop environment extensions specifically for the purpose of tweaking Ryzen processors.
The new patches are currently winding their way through review on the mailing lists, meaning mainstream kernel integration is on the horizon. For a DIY enthusiast who loves squeezing every last MHz out of silicon while maintaining a fully open-source software stack, this is easily the most exciting hardware-enablement milestone I've seen in a long time.

articles.title: I played Dawn of War 4, and it took me back to LAN parties, replaying campaigns repeatedly, and building massive armies for map domination just as I did in the first game over two decades ago — and I simply must have more
articles.text:
I’ve been watching my Dawn of War 4 armies dominate enemies, completely cover maps, and take more resource points than you can shake a Gretchen at, and it’s reminded me why I fell in love with the first game all those years ago
It’s been a long time since I’ve poured so many hours into Warhammer 40,000, but playing a bunch of the Dawn of War 4 campaign has absolutely captivated me, and almost made it feel like I was playing from my living room floor 30 years ago all over again.
After seeing a glimpse of the game last summer, I knew it was on the right track, but after a couple of weeks with Dawn of War 4, it’s safe to say that the series’ rip-roaring, gritty action, and moreish strategic map play is back with a vengeance, and channels all that made the first game brilliant.
My time with the chunky preview build has shown that King Art Games are an incredibly safe set of hands for the next Dawn of War game.
Going back to Kronus
The planet of Kronus provides the setting for Dawn of War 4, and while a part of me wonders whether it might have been more exciting to go for a brand new setting and premise, the familiar planet is still superbly executed by the new developer.
Each map is extremely well detailed and feels alive with wind-blown sand and tumbleweeds across barren landscapes, blinking lights and crumbling epic architecture in urban maps, and wonderfully icy and snowy maps providing some of the best backdrops.
No matter where you are, though, you’re always cheered on by some mega, epic battle music, and the individual unit audio from ambient mechanical whirring, distinct machine clunking, and furious fighting are all absolute chef's kiss level.
Underneath the aesthetic excellence, there is a real meaty campaign here. My preview build dived in and out of a few armies’ storylines, and the branching narrative is interesting and genuinely compelling, with twists that you can make decisions to impact through mission selection and choices (from what I’ve seen), while the accompanying cutscenes are also fantastic.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Even the in-game story moments help to give me the feeling of those excellent battle write-ups in the old White Dwarf magazines that I remember poring over for hours at a time.
Unrivaled units and chaotic combat
Moving your forces around that campaign is the true highlight: this is a properly meaty and fabulous strategy experience, and a 40K experience.
Taking control of the Orks or Adeptus Mechanicus in my preview, it really does feel like the perfect real-time recreation of seeing your miniatures on a tabletop. The action can be slower and methodical; or you can embrace some chaos and have fights on multiple fronts as you aim to use speed to your advantage over the battlefield.
There were multiple times in both scenarios where managing large masses of a mix of units was a genuine thrill, with each resource point captured, the mowing down of enemy infantry, or the blowing up of tanks with grenade barrages more satisfying than the last.
If you remember the best thing about moving units across maps in the Dawn of War games of yesteryear, then you’re in for a treat. Orks feel as wild and chaotic as they should; and the Adeptus Mechanicus have wonderful machine-focused units as well as biomechanic infantry that can pack more of a punch than you think, especially from cover.
However, Dawn of War 4 simultaneously feels more modern, and there’s an effort to streamline some controls to make things more straightforward. You can drag over a whole heap of enemies, and your units will automatically attack the ones most vulnerable to their attack type; and you can right-click on any unit’s ability so it will automatically trigger during missions.
Engaging with the units — be you a more casual player, or a really experienced one — is superb, and starts with them being a treat for the eyes. Units really look the part, and every combat encounter does too. King Art Studio’s attention to detail, with bespoke combat animations for every combination (it seems) that look genuine, and plenty of blood splatter and rag doll physics on show. Even the armor and weaponry of all units look radiant and detailed, down to the lustre on metals.
The machine endures
There’s a good mix of missions that keep things interesting and elevate the branching campaign, too. That’s a really great thing in a particular way, as my one ‘gripe’, if you can really call it that, is that Dawn of War 4 continues the series’ trend of sometimes being purely a numbers game.
Especially in base-building missions; if you can pace your play a bit, secure your territory, and build an army that’s massive, you’ll rarely fail. This can offset the nuances and ‘other’ factors to think about too when managing Orks and the WAAGH! that fuels them in battle, and the Adeptus Mechanicus and the Nosphere links that strengthen buildings and open up more development options.
That’s why the mix of missions is welcome: while those base- and army-building ones are heavily present, there’s usually a gauntlet or defence mission around the corner to mix things up — and I’ve probably enjoyed the latter two more on the whole.
Not that dominating a map is unenjoyable, of course. The power fantasy is real in Dawn of War 4 and can feel fantastic, but the game is also wonderfully successful at creating those ‘If I can just make it to that resource point’ or ‘if I can just hold off this enemy encounter’ or ‘if I can just create a couple of units quickly ot turn the tide here’ kind of moments, which are a thrill.
I could talk about more of the individual features in the game that make it shine, but the most important thing about my time with the game for preview is that everything adds up to an authentic Dawn of War experience and really captures the feeling and the essence of the series — as well as translating the turn-based tabletop game into a real-time action setting once again.
Dawn of War 4 successfully takes me back to early 2000s LAN parties, devouring campaigns over and over again, and building massive armies to crush my foes as I did in the first game over two decades ago — and now I just want more.

Prior to being TechRadar Gaming's Managing Editor, he was TRG's Deputy Editor, and a longstanding member of GamesRadar+, being the Commissioning Editor for Hardware there for years, while also squeezing in a short stint as Gaming Editor at WePC just before joining TechRadar Gaming. articles.title: Le nouveau Google Pixel 11 est déjà disponible pour 20% de moins sur Amazon
articles.text:
Pour contrer son prix plus onéreux, Amazon retire 180 euros au nouveau Google Pixel 11. L'occasion d'avoir un smartphone polyvalent avec une partie photo redoutable d'efficacité.
Pour finir l'année, Google a sorti son Pixel 11. La marque ne révolutionne pas sa gamme et continue sur la lancée du Pixel 10 avec un appareil qui brille sur sa partie photo. Malgré ce manque d'évolution, le Pixel 11 avait été lancé pour 100 euros de plus que la version précédente, mais Amazon réduit la facture avec une promotion de 18 %.
Sur Amazon, le Google Pixel 11 passe de 999 euros à 819 euros
Pourquoi choisir le Google Pixel 11 ?
- Pour les efforts sur l'appareil photo : Le Google Pixel 11 conserve le téléobjectif 5x, mais se dote d'un nouveau zoom numérique 30x, ce qui peut être intéressant pour les éléments à moyenne distance.
- Pour ce design toujours identifiable : La gamme Pixel s'est démarquée avec cette grosse barre de photo au dos qui fait tout le charme de ce smartphone.
- L'IA au service de l'utilisateur : Les fonctionnalités IA de ce Google Pixel 11 sont multiples pour convenir à chacun. Parmi elles, on retrouve un outil de retouche photo et il est aussi possible de traduire des conversations en temps réel.
Google mise sur la photo
Sans surprise, Google mise sur la partie photo. Cela se voit avec cette large bande photo au dos de l'appareil pour accueillir les différents capteurs. Parmi eux, on compte un téléobjectif 5x déjà présent sur la version précédente. Un capteur grand angle de 48 Mpx est aussi de la partie et l'ensemble brille par sa bonne restitution des couleurs, surtout la journée. Un zoom numérique 30x est aussi présent pour restituer les détails des éléments à moyenne distance.
Pour retoucher vos photos, vous pourrez compter sur l'intelligence artificielle pour améliorer vos clichés. Pour s'éloigner des photos, l'IA offre la possibilité de traduire des conversations en temps réel.
Enfin, un petit point sur l'autonomie. Le Google Pixel 11 peut tenir près de 18 heures avec une seule charge et est compatible avec la charge sans fil.
Toujours les mêmes défauts
Deux problèmes sont à pointer du doigt avec ce Google Pixel 11. Le plus gênant concerne certainement les performances surtout si vous êtes un joueur. Le smartphone de Google est équipé du Google Tensor G6. Sur le papier, ce processeur peut faire tourner toutes les applications même les jeux les plus gourmands. Cependant, la firme américaine a souhaité mettre au point un smartphone qui ne chauffe pas. Par conséquent, dans les jeux gourmands, un "throttling" est présent pour contenir la chauffe et il limite donc les performances de l'appareil.
Deuxième point négatif : le design et surtout la façade avant. La dalle OLED de 6,3 pouces brille avec un pic de luminosité de 3 000 nits, mais il pêche par ses bordures épaisses. Elles sont visibles et Google ne prend pas le pli de la sobriété comme de nombreux constructeurs peuvent le faire.
✅ Les points forts
- Une partie photo améliorée avec un téléobjectif x30
- Des fonctionnalités IA bien intégrées
- Un pic en HDR mesuré à 3 000 nits
❌ Les limites
- Des performances gaming limitées, encore un coup du throttling
- Des bordures épaisses, en 2026, cela fait un peu tâche
Au lieu de dépenser 999 euros pour acheter le Google Pixel 11, vous pouvez l'avoir pour 819 euros sur Amazon
Avec ce Google Pixel 11, la marque continue de s'appuyer sur ses points forts en améliorant son appareil photo et en lui offrant un boost d'autonomie appréciable.
Néanmoins, les défauts restent les mêmes avec ce "throttling" important qui peut ternir l'expérience gaming.

articles.title: OPPO Find X10, análisis: lo tiene todo para ser mi favorito del año en un mercado imposible
articles.text:
Con la recta navideña a punto de caramelo, OPPO se trae a España sus últimos móviles de gama alta. Yo he tenido la suerte de pasar unas semanas con el más "barato" de los dos, un teléfono que tiene poco de asequible y todavía menos de básico. Porque el OPPO Find X10 parte de los 1.400 euros, una cifra que obliga a exigirle mucho más que unas buenas especificaciones.
Después de varias semanas con él, tengo claro que es uno de esos móviles que dejan huella. Y también que OPPO ha conseguido plantearme una pregunta incómoda: ¿de verdad hace falta irse al modelo Pro para tener lo mejor de una marca?
✅ Cómpralo si…
- Buscas un gama alta de tamaño contenido y no quieres sentir que has renunciado a lo mejor.
- No quieres depender del cargador todos los días.
- Valoras una pantalla y sonido de gran calidad.
❌ No lo compres si…
- Priorizas la relación calidad/precio por encima de tener un móvil premium.
- Juegas durante sesiones muy largas y necesitas el máximo rendimiento sostenido.
- Prefieres un teléfono ligero y con buen agarre.
Lo esencial en 30 segundos
El OPPO Find X10 tiene algo que pocos móviles consiguen: hacer que te olvides de la ficha técnica. No necesita presumir en todo momento de sus características porque es en el día a día donde demuestra lo que vale. Y no siempre por las razones que esperaba.
Durante las semanas de prueba me he llevado unas cuantas sorpresas, especialmente en apartados donde parecía difícil innovar. También he encontrado detalles que no encajan del todo con su categoría. Porque una cosa es que OPPO haya construido un telefonazo y otra muy distinta que consiga justificar lo que cuesta. Ahí está la verdadera cuestión.
Es un móvil del que me es difícil decir algo malo, porque creo que apenas tiene inconvenientes. Desde su excelente pantalla a la cámara equipada para sacar el OPPO Find X10 de excursión: se ha comportado a las mil maravillas hasta cuando he querido exprimirlo a fondo. Es de los que cuesta olvidar.
9,0
A favor
- Autonomía sobresaliente
- Cámaras versátiles y fiables
- Mind Pilot aporta utilidad real
- Excelente construcción
En contra
- El precio es algo alto
- El ultra gran angular está un escalón por debajo
- Le cuesta sostener el rendimiento máximo
OPPO Find X10 5G Smartphone 12GB+256GB Hasselblad Doble 200MP, Glacier Blue | Garantía fabricante 4 años, vídeo cine 8K Log, LUMO True Colour Imaging, batería 7150mAh, 6,59", sin cargador
| Consigue 100€ de descuento utilizando el código XATAKA100 en la web de OPPO (Válido desde el 21 de octubre hasta el 30 de noviembre) | 
Nuestra experiencia con el OPPO Find X10
Diseño exquisito. En el cuerpo no se diferencia de la mayoría de móviles de gama alta, sin que esto sea malo: OPPO ha elegido materiales de calidad y unos acabados que se aprecian como tales. Es el tacto premium por definición. Con la desventaja de que el Find X10 es un móvil que se resbala fácilmente (OPPO no incluye funda en la caja). Es bastante compacto, el Snap Key lateral programable se hace querer y hasta el lector de huellas ultrasónico subraya la calidad general del teléfono. Tiene un diseño que enamora. Y me recuerda ampliamente a OnePlus, descanse en paz.
La experiencia multimedia definitiva. Decir que un móvil de 1.400 euros tiene una buena pantalla es casi de perogrullo, pero es tal que así: el OPPO Find X10 se ve genial, aporta gran nitidez y una colorimetría bien ajustada a cualquier contenido. Correcto en exteriores y con un sonido que queda al mismo gran nivel: hasta sobresale en potencia por su altavoz doble exterior (suena sin distorsiones y logra una presión sonora de 89 dB). Además de sacar un audio de calidad por el USB-C (y digital), el OPPO Find X10 incluye salida DisplayPort. No solo pude duplicar la pantalla en el monitor, también habilitar un modo de escritorio que expande las posibilidades del teléfono.
Lo mejor de MediaTek. El teléfono monta un procesador de gama alta muy potente: el MediaTek Dimensity 9600M. Lo he estado probando en juegos con excelentes resultados, sobre todo en calidad gráfica: puede con títulos a máxima resolución, aunque baja a la mitad el rendimiento tras unos diez minutos a tope. La estabilidad en los tests de 3D Mark fue del 45 %. Con unos números que se quedaron por debajo del Apple A19 Pro y del Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5: 2.435/7.662 en Geekbench 7.
Es un móvil que da de sí en cualquier situación, que ofrece memoria RAM y almacenamiento de sobra y que no se calienta en exceso durante los procesos de alta carga: medí un máximo de 42,5 ºC durante la serie de tests. Aguanta bien en mano durante largas sesiones de juego (es muy cómodo por su tamaño) y no pierde capacidades en otros aspectos clave, como en la cobertura 5G o WiFi 7. También ofrece gran calidad de audio durante las llamadas: la cancelación de ruido hace un excelente trabajo.
Batería de sobra. OPPO reduce ligeramente la capacidad con respecto al modelo chino (7.150 mAh frente a 8.000). Ese punto extra seguro que se nota, pero tampoco me he encontrado con dificultades: el móvil aguanta a la perfección cada jornada fuera de casa. Según mi uso, supera las nueve-diez horas de pantalla en uso medio e híbrido: 5G y WiFi. Con un consumo muy contenido con la pantalla apagada: durante la noche de ocho horas apenas se va un dos-tres % (incluso menos). Con un uso moderado, casi me alcanzó los tres días. Y un día y medio cuando estuve de viaje tirando del teléfono.
El móvil ofrece carga rápida de hasta 80 W (dispone de varios modos de protección para alargar la vida de la batería), es compatible con carga rápida inalámbrica de hasta 50 W y hasta tiene carga inalámbrica inversa. En cuestión de recarga, a mí me revivió en una hora y veinte minutos, aproximadamente.
Actualizado y con mucha IA. OPPO le ha dado un buen chute estético a ColorOS 17, basado en Android 17. La interfaz se ve moderna, agradable, el apartado gráfico está bien conseguido y llega cargada hasta los topes de funciones extra. Aparte de la personalización, OPPO incluye numerosas funciones relacionadas con la inteligencia artificial. La que más me ha gustado es Mind Pilot, un agente que puede utilizar modelos como ChatGPT o Manus. Necesita acceso a Internet, es una pega, pero funciona muy bien interactuando con el teléfono. OPPO debería garantizar, al menos, cinco años de actualizaciones Android y seis de seguridad. Es el compromiso que ya tuvo la familia OPPO Find X9.
Sólido en fotografía. El conjunto trasero sigue el esquema de principal/gran angular/telefoto periscópico. OPPO aporta sensores muy sólidos junto a objetivos que permiten hacer tomas en cualquier escena y terreno, tanto con buena iluminación como con baja. El tratamiento de la imagen es natural, con un gran esfuerzo en mantener el balance de blancos y los niveles de color. La correspondencia entre las tres cámaras se mantiene con solidez.
La cámara principal del OPPO Find X10 ofrece muy buenos resultados cuando la iluminación acompaña. Las fotografías tienen un nivel de detalle elevado, con buena definición de las texturas en edificios, vegetación y elementos alejados. El procesado es bastante contenido, aunque al ampliar las imágenes se aprecia cierta imperfección sobre los contornos y los detalles más finos.
El ultra gran angular mantiene una reproducción del color cercana a la cámara principal, sin cambios exagerados de saturación ni de balance de blancos. Sí se aprecia alguna diferencia de exposición, especialmente en los cielos, y una pérdida de detalle incluso con poco zoom (además de la deformación en los extremos de la imagen). Los colores tienden a ser naturales, sin hacer más vistosas las imágenes a fuerza de subir la saturación.
Las fotografías tomadas alrededor de los 65 mm equivalentes (2,8x) muestran una nitidez muy convincente, tanto en las fachadas lejanas como en los detalles de las esculturas. El aumento hasta los 130 mm (5,6x) sigue siendo aprovechable, con una buena conservación del detalle y sin una degradación demasiado evidente del color. A partir de ahí comienza a notarse el procesado, aunque a 10x sigue siendo un buen telefoto.
Las fotos tomadas de noche mantienen una exposición equilibrada y una reproducción bastante creíble de la iluminación ambiental. En las calles oscuras se aprecia la textura de las paredes y del suelo, aunque el procesado empieza a hacer de las suyas eliminando parte del detalle (con las correspondientes acuarelas). El teléfono también controla bien las altas luces de farolas y otras fuentes de iluminación.
Los retratos también me han dejado buenas sensaciones. El desenfoque aplicado al fondo es convincente, aunque a veces se nota un tratamiento excesivo a nivel de software. El bokeh es ajustable por software.
La cámara delantera mantiene la naturalidad de los colores, también el tratamiento de la piel. Conserva el detalle y no suaviza en exceso las imperfecciones, al menos si no se activan los modos de belleza. El recorte en el bokeh es bueno como norma general, con algunos defectos de contorno en los puntos más complicados.
Para comprobar cómo fotografía el OPPO Find X10 puedes acceder al álbum de cámara que he subido a Google Fotos.

OPPO Find X10, la opinión de Xataka
Cuesta encontrarle defectos de peso al OPPO Find X10. No es perfecto, pero sí un digno candidato a mejor móvil del año. Su principal obstáculo es el precio: la gama alta se ha disparado hasta un punto en el que incluso el modelo más accesible de una familia supone un desembolso considerable. Que el móvil más "accesible" de la familia X10 se vaya a 1.400 euros quizá sea consecuencia de la crisis de componentes, pero supone una gran barrera para la mayoría de usuarios (si este es el barato, como para irse a por el pro o el futuro Ultra). En la misma franja del X10 está el iPhone 18 Pro, por ejemplo.
Si tapamos la etiqueta del precio, el OPPO Find X10 no desmerece en nada a lo mejor del mercado, porque la elección de hardware y de software me parece excelente. Es uno de esos móviles compactos que te dan seguridad en el día a día, de los que te puedes fiar para cualquier cosa que se te ocurra. Ya sea navegar horas y horas por Internet, reproducir las series descargadas mientras vuelas a diez kilómetros del suelo o llevártelo de vacaciones como única cámara de viaje. Sé que va a tomar las fotos y vídeos que después querré recordar en el futuro. Y que responderá como debe en las tomas con zoom, algo que me parece primordial para un móvil de categoría.
En definitiva: el OPPO Find X10 es un móvil de bandera. En todos los aspectos. Por lo que vale, me parece imposible que decepcione. Porque tiene todo lo que yo le pido a un buen teléfono, incluido el esfuerzo de añadir valor al software: aparte de venir con un renovado ColorOS 17, OPPO es de los primeros que cuela un agente IA como extra. Con créditos de ChatGPT y de Manus incluidos, otro detalle positivo a tener en cuenta.
¿Te lo recomiendo?
Sin ninguna duda, siempre que tu presupuesto te permita gastar 1.400 euros en un móvil. El OPPO Find X10 es uno de esos teléfonos que disfrutas desde el primer momento y que, cuanto más utilizas, más cuesta abandonar. No es barato, tampoco pretende serlo. Pero sí ofrece una experiencia a la altura del precio, con una combinación de hardware y software que pocas pegas me ha dejado durante las semanas de análisis.
Si buscas un móvil de gama alta que destaque en prácticamente todos los apartados, el OPPO Find X10 es una apuesta segura. Incluso siendo el más "asequible" de la familia, no he sentido que necesitase subir un escalón para tener un teléfono todavía mejor. Y creo que ahí está su mayor mérito: OPPO ha conseguido que su modelo base sea redondo.

articles.title: Placer une pièce de monnaie sur son routeur Wi-Fi : pourquoi et à quoi ça sert
articles.text:
Placer une pièce de monnaie sur son routeur Wi-Fi : pourquoi et à quoi ça sert
L'astuce fait le tour des réseaux sociaux : poser une pièce, ou un bout d'aluminium, sur sa box internet améliorerait la connexion. La réalité physique est tout autre. Non seulement le métal ne renforce pas le signal, mais il peut le dégrader et faire surchauffer l'appareil. Voici ce qui marche vraiment.
C'est une astuce de grand-mère version numérique qui revient régulièrement sur YouTube : poser délicatement une simple pièce de deux euros sur le dessus de sa box internet permettrait d'obtenir enfin un réseau fluide et sans coupures. Entre démonstrations convaincantes et commentaires enthousiastes, la promesse est séduisante. Le geste est si simple et gratuit qu'on serait tenté de l'essayer sur-le-champ. C'est pourtant là que se niche le piège de ces recettes miracles qui circulent en ligne.
Une croyance séduisante mais sans fondement
L'idée paraît presque logique. Le métal réfléchit les ondes, alors une pièce posée sur la box redirigerait le signal Wi-Fi et étendrait sa portée. C'est sur ce raisonnement que repose l'astuce, largement relayée. Sauf qu'aucune preuve technique ne la soutient, et les spécialistes des télécoms sont unanimes pour la réfuter. Poser un objet métallique sur ou contre un routeur n'améliore rien, et peut même aggraver la situation.
Si certains utilisateurs jurent avoir constaté un mieux, il s'agit au mieux d'un effet placebo, au pire d'une coïncidence avec un simple redémarrage de la box au moment de la manipulation. La vérité est que l'amélioration du Wi-Fi ne passe jamais par un gadget posé sur le boîtier, mais par le placement de l'appareil et par ses réglages. La pièce, elle, ne fait qu'ajouter un problème là où il n'y en avait pas.
Pourquoi le métal nuit au signal, et à l'appareil
La physique explique clairement pourquoi cette astuce se retourne contre l'utilisateur. Les antennes d'une box sont des circuits calibrés au millimètre pour émettre sur des fréquences précises. Approcher un objet métallique conducteur perturbe leur environnement immédiat et décale leur fréquence de résonance, un phénomène que les ingénieurs appellent le désaccordage d'antenne. Résultat, une partie de l'énergie n'est plus rayonnée vers la pièce, mais réfléchie vers les circuits internes de la box, avec une perte d'efficacité qui peut dépasser 50 %.
Le métal déforme aussi le diagramme de rayonnement, ce halo en forme d'anneau selon lequel la box diffuse normalement son signal. Au lieu d'une couverture homogène, on crée des zones d'ombre et des réflexions incontrôlées. À cela s'ajoute un risque matériel : un objet posé sur le boîtier bloque les grilles de ventilation. La box chauffe, déclenche une sécurité qui bride ses performances, et souffre à la longue d'une usure prématurée. En cherchant à gagner quelques mégabits, on abîme donc l'appareil.
Les gestes qui améliorent vraiment le Wi-Fi
Bonne nouvelle, les vraies solutions sont tout aussi simples et, elles, réellement efficaces. La première tient au placement. Installez la box en hauteur, à environ 1,5 mètre du sol, et au centre du logement. Posée par terre ou cachée dans un meuble, elle perd jusqu'à 30 % de sa portée et risque la surchauffe. Éloignez-la des masses métalliques, des murs épais, mais aussi des perturbateurs comme le four à micro-ondes, les téléphones sans fil ou même un aquarium, l'eau absorbant fortement les ondes.
Asus ZenWiFi BT8
TP-Link Deco BE85
Côté réglages, quelques ajustements changent tout. Réservez la bande 5 GHz aux usages intensifs proches de la box, streaming ou visio, et gardez la 2,4 GHz, qui traverse mieux les murs, pour les objets connectés éloignés. Une application d'analyse réseau permet de repérer un canal moins encombré par le voisinage. Reliez en câble Ethernet vos appareils fixes, ordinateur de bureau ou console, pour libérer les ondes. Et pensez à redémarrer la box de temps en temps, puis à maintenir son logiciel à jour. Pour les grands logements, un système de répéteurs ou un kit CPL fera le reste. Autant de gestes qui, contrairement à la pièce de monnaie, reposent sur la science plutôt que sur la rumeur.

articles.title: Nvidia reportedly refused some neoclouds access to GTC Berlin for adding AMD and TPU chips
articles.text:
Rumor mill: Analysts with SemiAnalysis have uncovered what could be another troubling trend in the AI hardware industry. Nvidia is reportedly retaliating against some "neocloud" providers for integrating GPUs and other chips from rival manufacturers into their cloud offerings.
SemiAnalysis' latest "shocking" rumor allegedly confirms what the firm had already revealed in June. Several neocloud providers have reportedly been denied access to GTC Berlin, Nvidia's upcoming conference covering AI, GPUs, and related technologies. The Jensen Huang-led company apparently disapproves of cloud providers adding AMD GPUs, TPUs, and other third-party silicon to their offerings, and is making it harder for them to attend one of the industry's most important events.
Hyperscalers have apparently been spared Nvidia's "punishment" because they wield considerably more purchasing power than neocloud providers. The term neocloud is gaining traction as a way to describe a specific category of modern cloud providers that offer specialized IT infrastructure designed to efficiently handle AI workloads.
According to SemiAnalysis, neocloud providers are feeling Nvidia's pressure as the GPU maker attempts to discourage them from adopting competing GPU and AI hardware. The situation is reportedly so tense that some neocloud providers are now deploying AMD-based solutions without publicizing the move. This "quiet" approach might help them avoid further retaliation from Nvidia.
 – SemiAnalysis (@SemiAnalysis_) October 16, 2026
SemiAnalysis first disclosed Nvidia's alleged tactics earlier this year. At the time, the "silicon intelligence" company stated that Nvidia was punishing neocloud providers by withholding early allocations of upcoming chips. Financial support for IPOs and capital-raising initiatives was also reportedly at risk of drying up. Nvidia has directly funded some neocloud providers, which is why some observers have dismissed SemiAnalysis' latest claims as a non-story.
Nvidia launched its GTC conference in 2009, bringing together engineers, researchers, and developers for an event that has since become heavily focused on AI. Some observers also argue that the Santa Clara-based company is entitled to decide whom it invites to its own conference.
Nvidia has repeatedly faced accusations of abusing its dominant position in the GPU market to disadvantage competitors. In 2024, a former AMD GPU chief accused the company of behaving like a "GPU cartel" by delaying shipments to data centers, OEMs, and even resellers.
The AI boom is turning GPUs and other specialized accelerators into highly sought-after hardware. AMD is also benefiting from the trend, particularly in the data center market, where GPU manufacturers continue to struggle to meet demand from hyperscalers and other cloud providers.

articles.title: Custo-benefício: iPhone 16e volta a receber desconto de 43% na Amazon • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Custo-benefício: iPhone 16e volta a receber desconto de 43% na Amazon
iPhone 16e (128 GB) tem chip A18 e suporta Apple Intelligence; celular "baratinho" da maçã recebe desconto de 43% sobre o preço original no Pix
O iPhone 16e de 128 GB está saindo por R$ 3.299 no Pix na Amazon. O celular custo-benefício da Apple, que traz chip A18, 8 GB de RAM e suporta soluções de IA, recebe desconto de 43% sobre o preço original de R$ 5.799.
Embora seja um celular custo-benefício, o iPhone 16e possui desempenho de ponta graças ao chip Apple A18 e aos 8 GB de RAM. O kit otimizado dá conta de apps pesados e games, e até mesmo de rodar funções do Apple Intelligence localmente. Os 128 GB de armazenamento podem ser expandidos com planos do iCloud.
Sua tela Super Retina XDR OLED de 6,1″ tem brilho de 1.200 nits e reproduz imagens com cores vibrantes, além de oferecer visibilidade garantida em ambientes com muita luz. O vidro Ceramic Shield protege o display contra quedas e arranhões.
O kit de câmeras é o mesmo presente no sucessor iPhone 17e, formado por uma wide de 48 MP com OIS na traseira, que capta belas imagens ao ar livre, e uma frontal de 12 MP que tira ótimas selfies com o recurso Center Stage, que centraliza elementos. Ambas filmam em 4K a 60 fps.
O corpo de alumínio do 16e conta com a certificação IP68 para reforçar a durabilidade, recebendo uma camada extra de proteção contra poeira intensa e mergulhos acidentais. Assim, o celular resiste por muito mais tempo a acidentes.
Sua bateria de 4.005 mAh tem autonomia de até 26 horas de reprodução de vídeo, segundo a fabricante. O gadget pode receber uma carga rápida de 0 a 50% em apenas 30 minutos via cabo USB-C, garantindo seu uso por um dia inteiro.
O iPhone 16e de 128 GB (R$ 3.299 no Pix) foi atualizado para o iOS 27 e deve receber pelo menos mais quatro atualizações do sistema operacional. O celular acessível da Apple possui conectividade 5G, Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.3 e NFC.
Aviso de ética: ao clicar em um link de afiliado, o preço não muda para você e recebemos uma comissão.

articles.title: Synaptics Announces Astra SR200 Multimodal Edge AI Processors with Google Coral NPU
articles.text:
Wednesday, October 21st 2026
Synaptics Announces Astra SR200 Multimodal Edge AI Processors with Google Coral NPU
Synaptics Incorporated (Nasdaq: SYNA) today introduced the xMCU, a new class of microcontrollers that runs multimodal Edge AI, with the launch of the Synaptics Astra SR200 Series. Unlike conventional MCUs constrained by limited on-chip memory and compute, the xMCU combines heterogeneous, AI-native compute and acceleration with integrated high-bandwidth custom DRAM scalable to hundreds of megabytes, enabling larger AI models and richer multimodal workloads to run entirely on-device. The Astra SR200 Series of xMCUs is designed for the next generation of AI wearables, battery-powered sensing devices, connected cameras, streamers, and industrial vision and voice systems.
The SR200 Series is powered by the Synaptics Torq AI engine, which brings a standards-based hardware architecture and unified developer experience featuring the Coral NPU from Google Research. It also comes with the industry's first pairing of the Arm Cortex -M85 and Cortex -M52. Together with integrated vision and audio capabilities and hardware-rooted security, the SR200 Series brings unmatched system design efficiency and cost benefits to Edge and Physical AI designs.Setting a new standard for the industry, the Astra SR200 Series is engineered around the following core vectors: high-performance compute with extensible memory; transformer-ready AI acceleration; silicon-rooted security; multimodal integration; ultra-low-power architecture with tiered domains; and an open-source software ecosystem, offering developer choice and OEM design flexibility. 
The Synaptics Astra SR200 Series launches with three pin-compatible product lines, giving OEMs and developers a common hardware foundation and a shared SDK. The SR210 is designed to deliver 200 GOPS for power-optimized, always-on voice and sensing; the SR230 adds vision, display, and optional audio at 300 GOPS for mainstream multimodal devices; and the SR250 enables 400 GOPS with dual vision and display paths for premium, demanding edge applications. Developers can scale performance while preserving their software investment and system architecture.
In the SR200 Series of xMCUs, memory is the foundation, not an afterthought. A tiered architecture pairs up to 8 MB of SRAM with extensible, high-bandwidth, high-capacity custom DRAM that scales to hundreds of megabytes as AI models and workloads grow. Built around latency, retention, and power demands of Edge AI, this architecture runs workloads at one-third the power of typical system DRAM, eliminating the need for costly external memory in most applications at a fraction of the system power. 
At the heart of the family is the Synaptics Torq AI engine integrating the Coral NPU, optimized for low latency and high-efficiency execution of deep learning workloads, including CNN, transformer, and fully connected networks. Its open-source MLIR/IREE compiler supports industry-standard frameworks and model formats in place of proprietary vendor toolchains, extending Coral's Edge AI heritage into ultra-low-power, always-on IoT. 
A high-performance core, scaling to 800 MHz, tackles control, multimedia, and burst-compute workloads, while an efficiency core handles always-on sensor fusion, connectivity, and low-power inference. An optional Cadence Tensilica HiFi 5 DSP adds dedicated audio and acoustic ML processing, while an always-on domain manages voice activity detection, timekeeping, and wake-up. 
The SR200 Series integrates a multi-layered security engine that combines hardware isolation, cryptographic acceleration, anti-tamper detection, device lifecycle management, and secure boot. The implementation conforms to PSA Level 3 and CC EAL4+ certification targets, providing protection against software and physical attacks. 
The platform provides a broad peripheral and connectivity set, including high-speed octal SPI, SDIO and eMMC storage interfaces, UART, SPI, I2C, I3C, PWM, USB 2.0 and extensive low-power GPIO. Industrial variants add 1 Gb Ethernet with IEEE 1588 TSN support and two CAN-FD interfaces, supporting deterministic networking and real-time industrial control for Physical AI and Robotics applications. 
Supporting Zephyr RTOS and the open-source Torq NPU compiler, the SR200 Series brings groundbreaking performance and power efficiency to define a new category of MCU experiences for Edge and Physical AI.
Vikram Gupta, SVP and GM, Edge Compute & Connectivity Division, Synaptics"The next wave of AI will be defined by devices that understand their environment and act locally, while meeting tight power, cost, and form-factor requirements. With the Astra SR200 Series, we're introducing a new class, the xMCU, that brings applications-processor capability into the MCU domain, running multimodal AI workloads that traditionally require Linux and discrete DRAM. It gives customers a scalable foundation for everything from intelligent sensing to advanced Edge and Physical AI systems."
Yossi Matias, Vice President and Head of Google Research"Open technologies and strong partnerships are key to making Edge AI more accessible. Our ongoing work with Synaptics combines the Coral platform with Astra's scalable hardware and developer ecosystem to power next-generation, wearable-class devices. We share a vision of turning advanced research into reality through real-world products, empowering developers to create faster, more useful, and responsive experiences."
