articles.title: Rival chinesa da Starlink homologa equipamento no Brasil • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Rival chinesa da Starlink homologa equipamento no Brasil
SpaceSail deve oferecer conexão via satélite com velocidades de até 400 Mb/s de download. Preços e disponibilidade ainda não são conhecidos.
Resumo
- A SpaceSail, empresa chinesa de internet via satélite, homologou equipamento no Brasil.
- O equipamento tem velocidade de download de até 400 Mb/s e upload de até 100 Mb/s.
- A empresa planeja oferecer internet via satélite para uso fixo e móvel e pode iniciar as operações no Brasil ainda em 2026.
A competição nos serviços de internet via satélites de órbita baixa (LEO) deve esquentar no Brasil, pois a empresa chinesa SpaceSail certificou seu equipamento residencial no país. A antena tem código de modelo STG-S001-A0 e recebeu a aprovação da Anatel na segunda-feira (19/10), segundo a documentação obtida pelo Tecnoblog.
Desde fevereiro, a companhia está autorizada pela agência reguladora a operar em território nacional, período que começou a contagem de até dois anos para o início de suas operações.
Como é o equipamento da SpaceSail?
Externamente, o equipamento é visualmente similar ao concorrente americano, com design retangular e apenas uma porta, utilizada para alimentação e conexão cabeada com a internet, além de um LED de status e uma porta de diagnóstico coberta por uma tampa de borracha. São dimensões de 48 cm x 36 cm por 4 cm e peso de 4 kg e proteção IP65.
O cabo incluso terá 15 metros, permitindo a instalação em uma área externa ou telhado, utilizando conector USB-C fora do padrão. Na outra ponta, o cabo possui um conector RJ45 para cabos de rede Ethernet e um conector de alimentação para uso com a fonte inclusa.
A antena também é capaz de criar uma rede Wi-Fi 5, utilizada principalmente para a configuração inicial através do aplicativo da SpaceSail mas que também deve ser capaz de permitir acesso à conexão satelital. Na ficha técnica que consta do manual, as velocidades de download e upload serão de até 400 Mb/s e 100 Mb/s, respectivamente.
A SpaceSail pode oferecer alguns acessórios para o equipamento, como diversos tipos de suporte e uma bateria externa. Não espere poder utilizar um powerbank USB-C tradicional com a SpaceSail: a etiqueta menciona alimentação de 48 Volts a 4,5 Amperes, resultando em incríveis 216 Watts, valor bem próximo do limite da versão mais recente do USB Power Delivery.
O certificado de conformidade também dá mais uma pista sobre o serviço, ao afirmar que “O produto é destinado a múltiplos cenários (fixo e móvel)”. Ou seja, a SpaceSail deve oferecer opções de serviço fixo (similar ao Starlink residencial) e móvel (como o Starlink Móvel).
A fabricação da antena ficará a cargo da Shanghai Hanxun Information Technology Co., Ltd, na cidade de Nanquim.
Lançamento pode acontecer ainda em 2026
Como mencionamos, a SpaceSail, conhecida como Qianfan na China, recebeu autorização para operar no Brasil ainda em fevereiro. Durante este processo, a empresa afirmou planejar o início de sua operação brasileira no quarto trimestre de 2026.
Os entraves agora passam a ser operacionais e logísticos, como a importação dos receptores e a instalação de bases terrenos pelo Brasil.
Ainda não sabemos quando será o lançamento e nem os preços, mas, para fins de comparação, os serviços da Starlink vão de R$ 49 até R$ 619 mensais. A SpaceSail deve sofrer com a forte concorrência da empresa de Elon Musk, mas também do Amazon Leo, que será vendido no país pela Sky e cujo lançamento está atrasado.

articles.title: Telecom complaints up nearly 80%, CCTS says
articles.text:
Canada’s Commission for Complaints for Telecom-Television Services (CCTS) says it’s facing an unprecedented surge in complaints.
In an update posted on its website, the CCTS said its 2025-26 complaint period has so far received 53,195 complaints, a 79 per cent increase compared to the previous year. Of that, the commission has accepted 41,235 complaints — 74 per cent more than last year — and reports an 87.2 per cent resolution rate so far.
“This increase reflects unprecedented demand for our impartial, effective and free complaint-resolution services,” the CCTS said, noting that it’s continuing to accept complaints and help resolve them.
However, the commission also warned that the high volume of complaints is causing resolutions to take longer than usual, especially in cases requiring conciliation or investigation.
“As demand continues to increase, processing times may remain longer than usual,” the commission said.
The CCTS says its annual report will offer a fuller picture of the issues customers are facing when it arrives in January 2027. However, rising complaint volumes have been an ongoing problem for a while, with the commission’s mid-year 2026 report also showing a 53 per cent increase in wireless issues. Top complaints include incorrect charges, disclosure issues, service issues and price increases.
Tips to help with complaint process
To help alleviate some of the volume, the CCTS also shared some tips and reminders for Canadians to keep in mind before filing a complaint. For starters, the commission notes that people must try to resolve issues with their carrier first before filing a complaint with the CCTS.
Other tips include clearly explaining the problem and how the provider can resolve it, keeping copies of bills, contracts, chat transcripts, emails, and other documentation, and tracking when you contact your provider and who you speak with. The commission also advises Canadians to participate in “reasonable resolution steps” like troubleshooting or waiting for credits to appear. If all else fails — and importantly, if the issue falls within the commission’s mandate — then people should submit a complaint.
Carriers gutted customer service, outsourced roles
Notably, this comes amid an ongoing increase in issues with Canadian telecom providers, and in particular, Rogers, Bell, and Telus. The Big Three have spent the last few years gutting customer service roles and outsourcing jobs to overseas call centres, making it extremely difficult for Canadians to contact their providers.
Worse, if you actually manage to make it through the multi-hour hold times, getting anything resolved feels next to impossible. Customer service reps are actively incentivized to keep calls short and to sell new products and services, so anyone who needs help fixing an issue has to fight their way through several layers of employees, call transfers, and other mind-numbing bureaucracy — assuming reps don’t just hang up midway through your fourth hour on the phone.
That leaves the CCTS as one of the few recourses available to Canadians for resolving issues with their carriers. However, carriers are actively trying to undermine that too. Telus, for example, wants the CRTC to add additional requirements to filing complaints, like requiring proof that customers raised the issue to level two customer support — a truly Herculean feat.
Elsewhere, providers are asking the CRTC to scrap some of the scant consumer protections that currently exist, from caps on roaming overages to phone locking, and even clawing back sign-up bonuses from customers who cancel early.

articles.title: Review: Carrie is a triumphant remix with one major flaw
articles.text:
Carrie White, the telekinetic prom queen from hell, is one of the most beloved horror icons in popular culture. First introduced in Stephen King’s 1974 novel, Carrie, the character was immortalized in director Brian De Palma’s 1976 adaptation, widely regarded as one of the best horror films of all time. It’s certainly one of the best King adaptations. So Mike Flanagan faced a massive challenge when he signed on to create an eight-episode miniseries for Prime Video based on the book, released just in time to mark the 50th anniversary of de Palma’s film.
I was among the skeptics who questioned why a Carrie miniseries was even necessary, although as a diehard Flanagan fan (“Flana-fan”?), I was willing to give him the benefit of the doubt. If anyone has an affinity for smartly adapting horror in general, and King’s work in particular, it’s Flanagan. And you know what? With one (very big) exception, Flanagan pulls it off, giving us a richly textured version of the story that is as much about kindness and lost innocence as bloody, vengeful rage—although we get plenty of the latter, too.
(Many spoilers below for the novel and the 1976 film, but there are no major reveals for the new series until after the second gallery. We’ll give you a heads-up when we get there.)
King initially meant to write a short story after reading an article in Life magazine about telekinesis. He imagined a scene where a bullied young girl gets her first period in a high school locker room as the centerpiece of the story but struggled to capture how his female character would react in that situation. He wrote three pages and tossed them in the trash. Fortunately, his wife Tabitha salvaged the pages and convinced King to try again. He eventually expanded it into a full-length novel, basing Carrie on two girls he knew in high school who had been bullied relentlessly.
Fun fact: In an early draft of the infamous prom scene, King had Carrie grow horns and use her telekinetic powers to take out an airplane flying overhead. His editor convinced him to go with a more “subtle” ending. Granted, dumping pig’s blood on his protagonist and having her destroy the entire town in revenge is hardly subtle, but it’s a vast improvement on devil horns.
Carrie was not an instant bestseller; it was the mass-market paperback edition that sold over a million copies and put King on the map as a writer. It also piqued the interest of director Brian De Palma after a mutual friend of King’s recommended the book. De Palma instantly recognized the film potential and optioned the rights before searching for the perfect actress to play Carrie.
Sissy Spacek was still relatively unknown, although she’d had a breakthrough role in the 1973 neo-noir drama Badlands. Her husband, a production designer, convinced her to audition for the film. She wasn’t de Palma’s first choice for Carrie, but Spacek was determined to win him over, even rubbing Vaseline in her hair and wearing her seventh grade sailor dress to the audition. She got the part, and the rest is cinematic history.
De Palma kept most of the novel’s key scenes intact in his adaptation, with a few changes. For instance, in the book, Carrie kills her mother, after the latter stabs her, by telekinetically stopping her heart, calling it a “gift” since Margaret White has always longed for “darkness.” In the film, Carrie impales Margaret (Piper Laurie) with flying kitchen knives, crucified within a door frame, before perishing herself. The director also tried to include a framing device in which stones fall from the sky onto the White family home—a key moment from Carrie’s childhood in the book—but in the opening scene the rocks just looked like falling raindrops, and there was a mechanical malfunction while filming the house’s final destruction by falling stones. So De Palma opted to destroy it by fire instead.
In the novel, survivor Sue Snell is psychically drawn to a dying Carrie, experiencing the tormented girl’s final moments in a kind of mind meld as she comforts her. De Palma opted to end Carrie with one of the best jump scares in film. A repentant Sue (Amy Irving) visits Carrie’s grave with flowers, only to have a hand shoot from under the soil and grab her arm; Sue wakes up screaming from her nightmare, still traumatized by the events on prom night. De Palma shot the scene backward to make it feel like a dreamscape. And that was actually Spacek’s hand bursting up through the soil; she let herself be buried on set to pull it off.
“They’re all going to laugh at you”

Carrie was a critical and box office hit, snagging Oscar nominations for Spacek and Laurie—a rare thing for a horror film. And the film has withstood the test of time, as compulsively watchable 50 years later as it was in 1976. The tragic story of an emotionally damaged, tormented girl with supernatural gifts, pushed to her breaking point, seems to resonate with something psychologically primal in all of us. Others have tried and failed to recapture that magic. The less said about the 1999 sequel, the 2002 TV film, the 2013 remake, and the 1988 Broadway musical, the better.
Enter Flanagan, who boldly set out to reinvent Carrie for the 21st century. The showrunner has a gift for creatively remixing classic material in interesting ways, while remaining true to the spirit of the original. Another strength is his ability to build memorable, multifaceted characters, and he has eight episodes, not two hours, to do so. Flanagan reclaims certain elements, such as the stones raining down on the Whites’ house. The novel was also partly epistolary, including segments of fictional court transcripts and news coverage created by King (who enjoyed mimicking different writing styles). Flanagan incorporates video interviews as a framing device, in which surviving witnesses recount their memories of the tragic events.
But there are also significant changes. Carrie in King’s novel and De Palma’s film is a flinching, socially inept, mousey misfit. She lost her father as a baby and has been bullied all her life, not to mention being physically and emotionally abused at home by her religious zealot mother. In Flanagan’s version, Carrie (Summer H. Howell) has been homeschooled since birth. The death of her conspiracy theorist father (Tahmoh Penikett) in a freak construction accident forces Carrie and her mother, Margaret (Samantha Sloyan), into the real world after years of hardly ever leaving the house. (A social worker describes the family as having been a “cult of three.”)
This Carrie is smart, two grades ahead in terms of academic achievement, surprisingly open and curious, and an avid reader—thanks to the kindness of a next-door neighbor who would regularly leave books for Carrie to read on the sly by hiding them in a shared birdhouse. None of her fellow students catch her frequent literary allusions, but the principal, Henry Grayle (Matthew Lillard), does. So does Peter Morton (Tom Bagley), the gay guidance counselor. He and Carrie exchange a few of their favorite book quotes, after which he shows her the wonders of the high school library (“It’s all for you”).
But Flanagan’s Carrie is also extremely sheltered and unprepared for the harsh realities of high school in the 21st century, in addition to grieving for her father. First her gold cross sets off the metal detector. Then she thinks the school shooting drill is for real and has a panic attack. She’s never played volleyball or any team sport, so gym class is a disaster.
And then comes the infamous locker room scene and Carrie’s first period. De Palma’s camera lingered just a bit too longingly on the naked adolescent girls in the showers, although the scene did capture Carrie’s extreme vulnerability in that moment. Flanagan’s version has Carrie start her period fully clothed—but wearing white pants. High school bully Chris (Alison Thornton) pushes her into the shower before leading the other girls in a chant of “plug it up” while pelting her with sanitary napkins and tampons. And of course it’s all captured on multiple cell phones.
The 22-year-old Howell, best known to date for playing Alison Pierce in the Chucky franchise, beat out 1,400 young actresses to play Carrie. She didn’t even read King’s novel or watch the 1976 movie, so she could interpret Flanagan’s take on the character. Spacek defined the role, but Howell redefines it with just as much assurance. She hits every single note, registers every small shift in expression and emotion, in a stellar performance that should cement her status as a gifted young actress on the rise.
WARNING: Major spoilers for the Mike Flanagan series below. Stop reading now if you haven’t finished watching.)

Lillard brings a jaded weariness to Principal Grayle—a once-idealistic educator whose kindness has been beaten into submission. But he still shows some fire when Chris’ high-powered lawyer father, John (Michael Trucco), threatens to sue the school, reminding John (in a moment lifted from the novel) that, by his reasoning, the school could counter-sue and that Chris’ long history of bullying would be laid open during discovery.
In the De Palma film, John Travolta’s Billy was a dim-witted jock, bonded to Nancy Allen’s vapid Chris by hormonal lust and their shared nasty, brutish natures. Neither had any redeeming qualities. That’s not the case in Flanagan’s series. Arthur Conti’s Billy is a high school dropout who works on a farm when not dealing drugs to partying high schoolers. He’s dark and broody, smart and sarcastic, a compulsive rule-breaker. And he’s dangerous—catnip for a spoiled, rebellious golden girl like Chris, whose perfect life has unexpectedly hit the skids. Her parents are divorcing, the father she idolizes is facing financial ruin, and since she didn’t apply for financial aid in time, she can’t join her bestie, Sue (Siena Agudong), at Duke University in the fall.
None of this excuses Chris’ malicious behavior, not just toward Carrie but toward her future stepsister, Brooklyn (Rowan Danielle), and the school as a whole, mostly via a fake Instagram account devoted to smearing students and faculty alike. It’s Carrie who asks the key question: Why go to such great lengths to target Carrie particularly? Chris’ answer—“I don’t know. You were weird, and you pissed me off”—speaks to her profound lack of self-awareness. Yet her recklessness and stubborn pride seal her doom. Chris is given many chances to reverse course, face accountability, and do the right thing; however torn, she can never bring herself to do it until it is much too late.
Flanagan improves on both De Palma’s film and King’s novel in his treatment of faith, embodied in Carrie’s mother, Margaret White. Margaret is a cartoonish caricature in those earlier incarnations, with her candles and crucifixes, sexual repression, and psychotic rants about sin and atonement. Flanagan understands the complicated nature of faith; he created the exquisite Midnight Mass, after all, which also starred Sloyan (part of the “Flana-fam” of actors) in a pivotal role.
Sloyan was the perfect choice to play Margaret. She’s a grieving widow who has spent the last 15 years shutting out the world out of fear, ill-equipped to hold down even a job as a checkout clerk. She can’t help judging customers for, say, buying vibrators and condoms and helpfully lecturing them on their poor life choices. She’s intelligent, like Carrie, and has clearly done an excellent job homeschooling her daughter. However nutty her specific beliefs might be, she is not always wrong in her assessments; she’s just so rigidly unlikable, nobody wants to cede her the points.
Where King’s Margaret actively disliked her daughter—viewing her as the polluted spawn of the night her drunken husband effectively raped her—Sloyan’s Margaret clearly loves Carrie, wanting only to protect her from a world of sin and depravity. (She also clearly loved and depended upon her late husband.) She wages battle on behalf of her bullied daughter with admirable ferocity. Flanagan understands another crucial aspect of Margaret’s faith: it’s all about control. So when Margaret feels that control slipping away—when she’s forced to work and confront the ugliness of the world or when Carrie pushes back on her authority—she throws herself into re-exerting her control, even if that means locking Carrie in the prayer closet for hours on end to save her immortal soul.
Above all, Flanagan understands how even a mother’s love can be poisoned by fear when Carrie uses her newfound powers to wrest control of the household from her mother. The final interaction between mother and daughter starts with Margaret washing away all the blood in the bath, recalling how she did the same thing the night Carrie was born. As they prepare to pray together, Carrie asks if god can forgive her for what she has done. “Even if god doesn’t, I forgive you,” Margaret replies, before tearfully asking if Carrie can forgive her—for what we know (but Carrie doesn’t) will be Margaret’s attempted murder of her own child

King’s novel alludes to Margaret’s grandmother having similar telekinetic abilities, which Margaret had always attributed to witchcraft, and the novel ends with an Appalachian woman writing a letter to her sister in 1988, telling her about her 4-year-old daughter’s emerging telekinetic gifts. He even hints at a recessive “TK” gene as the cause. Flanagan turned all that into a cult of women with supernatural gifts, led by Adelaide (Kate Siegel), who sense Carrie’s nascent power and track her down. (Here it is Adelaide, not Carrie, who stops Margaret’s heart after interviewing her as a witness.) He also introduces Emmaline (Thalia Dudek), who befriends Carrie and encourages her worst instincts, only to be revealed as an astral projection of the real Emmaline. (She is definitely not a high school student.)
Of course, everything comes down to that famous prom scene, with Carrie being crowned queen before being doused with pig’s blood. De Palma’s sequence followed that moment with an eerie silence, the only sound that of the clanking empty bucket, before all hell breaks loose. Flanagan chooses to have Carrie telekinetically explode everyone’s cell phone and have the screen cut to black as we hear agonized screams to close the penultimate episode. Yet the final episode opens with another interview segment; those segments keep interrupting the action, which is a bit frustrating but forgivable. (There are already fan cuts popping up on YouTube stitching together the prom night footage without the breaks.)
There is really only one flaw in Flanagan’s Carrie, and it’s a major change from the source material: Carrie is not solely responsible for the prom night carnage—and she survives (a twist that also featured in the 2002 TV film). Sue admits she knew Carrie was “fucked” on the very first day because she was genuinely kind and innocent, admirable qualities that make certain people like Chris feel inferior and lash out with cruelty. But plenty of others found Carrie disarmingly likable. We see glimpses of a darker Carrie—telekinetically breaking Chris’ nose in class, for instance, and telling her to “plug it up” as she walks past. Honestly, Chris deserved it. But Carrie only feels shame and guilt over her actions, rejecting Emmaline’s celebratory gloating over the incident.
Is this a person so psychologically damaged that she would quickly turn murderous and take out an entire town in revenge for a vicious prank? Flanagan doesn’t seem to think so, since he blinks and lets Emmaline “take the wheel” after poor Tommy (Joel Oulette) is killed when Carrie brings down an overhead walkway. Emmaline (who is that damaged) temporarily possesses Carrie to inflict the worst of the ensuing deadly havoc on her behalf. That one creative decision takes away Carrie’s agency at the most crucial moment and seriously undercuts the foundation on which the whole character arc rests.
Of course, Carrie does plenty of damage on her own, including crushing Billy and Chris to death after flipping their car when Billy tries to run her down. She’s both horrified and strangely elated by what she’s done. But she just feels horror when Emmaline vanishes abruptly, and Carrie realizes what she’s done to the town, limping home for the final confrontation with her murder-minded mother. That’s the devastating revelation that truly breaks her: She’s a monster in the eyes of her own mother.
Somehow that one huge misstep isn’t enough to sink this compelling series—a tribute to the power of the core story.
As for why Carrie survives, Flanagan has plans for another two seasons, taking us into uncharted territory with King’s blessing. Prom night set Carrie down a dark path, drunk on her newfound power, with a weakened moral compass. She’s unwittingly caught between two different factions seeking to exploit her immense power—her new bestie, Emmaline, and Adelaide’s group—plus another group that seems intent on killing Carrie and others like her. It will be interesting to see what Flanagan comes up with, given the chance, now that he’s freed from the constraints of the original novel.
All eight episodes of Carrie are now streaming on Prime Video, as is the 1976 film.

articles.title: Trump says data centers should pay locals to get them on side — but last time they offered $10,000 and the residents called it a bribe
articles.text:
Trump says data centers should pay locals to get them on side — but last time they offered $10,000 and the residents called it a bribe
Data center developers could end up paying residents for approval
- President Trump says data center developers should offer a 'dividend' to get local community approval for campuses
- Nebius CRO says the company is "100% in principle" considering some form of local investment
- Paying local residents to approve a local data resident didn't go so well in Hazle, Pennsylvania
President Trump has told data center companies that one way to get local residents to support new developments is to “make deals” with local residents.
Trump suggested offering communities a “dividend,” adding, “I have watched the process closely, and Data Centers that were highly unpopular in a certain area, have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck.”
“MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!! GREAT FOR THE U.S.A.,” the President wrote on Truth Social. But as one town has already demonstrated, these payments are viewed as a bribe that threaten to turn communities against each other.
Dividend or bribe?
As the November 2026 midterm elections draw closer, data centers have become a make-or-break topic for some candidates. Data center developers and AI companies have been channeling millions of dollars into political action committees in an effort to get a more favorable view of data centers.
Multiple states are considering enacting moratoriums on AI data center development, which if approved could cost developers and AI companies billions in lost investment. Environmental concerns and issues relating to noise and light pollution are high on the list for residents protesting against local developments.
NorthPoint Development is currently seeking to build an AI data center in Hazle, Pennsylvania, and offered each household $10,000 in an attempt to convince residents to get on board with having the campus approved. But the residents did not react as planned, calling the payment a bribe and turning it down over fears it could split the community in two - those who live near the campus and declined and those who live further away and took the payment.
When questioned by Trump’s proposal, Marc Boroditsky, CRO of Nebius told CNBC that the company is “100% in principle” having discussions about potential investments in local communities.

The concept that the president identified... it’s not crazy to consider something like that"

articles.title: Waymo starts offering rides at the Las Vegas airport | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Waymo is now shuttling customers to and from the Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas, with pickups and dropoffs happening at dedicated “autonomous vehicle zones” at Terminal 1 and Terminal 3, the company announced Wednesday.
This is the sixth major airport that Waymo is serving. The company already offers rides at Phoenix Sky Harbor, Nashville International, San Antonio International, San Francisco International, and San José International airports.
Waymo only just started offering rides to the public in Las Vegas in September, but is already serving a 24-square-mile area in the city. The company said the rides to and from the Las Vegas airport will be limited at first to just a few riders, before opening up to all customers.
Amazon-owned Zoox already offers rides at the Vegas airport, and more robotaxis are coming to Sin City. In August, state regulators approved permits that will allow Tesla and Uber to put thousands of them on the city’s streets in the next year.

articles.title: Trump announces mandate forcing AI data centers to pay energy dividends to the local community — says excess energy should be given or sold back to prevent increases or even bring down costs
articles.text:
Trump announces mandate forcing AI data centers to pay energy dividends to the local community — says excess energy should be given or sold back to prevent increases or even bring down costs
Excess electricity generated could also make its way to the local community.
President Donald Trump has issued a call for data center builders and AI hyperscalers to pay communities a dividend in order to overcome energy-related price hikes, or even to reduce prices, in order to make data centers more palatable to local communities. In a post on Truth Social post, he warned that data centers would be mandated not only to make their own electricity, as he has previously stated, but also to give or sell excess energy back to the local community.
Local communities all over the United States have protested against AI data centers, often owing to their outsized impact on local communities. Rising electricity costs, noise pollution, water shortages, air pollution, deforestation, and more are the things that small communities have to deal with because of these companies.
To ease the pain of local communities, Trump is demanding that these large companies provide the communities they affect with something that will hopefully make their presence more acceptable. The Trump Administration is keen to stay ahead of China in the AI arms race and is looking for solutions to win back some favor by making the data centers pay something back to the affected communities; how that will practically transpire is yet to be seen. Considering the electricity-focused post, the dividend might be in the form of partially paying rising electricity costs to alleviate a pain point that directly affects many homes within the vicinity of data centers. The Trump Administration had ordered these companies to make their own electricity, as we’ve covered previously. Excess electricity from their generation could be used to further lower the electricity cost for the locals, including a recently passed act that orders data centers to shoulder the cost for grid upgrades to avoid taking it from the taxes of local communities.
“Data Centers that were highly unpopular in a certain area have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck.” Trump further says in his post, aiming to have more data centers built, “MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!!," the President said in closing.
Whether the dividends will be enough to win over communities is yet to be known, as the economic aspect is only one facet of the problem. There are still plenty of problems to face; enormous water consumption, ecological damage, and pollution are still major challenges that make AI data centers a hard sell anywhere they’re located.

articles.title: Pfandsystem im All: Warum eine Kaution von 200.000 Dollar pro Satellit sogar der Raumfahrt nützt
articles.text:
200.000 Dollar Pfand pro Satellit: Wie eine Kaution das Problem mit Weltraumschrott lösen soll
Vor jedem Start in eine erdnahe Umlaufbahn sollen Raumfahrtunternehmen künftig eine Kaution in Höhe von 200.000 US-Dollar hinterlegen, wie in einer im Wissenschaftsmagazin Nature Communications veröffentlichten Studie vorgeschlagen wird. Das Treuhandmodell stammt von einer internationalen Gruppe um den Forscher Indigo Brownhall vom britischen University College London und den Umweltökonomen Daniel Kaffine von der US-amerikanischen University of Colorado Boulder: Betreiber:innen erhalten den hinterlegten Betrag samt Zinsen nur dann zurück, wenn sie den Satelliten nach Missionsende kontrolliert aus dem Orbit entfernen.
Den Berechnungen zufolge bleibt durch das Pfand jährlich mehr als ein Drittel weniger Schrott im All zurück, während der wirtschaftliche Nutzen der Raumfahrt wegen des geringeren Kollisionsrisikos um bis zu 27 Prozent wächst. Lassen Unternehmen ihre ausgedienten Flugkörper hingegen im All zurück, verfällt das Geld und fließt in einen staatlich verwalteten Fonds, über den sich im Simulationszeitraum von 25 Jahren bis zu drei Milliarden Dollar für aktive Aufräummissionen einsammeln ließen.
Warum Regeln der FCC und der ESA beim Weltraumschrott bislang versagen
Nach Angaben der Europäischen Weltraumorganisation (ESA) bewegen sich derzeit mehr als 57.000 Trümmerteile mit einer Größe von über zehn Zentimetern sowie rund 1,5 Millionen Objekte über einem Zentimeter unkontrolliert um die Erde. Zwar verlangen internationale Richtlinien eine Entsorgung binnen 25 Jahren und die US-Kommunikationsbehörde FCC schreibt für den niedrigen Erdorbit eine Frist von fünf Jahren vor, doch zwischen 2010 und 2024 verblieben 60 Prozent aller Satelliten in Bahnen ohne natürlichen Wiedereintritt nach dem Ende ihrer Betriebsdauer im All.
Der Grund für diese geringe Einhaltungsquote liegt im Treibstoffverbrauch: Um einen Satelliten am Ende seiner Laufzeit abzubremsen und in der Erdatmosphäre verglühen zu lassen, müssen Betreiber:innen Treibstoff aufsparen, der ihnen sonst für den laufenden Geschäftsbetrieb und weitere Einnahmen zur Verfügung stünde. Welche geringen Folgen Verstöße bisher hatten, zeigte sich im Oktober 2023, als die FCC gegen den US-Satellitenfernsehanbieter Dish Network wegen des im Orbit verbliebenen Satelliten Echostar-7 erstmals überhaupt eine Strafzahlung von 150.000 Dollar verhängte.
Gegenüber Space.com erklärte Mitautor Daniel Kaffine, das vorgeschlagene Kautionssystem orientiere sich an einem US-Modell aus den 1960er-Jahren, bei dem Ölkonzerne vorab Geld hinterlegen müssen, damit verwaiste Bohrlöcher nach dem Ende der Förderung versiegelt werden: „Wenn die Ölbetreiber:innen nach Abschluss der Förderung aufräumen, bekommen sie ihr Geld zurück.“
Simulation über 25 Jahre: Warum direkte Abstürze mehr bringen als Abklingbahnen
Für ihre Untersuchung koppelten die Wissenschaftler:innen das ökonomische Entscheidungsmodell OPUS mit einem physikalischen Trümmermodell des Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge über einen Zeitraum von 25 Jahren in Höhen zwischen 200 und 2.000 Kilometern. Dabei zeigte sich, dass bei Kautionen zwischen 100.000 und 200.000 Dollar die Wahrscheinlichkeit von Zusammenstößen stärker sinkt, wenn das Pfand nur bei einem direkten, durch Triebwerke gesteuerten Absturz binnen weniger Monate ausgezahlt wird. Wenn für die Rückzahlung bereits das Absenken in eine tiefere Abklingbahn genügt, in der das Objekt erst über fünf oder 25 Jahre durch die Reibung der oberen Luftschichten abstürzt, kreuzen die manövrierunfähigen Satelliten noch jahrelang tiefere Flugbahnen und erhöhen dort das Kollisionsrisiko.
Höhere Kautionen von 500.000 Dollar, was im Modell rund 17 Prozent der durchschnittlichen Gesamtkosten eines Satelliten entspricht, reduzieren die unkontrollierte Schrottmasse zwar um 50 bis 65 Prozent, doch ab einer Million Dollar flacht der Nutzen ab, weil die finanzielle Hürde den Start wirtschaftlich sinnvoller Nutzlasten bremst. Gegenüber einer laufenden Nutzungsgebühr nach dem Vorbild einer Maut im Orbit, wie sie Kaffine 2020 in einer Studie in den Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) untersucht hatte, bietet die Kaution laut den Autor:innen den Vorteil, dass regelkonforme Unternehmen unter dem Strich kein Geld an den Staat verlieren.
EU Space Act und Starlink: Wie Europa den Standard im Alleingang durchsetzen könnte
Auf Ebene der Vereinten Nationen in New York gelten verbindliche Abkommen gegen Weltraumschrott als kaum erreichbar, weil im zuständigen Weltraumausschuss alle Mitgliedstaaten einstimmig abstimmen müssen. Die Simulation belegt jedoch, dass schon ein einzelner Wirtschaftsraum mit einem Weltmarktanteil von 20 Prozent die Zahl nicht-konformer Satellitenwracks um bis zu 18 Prozent senken kann, selbst wenn ein Teil der Anbieter auf unregulierte Drittstaaten ausweicht.
Als möglichen Hebel nennen die Forscher:innen den geplanten EU Space Act der Europäischen Kommission in Brüssel, der bereits Lizenzgebühren von 100.000 EUR sowie Startgebühren zwischen 200.000 und 1,5 Millionen EUR vorsieht. Ähnlich wie bei der Datenschutz-Grundverordnung könnte die Europäische Union den Zugang zu ihrem Binnenmarkt mit rund 400 Millionen Verbraucher:innen daran knüpfen, dass auch US-Unternehmen wie SpaceX für sein Starlink-Netzwerk eine Kaution hinterlegen.
Trotz der positiven Bilanz in den Modellrechnungen räumen die Autor:innen mehrere Schwachstellen ein, die den Erfolg eines solchen Pfandsystems in der Praxis schmälern könnten. So entfällt der finanzielle Anreiz zur Entsorgung, wenn ein Betreiberunternehmen während der mehrjährigen Laufzeit seiner Satelliten insolvent wird, während finanzstarke Konzerne moderate Kautionen als reguläre Betriebskosten verbuchen könnten, um ihre Satelliten zugunsten zusätzlicher Einnahmen bis zum letzten Tropfen Treibstoff weiterzubetreiben.
Zudem berücksichtigt die Simulation bei ausgebrannten Raketenoberstufen lediglich den bereits vorhandenen Bestand und klammert neu hinzukommende Raketenkörper sowie unvorhersehbare technische Defekte aus, durch die ein Satellit noch vor dem Bremsmanöver ausfällt. Wie oft unkontrollierte Objekte im All derzeit durch Explosionen oder Kollisionen zerbrechen, dokumentierte laut Space.com zuletzt das US-Weltraumüberwachungsunternehmen Leolabs, das allein in den vergangenen sechs Monaten mindestens vier solcher Vorfälle mit hunderten neuen Trümmerteilen registrierte.
Nicht zuletzt verlagert eine höhere Entsorgungsquote das Umweltproblem teilweise aus dem Orbit in die obere Erdatmosphäre. Wie Forscher:innen der US-Wetter- und Ozeanografiebehörde NOAA in einer im Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres veröffentlichten Untersuchung nachwiesen, setzt das vermehrte Verglühen von Satelliten Metallpartikel wie Aluminiumoxid in der Mesosphäre frei, was die Temperaturverteilung verändern und die Ozonschicht schädigen kann.

articles.title: Faille PHP : des milliers de sites pourraient être coupés d’Internet cet après-midi, l’UE tire la sonnette d’alarme
articles.text:
Faille PHP : des milliers de sites pourraient être coupés d’Internet cet après-midi, l’UE tire la sonnette d’alarme
Rendez-vous à 16 heures. Deux brèches notées 9,2 sur 10 ont été découvertes dans PHP, le langage qui fait tourner près de sept sites sur dix, et elles ont fuité avant l'heure. Bruxelles conseille déjà de débrancher les sites impossibles à corriger, et plus d'un site PHP sur trois tourne sur une version que personne ne réparera.
Mardi 20 octobre au soir, l'équipe de sécurité de PHP a diffusé un avis aussi laconique qu'alarmant. Une mise à jour corrigeant deux vulnérabilités critiques, chacune notée 9,2 sur l'échelle CVSS v4.0, sortira ce mercredi 21 octobre à 14 h UTC, soit 16 h à Paris. Une fuite a précipité le calendrier. Quelques heures plus tôt, un message posté sur le forum Hacker News, effacé depuis, annonçait deux failles et leur divulgation prévue le 22 octobre. Les chercheurs de watchTowr, dans la confidence, ont aussitôt confirmé.
We were all supposed to wait until Thursday at 11am ET. 
Information has leaked wrt zero-day embargoed RCE vulns in PHP. We can confirm that they're real. CVE-2926-109618/619
We cannot share further information right now. Take this seriously and apply patches when available. pic.twitter.com/kguM8fpq13
— watchTowr (@watchtowrcyber) October 20, 2026
Failles PHP : une porte ouverte sur des millions de serveurs
PHP garde le mode opératoire sous scellés. D'après watchTowr, les deux brèches, référencées CVE-2026-109618 et CVE-2026-109619, permettraient d'exécuter du code à distance. Un pirate pourrait donc prendre la main sur un serveur sans le moindre identifiant. WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Magento et PrestaShop reposent tous sur ce langage, présent sur 69,3 % des sites dont la technologie serveur est identifiée, selon W3Techs.
	
Les deux sont notées 10 et toucheraient les versions 5, 6, 7 et 8 de PHP.
Maigre consolation : aucune attaque n'a été repérée à ce stade. Le compte à rebours tourne pourtant. Les détails techniques paraîtront avec le correctif, et attaquants comme défenseurs partiront de la même ligne de départ. PHP se réserve même le droit d'avancer l'horaire si les informations circulent ou si une exploitation apparaît.
Mise à jour PHP : ce que doivent faire les propriétaires de sites
Dans son avis du 20 octobre, le CERT-EU, l'équipe de cybersécurité des institutions européennes, demande de se tenir prêt à corriger immédiatement. À défaut, il recommande d'envisager l'isolement des applications exposées sur Internet. Voilà d'où viennent les rumeurs de coupures : des sites débranchés de leur plein gré, faute de remède.
Seules les branches 8.2 à 8.5 recevront un correctif. Or 27 % des sites PHP tournent encore sous PHP 7, et 7,7 % sous PHP 5, une version née en 2004.
Sur un hébergement mutualisé, la tâche revient à l'hébergeur : interrogez-le sur son calendrier. Sur un serveur administré soi-même, la commande php -v révèle la version installée. Prévoyez une sauvegarde fraîche et un créneau de maintenance dès ce soir.

articles.title: On a reçu l'iPhone Duo : nos premières impressions et nos doutes — Frandroid
articles.text:
Ça y est, on a reçu l’iPhone Duo à la rédaction de Frandroid. En attendant notre test complet qu’on vous proposera dès que possible (mais sans nous précipiter), voici mes premières impressions sur le premier smartphone pliable d’Apple.
J’ai organisé mon fil de pensée point par point pour retranscrire mes toutes premières heures avec l’iPhone Duo.
L’animation à l’ouverture est bluffante
Une chose a beaucoup fait parler à l’annonce de l’iPhone Duo : l’animation à l’ouverture et à la fermeture créant un effet de transparence. Ce détail a tellement marqué les gens qu’un bidouilleur a rapidement imité l’effet sur le Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8.
J’ai enfin pu me faire ma propre idée et, même si c’est vraiment un détail, ça donne tout de suite envie de découvrir et de manipuler l’iPhone Duo.
Sachez aussi que le smartphone d’Apple ne se verrouille pas dès qu’on le ferme. C’est un choix assumé d’Apple qui estime que ce geste signifie simplement qu’on veut changer de format, pas qu’on veut mettre un terme à l’utilisation. Un petit paramètre pour laisser les gens choisir ce qu’ils préfèrent n’aurait pas été de trop.
Un format qui pèse, surtout fermé
Premier constat en le sortant de sa boîte : l’iPhone Duo n’est pas un poids plume. Avec 254 grammes, c’est l’iPhone le plus lourd jamais commercialisé par Apple (le Galaxy Z Fold 8 pèse 201 grammes). Fermé, il mesure 11,3 millimètres d’épaisseur, et c’est là que ça se ressent le plus. Cela ne dégrade pas pour autant la prise en main, qui reste bonne, mais on sent bien qu’on tient, en quelque sorte, deux écrans dans la main.
Dès qu’on le déplie en revanche, cette impression s’efface très vite. Le poids, bien réparti, passe clairement au second plan et on profite simplement de la grande surface d’affichage.
Un écran interne mat qui change la donne
L’un des choix les plus marquants d’Apple concerne le revêtement mat de l’écran interne. Après ces premières heures d’utilisation, son impact est évident : les reflets ne se diffusent pas du tout de la même manière qu’avec une dalle brillante, et le rendu des couleurs change lui aussi. Revers de la médaille, les noirs tirent un peu vers le gris.
Sur des contenus aux couleurs vives, avec une luminosité bien poussée, le rendu reste en revanche franchement réussi. Ça pète bien et ça flatte la rétine. En comparant avec un Galaxy Z Fold 8 de Samsung, ma préférence a d’ailleurs varié d’une image à l’autre : sur une scène sombre, j’avais tendance à préférer le Fold ; sur une image très colorée, c’est plutôt l’iPhone Duo qui l’emportait.
Sur le reste de l’interface, l’effet mat, rappelant celui d’une liseuse, est vraiment plaisant. Je n’ai en revanche pas encore pu vérifier si les photos et vidéos prises avec l’iPhone Duo s’affichent fidèlement sur le grand écran, ou si le revêtement mat fausse leur rendu. Je regarderai ça de près pendant le test.
Touch ID : une petite friction
L’iPhone Duo mise sur un lecteur d’empreintes Touch ID intégré au bouton latéral. Mais il faut d’abord appuyer sur le bouton pour réveiller l’appareil avant de pouvoir le déverrouiller avec son doigt. Sur le Galaxy Z Fold 8, dont le capteur est lui aussi placé sur la tranche droite, il suffit de poser le pouce ou l’index pour déverrouiller directement.
Cette étape en plus agace un peu au quotidien, dommage sur un produit aussi soigné par ailleurs. On regrette aussi de ne pas avoir la moindre reconnaissance faciale.
Apple n’a pas mis de Face ID sur l’iPhone Duo : Touch ID est sa seule méthode biométrique. Pour éviter l’appui sur le bouton, il reste la possibilité de déverrouiller le téléphone avec une Apple Watch, plié comme déplié.
Une interface pensée pour les droitiers
Le dock d’applications reste toujours positionné à droite, et c’est plutôt bien vu. Quelle que soit l’application utilisée, que l’écran soit ouvert ou fermé, les boutons restent accessibles du même côté, sous le pouce.
Toutes les applications ne sont toutefois pas encore parfaitement adaptées au format et affichent juste une barre noire verticale. Je ne m’en inquiète pas outre mesure : Apple dispose d’une force de frappe considérable auprès des développeurs, et les interfaces devraient rapidement suivre. Difficile d’imaginer une application comme YouTube, par exemple, ne pas se mettre à jour pour l’occasion. Ce qu’on voit déjà est en tout cas prometteur.
En revanche, pour les gauchers, ce choix de fixer le dock à droite risque de poser souci. On surveillera de prochaines mises à jour d’iOS pour voir si Apple apportera une solution (si le problème est vraiment signalé par les utilisateurs).
L’iPhone Duo n’abandonne pas le Flex Mode
Alors que Samsung a malheureusement abandonné le Flex Mode sur son Galaxy Z Fold 8, qui a lui aussi un format passeport (le Fold 8 Ultra le conserve), l’iPhone Duo propose un mode semi-plié permettant d’utiliser le téléphone quand il est « assis ». C’est-à-dire plié à 90 degrés.
Sur les applications compatibles, comme Netflix, la vidéo s’affiche ainsi sur la moitié supérieure tandis que les boutons d’interaction s’affichent sur la partie inférieure, posée sur la table.
Bref, ici, Apple marque des points.
Une charnière remarquable
La charnière est l’un des points les plus réussis de cette prise en main.
L’ouverture comme la fermeture sont agréables, avec un niveau de résistance parfaitement dosé. C’est à la fois plaisant à manipuler et rassurant sur la qualité de fabrication.
Une caméra sous l’écran qui se fait oublier
La caméra placée sous l’écran interne est très bien dissimulée. Il faut vraiment jouer avec les reflets pour la repérer, et à l’usage, écran allumé, on l’oublie très vite. De quoi profiter d’un affichage plus immersif, sans interruption.
Évidemment, il ne faut pas en attendre une qualité photo comparable aux autres capteurs photo du smartphone. Apple la présente d’ailleurs comme une caméra FaceTime, qui filme en 1080p à 60 images par seconde. Pour les appels vidéo, elle fera l’affaire.
Des animations aux petits oignons
iOS a été adapté au format avec beaucoup de soin, jusque dans des détails parfois anecdotiques. Si je referme le smartphone à moitié et que je m’arrête en cours de route, l’application ouverte se réajuste aussitôt : plutôt que de laisser du texte s’afficher au niveau de la pliure, elle se divise en deux parties, à gauche et à droite.
C’est tout bête, et personne n’utilisera vraiment son téléphone de cette manière. Mais c’est amusant, et cela montre à quel point Apple a peaufiné l’expérience logicielle.
Un multitâche limité à deux applications
Le multitâche est plutôt bien géré, mais il se limite à deux applications affichées simultanément (le Xiaomi 18 Fold rigole). Bonne idée en revanche : lorsqu’une application occupe une moitié de l’écran, l’autre peut être utilisée comme un smartphone classique, avec l’écran d’accueil, pour continuer à naviguer librement. Il est aussi possible d’associer deux applications pour qu’elles restent liées, et les rouvrir ensemble depuis le multitâche.
Il manque toutefois une option pour sauvegarder ces paires d’applications. Chez Samsung, un duo ou un trio d’applications peut être enregistré et relancé en un geste depuis le dock. Rien de tel chez Apple pour le moment, mais j’ai espoir que cela finira par arriver.
MagSafe, l’avantage qui compte
Enfin, l’iPhone Duo est compatible MagSafe, avec des aimants intégrés. C’est un vrai avantage face au Galaxy Z Fold 8, qui n’en a pas et nécessite une coque spécifique pour profiter de la recharge magnétique Qi2.
Je l’ai testé sur un support : une fois déplié, ce n’est pas très pratique, puisque soit le support bascule, soit le smartphone glisse, déséquilibré.
Prix et disponibilité de l’iPhone Duo en France
Les précommandes de l’iPhone Duo sont ouvertes depuis le vendredi 16 octobre à 14 heures sur le site d’Apple, dans l’application Apple Store et chez les revendeurs officiels, pour des premières livraisons et une disponibilité en boutique ce vendredi 23 octobre. Attention cependant, il y a de gros soucis au niveau des stocks.
    À lire aussi : 
N’espérez pas vous rendre dans un Apple Store pour trouver des stocks d’iPhone Duo
L’iPhone Duo existe en deux coloris : Blanc stellaire et Ciel nocturne. Côté prix, l’iPhone Duo devient l’iPhone le plus cher jamais commercialisé par Apple.
Voici la grille tarifaire en France :
- 256 Go : 2 339 €
- 512 Go : 2 589 €
- 1 To : 3 089 €
- 2 To : 3 839 €
Attention enfin avant de craquer : l’iPhone Duo fonctionne uniquement en eSIM, sans tiroir pour carte physique, il faudra donc vérifier que votre forfait est compatible.

articles.title: The past, present, and future share a show floor at Pinball Expo 2026
articles.text:
It’s October in the Midwest, which means it’s time for the pinball world to descend on a convention center in Chicagoland for the annual Pinball Expo. Once thought to be an entertainment sector slowly bleeding out, pinball has come back in a big way in recent years. I visited one of Chicago’s last old-school manufacturers before heading down the road to see what’s new in the silver-ball universe.
Behind the silver ball
Hundreds gathered on a brisk fall Friday morning outside Stern Pinball’s headquarters in Elk Grove, Illinois, waiting to enter a Wonka-like wonder factory where piles of raw parts become licensed creations from Jaws to the brand-new Fallout. Stern invited me to tour its offices and factory floor before heading off to the convention in nearby Schaumburg, Illinois.
An early-morning line begins to form outside of Stern HQ as buses of Pinball Expo attendees arrive for tours.
An early-morning line begins to form outside of Stern HQ as buses of Pinball Expo attendees arrive for tours.
As I stood with my tour group in Stern Pinball’s HQ lobby, mouth agape at the dozens of machines lining the walls, we were greeted by the man himself, Gary Stern, who gave us some background on the company’s 40-year history. After a stop at Gary’s podium, we were ushered to the factory floor entrance, where Stern employee and legendary game designer George Gomez briefed us on the tour rules and answered questions. According to Gomez, “at any given time, Stern controls 90 percent of the current pinball market, and everybody else splits the rest.”
Gary Stern greets visitors at the Stern factory tour.
Gary Stern greets visitors at the Stern factory tour.
While the industry may be expanding toward something more reminiscent of its glory days, there’s no doubt who still rules the market. With a steady stream of new license releases, Stern has cemented itself as the brand in modern pinball.
Stern HQ. I think I could work in this office…
Credit:
Nick Indge
Stern HQ. I think I could work in this office…
Credit:
Nick Indge
What I saw on the expo floor, though, showed me that the remaining 10 percent of the market is doing some really interesting things, and hobbyist projects are booming. From modular home setups to open development kits that let anyone with silver-ball dreams try their hand at game design, there was something for everyone. In short, it’s a very exciting time to be a pinball fan.
The Stern pinball headquarters in Elk Grove Village, Ill.
The Stern pinball headquarters in Elk Grove Village, Ill.
A view of the machine collection inside of Stern Pinball’s offices.
Nick Indge
A view of the machine collection inside of Stern Pinball’s offices.
Nick Indge
A lineup of Stern releases from the 2012-2014 era.
Nick Indge
A lineup of Stern releases from the 2012-2014 era.
Nick Indge
A view of the machine collection inside of Stern Pinball’s offices.
Nick Indge
A lineup of Stern releases from the 2012-2014 era.
Nick Indge
A row of game releases at the Stern HQ offices.
Nick Indge
Some of the more recent modern releases lined up at Stern HQ.
Nick Indge
Latest from the show floor
Stern’s latest offering, Fallout, stood near the entrance of a convention floor packed with the latest machines from manufacturers like Jersey Jack, Barrels of Fun, Spooky Pinball, and others. I’ve attended this show for the last four years, and each year seems to bring new companies into the fold. Despite more than 25 years of advances in home entertainment, nothing quite matches the tactile thrill of launching a metal ball around a wooden cabinet.
The new Fallout machine from Stern Pinball.
Credit:
Nick Indge
The new Fallout machine from Stern Pinball.
Credit:
Nick Indge
Several companies showed off their latest attempts to bring pinball into virtual reality without abandoning physical controls, letting players wear a VR helmet while pressing real buttons on a pedestal setup. It’s a fun novelty that demonstrates what’s possible, but if the lines at the expo were any indication, most people still prefer walking up to a physical machine and enjoying the tactile controls, visuals, and sounds that come with it.
American Pinball’s upcoming remake of Circus Voltaire.
Nick Indge
American Pinball’s upcoming remake of Circus Voltaire.
Nick Indge
The new Bon Jovi game from Barrels of Fun.
Nick Indge
The new Bon Jovi game from Barrels of Fun.
Nick Indge
Spooky Pinball’s latest: Beetlejuice.
Nick Indge
Spooky Pinball’s latest: Beetlejuice.
Nick Indge
The new Bon Jovi game from Barrels of Fun.
Nick Indge
Spooky Pinball’s latest: Beetlejuice.
Nick Indge
The new Sonic the Hedgehog pinball by Jersey Jack.
Nick Indge
The floor of this booth was an especially nice detail.
The modular market
One of the biggest questions facing anyone buying a pinball machine for home use is what to do when you get bored with a $10,000 game. Until recently, the options were to sell it, find someone willing to trade, or build your own virtual pin setup with screens instead of physical playfields. The Multimorphic P3 team saw an opportunity for another approach.
Multimorphic’s Portal pinball machine is a part of their P3 lineup of swappable table designs.
Multimorphic’s Portal pinball machine is a part of their P3 lineup of swappable table designs.
According to Multimorphic co-creative director Stephen Silver, “The way the P3 is designed is that the lower two-thirds is a ball-tracking interactive display… We have floating mechanisms above the screen, floating flippers, floating slings, floating targets. And the upper third is a swappable play field. We’ve got 10 different play fields now that we can swap and change the entire game.”
As demonstrated by the much-hyped Dungeon Crawler Carl prototype (whose lines never seemed to get shorter), the P3 system uses a playfield screen that can react to ball movement in real time, and the game can change to match player choices. In Dungeon Crawler Carl, for instance, the display layout changes based on which book in the series the player chooses.
“We’re planning on doing seven books in the game… you can play them in any order you want,” Silver explained. ” The idea being that you get to Faction Wars—the events of the seventh book—it’s a perfect wizard mode. When we started this, Faction Wars was the last book in the series. It still feel(s) like a good wrapping-up point for this story that we’re telling. In the future, we could always be open to adding more books, but right now that’s the plan.”
The first two entries in the book series had playable pin versions on the show floor, and Silver says that “every single book itself is the equivalent depth of a ’90s Williams game… It’s like seven really solid games in one,” Silver said.
Dungeon Crawler Carl will enter production “at the end of the year, and then it should be rolling out to delivery early next year,” he said.
Multimorphic’s upcoming Dungeon Crawler Carl pinball.
Multimorphic’s upcoming Dungeon Crawler Carl pinball.
The platform’s versatility extends beyond in-house designs. Multimorphic offers a free software development kit (SDK) that lets community members design and distribute their own table creations for the P3 system. Machine owners can swap physical overlay kits or remove them entirely to play original games on the reactive screen.
“There are 30 different games available on the system now because you can do software-only games,” Silver said. “It’s the only third-party development platform in pinball. So anybody can download the free SDK and develop third-party software games… and release it through our store to an audience of P3 owners that are hungry for new content.”
Dungeon Crawler Carl cabinet artwork by Brad Albright. Voice actor Jeff Hays also reprises his audiobook roles for the machine.
Dungeon Crawler Carl cabinet artwork by Brad Albright. Voice actor Jeff Hays also reprises his audiobook roles for the machine.
Pocket Pinball and pinball construction set
Sitting on one of the more unassuming tables of the PinExpo show floor was Pocket Pinball, a free Android APK that lets users load any Visual Pinball X (VPX) table on their phone or tablet. But the project’s developer, Johnny Zen, had something else to show off: a closed beta for his Pinball Construction Set. An homage to the 1982 classic Bill Budge Apple II game of the same name, the browser-based tool lets users design their own pinball machine with an easy drag-and-drop interface. Multimorphic may have the only free pinball SDK for now, but if Zen has his way, that won’t be true for long.
Pocket Pinball running on my tablet.
Pocket Pinball running on my tablet.
Whereas most modern pinball designs start at the CAD desk, the upcoming Pinball Construction Set keeps the process entirely within a browser. Zen compares the system to building a coaster in Roller Coaster Tycoon: Users can choose between three styles or start with a blank slate. After selecting a template, such as a standard or wide-body layout, they can add traditional design elements like ramps, targets, and scoops by clicking and dragging them into place.
The program is still in closed beta, but aspiring pinball developers can register their interest to be notified when it becomes publicly available. Zen also plans to add a marketplace where users can commission artwork from freelance artists. “If you needed some artwork for your apron or playfield, you basically look at the artist profiles, then the app will send the artist’s team the exact measurements of what you need,” he said.
Homebrew heaven
One of the most exciting trends in pinball’s modern resurgence is the rise of homebrew design, with passionate hobbyists turning basement-built machines into careers with some of the industry’s biggest players. Often serving as playable resumes, homebrew games give aspiring designers a chance to flex their creative muscles without the licensing restrictions that come with producing commercial machines.
Who Shot Mr Burns? This impressive homebrew looks ready for the arcade floor.
Who Shot Mr Burns? This impressive homebrew looks ready for the arcade floor.
One of this year’s homebrew highlights was Shaolin Flow, an ode to the great Hong Kong action movies that those of us who grew up in the ’90s watched on Saturday afternoon network TV. Complete with an optional Wu-Tang soundtrack, Shaolin Flow lets players choose between traditional flipper-button controls and a more punchy approach. Two fist-shaped sensors sit atop the playfield, to the left and right of the flippers. Players activate the flippers by throwing punches over the sensor.
What initially looked like a gimmick quickly proved to be a great time. Adding a physical element to an already physical game felt more natural than I expected, and the absence of any perceptible input lag made the experience seamless.
Passing your fists over the green sensors allows you to control flippers by punching.
Passing your fists over the green sensors allows you to control flippers by punching.
As the tools for designing and building pinball machines become more accessible, the homebrew scene continues to grow. Each year brings more entries to the floor, transforming what was once a smaller corner of proudly displayed projects into a dedicated, walled-off section featuring games from the future stars of pinball design. This year’s homebrew showstopper could see its creator designing a licensed table for one of the industry’s major manufacturers by the following year’s show.
An Akira-themed homebrew pinball machine.
Nick Indge
An Akira-themed homebrew pinball machine.
Nick Indge
A Minecraft-themed homebrew table.
Nick Indge
A Minecraft-themed homebrew table.
Nick Indge
A Beastie Boys homebrew pinball machine.
A Beastie Boys homebrew pinball machine.
A Minecraft-themed homebrew table.
Nick Indge
A Beastie Boys homebrew pinball machine.
So much more
Project Pinball is a charity that raises money to place pinball machines in children’s hospitals. Great cause!
Credit:
Nick Indge
Project Pinball is a charity that raises money to place pinball machines in children’s hospitals. Great cause!
Credit:
Nick Indge
Pinball Expo isn’t just an industry trade event; it’s also a celebration of every era of pinball history. Volunteers haul machines from their personal collections to the show floor, where the general public can play them all weekend. And it’s not just balls and flippers. Walk the aisles, and you’ll see artists, merch and crafts vendors, accessories, retro video games, traditional arcades, and enough aftermarket mod kits to turn any pinball machine into a second hobby.
Pieces of the world’s largest Sonic collection on display.
Nick Indge
Pieces of the world’s largest Sonic collection on display.
Nick Indge
Ever wanted to learn how to solder? There’s a booth for that.
Nick Indge
Ever wanted to learn how to solder? There’s a booth for that.
Nick Indge
A selection of custom playfield accessories to add some extra flavor to your pinball table.
A selection of custom playfield accessories to add some extra flavor to your pinball table.
Ever wanted to learn how to solder? There’s a booth for that.
Nick Indge
A selection of custom playfield accessories to add some extra flavor to your pinball table.
A booth selling original pinball machine manuals and schematics.
Nick Indge
Pinball artist Brian Allen’s artwork booth.
Nick Indge
A retro gaming booth.
A vendor selling custom light-up pinball logo signs.
Nick Indge
Ever wanted to play pinball with the drums from Donkey Kong? There’s a mod for that.
Nick Indge
The floor of this booth was an especially nice detail.
The future
See you later, Flippy!
See you later, Flippy!
For decades, pinball production was concentrated among a handful of major manufacturers in the Chicagoland area. While the region might still be the industry’s epicenter, newer challengers to Stern’s dominance, like Texas-based Barrels of Fun or European producers like Dutch Pinball, show that things are changing.
Today, aspiring developers can turn a good idea into a playable VPX table without ever putting down their phone. Whether it’s a bedroom developer working with a free SDK or one of the industry’s biggest players, pinball is being made by more people in more places, and fans are all the better for it.
Nick Indge is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica covering hardware, embedded systems, and self-hosted infrastructure. A former security investigator turned tech writer, he writes to help readers escape subscription traps and regain ownership of their digital lives. He lives in Chicagoland with his family and a goofball husky.

articles.title: Sam Altman creador de ChatGPT ahora lanza herramientas para distinguir humanos de deepfakes en bancos y videollamadas
articles.text:
World presentó un conjunto de herramientas de verificación de identidad pensado para bancos e instituciones financieras, con el objetivo de distinguir a personas reales de sistemas automatizados y deepfakes. El anuncio lo hizo Alex Blania, cofundador del proyecto impulsado por Sam Altman, director ejecutivo de OpenAI, durante la conferencia Money20/20.
Se trata del primer producto que World diseña de forma específica para un sector industrial, y llega en un momento en el que la inteligencia artificial multiplica los riesgos de fraude y suplantación.
El paquete, bautizado World ID, combina tres soluciones distintas: una aplicación de identidad digital, una extensión para verificar participantes en videollamadas de Zoom y un sistema para que agentes de IA puedan actuar en nombre de los usuarios. Cada componente apunta a un escenario distinto donde la confianza entre humanos y máquinas se ha vuelto un problema para las empresas.
Cómo funciona World ID para verificar identidad bancaria
La aplicación World ID funciona como un repositorio de credenciales digitales que certifican la identidad de cada usuario. Estas credenciales permiten demostrar que determinada acción fue ejecutada por una persona real y no por un programa automatizado, un aspecto cada vez más relevante para las instituciones financieras.
Sandro Herbig, presidente de Tools for Humanity, explicó que el avance de la inteligencia artificial está elevando la necesidad de las empresas de contar con mecanismos de verificación confiables. Según indicó, World ID busca aportar una capa adicional de confianza tanto en los sistemas internos como en los externos de los bancos.
Por ahora, World no identificó ninguna entidad bancaria que haya adoptado formalmente la herramienta, ni dio a conocer su costo. Sí mencionó como socios de diseño a OpenExchange, Bain Capital, VanEck Funds y Outtake, compañías que participaron en el desarrollo del producto sin que se haya confirmado su implementación comercial.
La urgencia detrás de este lanzamiento tiene respaldo en cifras concretas. World citó una proyección de Deloitte según la cual las pérdidas por fraude facilitado con IA en Estados Unidos podrían escalar de 12.300 millones de dólares en 2023 a 40.000 millones de dólares en 2027, un salto que explica el interés del sector financiero en herramientas de este tipo.
World ID para Zoom combate deepfakes en videollamadas
Uno de los componentes del paquete apunta directamente a un problema que ha crecido con la sofisticación de la inteligencia artificial generativa: la suplantación de identidad en videoconferencias. World ID para Zoom verifica a los participantes de las llamadas y detecta posibles deepfakes durante la interacción.
Esta función no es completamente nueva. Había comenzado una fase de pruebas limitada en abril, y tras ese período acotado, la herramienta ya quedó disponible para todos los usuarios. El objetivo es que las empresas puedan confirmar, en tiempo real, que la persona que participa de una reunión virtual es quien dice ser.
AgentKit habilita pagos y acciones de agentes de inteligencia artificial
La tercera pieza del anuncio, conocida como World ID for Agents o AgentKit, resuelve un problema distinto: permite que los usuarios autoricen a agentes de IA a presentar credenciales en su nombre. La herramienta busca simplificar las interacciones entre sistemas automatizados y plataformas externas sin perder el rastro de quién autorizó cada acción.
Este desarrollo no surge de manera aislada. En marzo, World ya había presentado una versión de prueba de AgentKit compatible con el protocolo de pago x402, de Coinbase, que permite a los agentes de inteligencia artificial realizar pequeños pagos con criptomonedas estables por servicios digitales.
La actividad en torno a ese protocolo ya muestra volumen: se han procesado más de 138 millones de transacciones a través de x402, entre ellas micropagos por datos, recursos informáticos y acceso a modelos de IA. No obstante, todavía no es posible determinar qué proporción de esas operaciones responde a una demanda comercial sostenida en el tiempo.
World sostiene que más de 18 millones de personas ya verificaron su identidad como seres humanos únicos dentro de la red. Esa base de usuarios es la que el proyecto busca capitalizar con una expansión hacia servicios financieros que combinen identidad digital y pagos.
En esa línea se inscribe World Money, una aplicación para pagos con criptomonedas estables que la compañía lanzó en septiembre. El producto se suma a un conjunto de herramientas que World desarrolla en paralelo junto con actores del sector de servicios financieros.

articles.title: Foursquare co-founder says equity holders saw no returns from the company's acquisition | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Last month, advertising company Infillion acquired location-data platform Foursquare, a once popular social network, at an undisclosed value. Now, in a new blog post, Foursquare co-founder and former CEO Dennis Crowley said that investors didn’t see any returns from the sale.
Crowley referenced a post by an angel investor, inferred that neither preferred nor common stockholders got any value out of the deal, and said he was disappointed by the outcome.
“I was heartbroken by this ending. So many people put so much time and energy and passion and love into building Foursquare — the company, the products, the brand, the culture. If you were part of it (or even close to it), you know exactly what I’m talking about. To our ~1600 former employees over 17 years, I am sorry the Foursquare story ended in such a way that makes it seem like our collective efforts were worth … nothing?” he said in the post.
Crowley said that the company did well after it started focusing on enterprise business and had consecutive years with over $100 million in revenue. In 2019, the company raised capital from a private equity firm and in 2021 brought in the banker who led the raise as CEO. Crowley blamed the final outcome on that transition, saying that the management of the company wasn’t able to preserve or create new value.
Foursquare, which had raised over $411 million in funding according to PitchBook data, eventually shut down its app in 2024.
Several people reacted to Crowley’s post and said that Foursquare was very useful to them in discovering new places in their cities and also gave ideas for new apps. After Foursquare, startups like Zenly and Jagat, along with Instagram and Snapchat, have explored social maps.

articles.title: I asked ChatGPT to recreate 5 classic video games, including Snake, Pong and Tetris — then challenged it to make them even better
articles.text:
ChatGPT can now create games you can play right inside a conversation — I challenged it to recreate 5 classics, then gave them a crazy twist
Can ChatGPT really recreate my favorite retro arcade games?
OpenAI recently introduced GPT-6, a new model of ChatGPT. You've probably heard about a lot of its new features but one that I don't think has had nearly enough attention, especially considering how much fun you can have with it, is Intelligent UI.
It allows ChatGPT to generate interactive experiences directly within a conversation. OpenAI explains: “With Intelligent UI, responses can include graphics, tappable buttons, forms, charts, and interactive experiences you can use directly in your conversation.”
What's interesting is there isn’t a single format. Which means, depending on what you ask, ChatGPT might create an interactive diagram, a calculator, a mood board, a map or even a little gaming console.
There are some genuinely useful applications here, from making complicated subjects easier to understand to building simple tools on the spot. But I was particularly interested in something a little less practical — games.
ChatGPT can now create games you can actually play within the chat window. And while there are all sorts of possibilities for educational games, quizzes and entirely new creations, I wanted to see what would happen if I asked it to recreate some old favorites.
So I started with five classic games, including Snake, Pong and Tetris. I gave ChatGPT simple prompts to see how faithfully it could recreate them. I then asked it to reinvent each game with new aesthetics, unexpected gameplay mechanics and a few deliberately chaotic twists. Think Snake in a neon cyberpunk world and Tetris with rules that change every time you clear a line.
Here's what happened when I put ChatGPT's new game-making abilities to the test.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Snake gets a neon makeover
The prompt: "Create a playable version of the classic Snake game directly inside this conversation."
ChatGPT got the basics right straight away. The game was instantly recognizable, with responsive controls and even a slider to adjust the speed. It looked good and, importantly, it was actually fun to play for a couple of games.
I then asked it to give Snake a neon cyberpunk makeover, complete with moving obstacles, special power-ups and a speed increase every five points. Say hello to Neon Snake.
There was one small hiccup. Instead of creating the new game directly in the chat window, ChatGPT initially gave me the code. Which wasn't much use when the whole point was to play it there and then.
I tried another prompt asking it if it could make it directly playable in the conversation and that worked. The results of that experiment were fun. The neon aesthetic looked good, everything was color-coded and the new mechanics gave the classic (and, let’s be honest, sometimes boring) game an extra layer of challenge.
Tetris gets new rules
The prompt: "Create a playable game inspired by Tetris directly inside this conversation."
This one worked really well from the start. I’d just assumed it would be a bit buggy and glitchy because there’s so much going on compared to Snake, but the controls were intuitive and responsive, and the classic block-stacking mechanic was all there.
But what if Tetris changed the rules every time you cleared a line? That was the idea behind my follow-up prompt.
I asked ChatGPT to introduce unexpected twists, which could include rotating the board to adding unusual block shapes or special powers that could destroy part of the grid.
And it delivered. The changing rules introduced a fun element of unpredictability to a game that's usually all about getting into a rhythm. I also came away thinking about how much further you could take this. There are so many opportunities to experiment with different rules, challenges and power-ups.
Space Invaders becomes a First Contact situation
The prompt: "Build me a fully playable retro arcade game inspired by Space Invaders"
Again, ChatGPT recreated the classic arcade experience surprisingly well. It looked and played like the original, with straightforward controls and all the fun of shooting at waves of approaching aliens.
But I wanted to see whether it could do something a bit more imaginative than adding extra enemies or making everything move faster. So I asked it to introduce a choice: what if I could defend Earth by fighting the aliens or negotiating with them?
I wanted waves of pixel-art enemies, but also decisions between rounds that could unlock weapons, stop an invasion or make the next attack more dangerous.
ChatGPT called its reinvention First Contact, which I loved. Up until this point it was calling most of the games "chaos" or "chaotic" so this felt more inventive.
It was a fun way to introduce a new dimension to a familiar game. But did it work well? I don't know, I couldn't ever make it past the first level. This experiment really suffered with my poor alien-fighting abilities.
Haunted Pac-Man
The prompt: "Create a fully interactive retro maze game inspired by Pac-Man that I can play directly inside this ChatGPT conversation."
This was easily my favorite of the five, but I have always adored Pac-Man. ChatGPT's first attempt was a fun, responsive maze game with the familiar mechanics of moving around, collecting things and trying to avoid enemies. Bonus points for the fact it renamed it Maze Muncher.
For the reinvention, I decided to lean into Halloween. I asked it to turn the game into a haunted 1980s arcade, with me playing a little ghost hunter instead of Pac-Man.
I also wanted the maze itself to change. Every ten orbs collected would trigger a surprise, like shifting walls, new passages or an extra ghost. And I asked for temporary power-ups that would let me chase the ghosts for a change.
ChatGPT handled this well but didn't wait until I'd collected orbs. It was super fast-paced and there were new ghosts, secret passages and changing mechanics from the start. It was quick, easy to control and genuinely fun to play.
Pong reinvented
The prompt: Build me a fully playable version of Pong inside this conversation.
Pong might be the simplest game of the bunch, but ChatGPT made a really solid version. The controls were easy, the aesthetics were nice and it even offered easy, normal and hard difficulty settings.
I decided to ruin that simplicity and asked ChatGPT to create a more chaotic version where every point triggered a random modifier. The ball could split in two, the paddles could shrink, gravity could change or an obstacle could appear in the middle of the court.
The result definitely delivered on the chaos. The familiar back-and-forth gameplay was still there, but the changing rules made each rally a little less predictable. It was also a reminder of how much fun you can have with a simple idea. You don't need to reinvent every part of a game to make it entertaining.
I was genuinely impressed with how well all five games worked, especially considering how simple my original prompts were.
Yes, there were a few hiccups along the way, like ChatGPT deciding to give me code instead of a playable game a couple of times. But overall, the controls were responsive, the games looked good and the reinventions were more imaginative than I expected.
What I enjoyed most was how easy it was to experiment. You could take a game you already know, change the aesthetic, introduce an unexpected mechanic or come up with something completely ridiculous and see what ChatGPT made of it.
I can imagine this being a fun way to waste half an hour, especially if you loved these games growing up. Although, after all this experimenting, I do feel like I should remind you that the originals are still out there, and they're well worth revisiting too.
