articles.title: Staples hackers created more than 15,000 gift cards, then went on a shopping spree
articles.text:
What we know so far: Hackers took over Staples customer-service sessions and used them to issue more than 15,000 gift cards worth over $5 million, according to a newly unsealed search warrant application. The breach linked a corporate software intrusion to an organized retail theft operation, letting the group turn unauthorized system access into merchandise. It also exposed how weaknesses in one company's internal tools could support fraud across multiple retailers.
The attackers obtained the session data from the memory of a support application the retailer believed could only be reached from its own computers. The breach gave a Chinese organized crime group a way to generate gift cards for retailers including Target and Sephora. Members of the operation then used the cards to buy electronics and other merchandise, much of which was shipped to China.
The court document describes the compromised system as Nexus, an internal customer-support application. It does not name Staples, but 404 Media identified the company through its Massachusetts headquarters, its use of Blackhawk Network to fulfill gift card orders and the Nexus name. The publication also found a reference to Nexus on a former Staples executive's LinkedIn profile.
Staples did not respond to 404 Media's requests for comment.
The hackers reached Nexus from outside the company's network and made multiple heap-dump requests, the warrant application says. A heap dump captures the data held in an application's memory at a given moment.
The information returned by those requests allowed the attackers to hijack sessions belonging to customer-service representatives who were already logged in. They then used those sessions to issue gift cards and send them to email addresses they controlled.
The document describes how the attackers moved from application-memory data to authenticated employee sessions. It does not establish how they first gained outside access to Nexus.
Homeland Security Investigations learned of the attack in October 2023, when the company reported that more than 15,000 gift cards had been fraudulently issued through its systems.
Once the cards reached the group's email accounts, participants could display them on their phones for cashiers to scan.
At a Target in New Hampshire, 35 gift cards linked to the Staples breach were used within one hour to buy Apple, Bose and Powerbeats products. The purchases also involved cards from other sources.
Surveillance footage showed four men approaching checkout counters one after another, sometimes interacting with each other and the cashiers. Investigators described the men presenting a card on a phone, having it scanned, then finding another card and repeating the process until they had used all the cards available to them.
Target employees told investigators the men visited almost daily and regularly made large purchases of Apple products with gift cards.
Records from other stores showed the scale of the spending. Target identified 3,850 cards worth about $141,000 that were used in 300 transactions across 85 stores in 18 states over two days.
Sephora reported that about 330 cards worth $58,600 had been redeemed online across 1,500 transactions. Lowe's reported 450 cards totaling $226,000 used online and in person at more than 22 locations.
In total, the group redeemed about 4,630 cards from the breach, worth about $425,000. That was only a portion of the more than $5 million in cards the hackers had issued.
The breach was linked to a larger gift card conspiracy that used warehouses to hold merchandise before shipping goods to China. The Justice Department announced prison sentences for three Chinese nationals involved in the operation in April. Its announcement mentioned attacks on US businesses but did not identify Staples.
The broader group acquired more than $100 million in gift cards.

articles.title: Fuse Energy bets on NVIDIA GPUs as it expands from energy supply into AI infrastructure | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Fuse Energy, a British energy company, has opened reservations for Fuse Compute, its first commercial AI product, offering access to NVIDIA GPUs in UK data centres powered by Fuse – marking a new step into AI infrastructure by the EnergyTech startup.
Interested parties can register interest and reserve capacity today, with the first GPUs slated to come online in December 2026. The ambition here is to own the full AI stack: power, land, data centres and AI compute.
“Power is the biggest hurdle to building AI infrastructure, and it’s the part we already know how to do,” says Alan Chang, CEO and co-founder of Fuse Energy. “Every AI company is fighting for the same scarce GPUs, and the grid can’t connect data centres fast enough to keep up. Fuse Compute puts that expertise to work for the companies building the future of intelligence, and makes sure that future is built in Britain.”
This is an interesting new direction for an energy company whose focus is simplyfying gas and electricity management. Fuse has raised €178 million ($199 million) since its founding in 2022.
Our earlier coverage traces Fuse’s expansion from supplying 50,000 UK homes in July 2025, when it reported €76 million in annualised revenue and raised €8.5 million, to more than 200,000 households and €341 million in annual recurring revenue by December, when it secured another €59 million.
By June 2026, Fuse was supplying more than 300,000 households and had closed a €25 million Series B extension, while reporting monthly EBITDA profitability since December 2025.
Its expansion into AI compute comes amid significant funding for companies developing the underlying infrastructure. In the UK, Nscale raised €1.7 billion for vertically integrated AI compute, Volta reportedly secured €259.8 million across two rounds to develop AI factories, and Orbital Industries raised €43 million for industrial hardware including data-centre technologies.
Elsewhere, Finland’s Verda raised €164.8 million for AI cloud expansion and Spain’s iPronics secured €107.6 million for optical networking. These 2026 infrastructure financing announcements totalled approximately €2.4 billion, excluding Fuse’s historical funding.
The company says that AI is creating more demand for compute than the UK can supply. The UK Government’s Compute Roadmap estimates the country will need at least 6GW of AI-capable data centre capacity by 2030, yet new data centres face waits of up to a decade for a grid connection.
Power has become the main constraint on how quickly that capacity can be built. The Government aims to expand the UK’s public compute capacity 20x by 2030, but the country has few home-grown providers of large-scale compute, leaving many British AI companies reliant on capacity hosted overseas.
Fuse’s move into compute builds on its experience in power. Its most recent solar site was built at around 30% below the industry average cost per megawatt. It holds a power generation pipeline of more than 1GW and a data centre connection pipeline of 142MW across 15 projects. This will allow it to energise and construct high-density AI sites quickly and cheaply.
Fuse Compute will offer bare-metal, single-tenant NVIDIA GPU nodes in UK data centres, with UK jurisdiction and a UK data path. The first 128 NVIDIA B300 GPUs are due to come online in December 2026, followed by 1,024 in Q2 2027, a further 22MW in Q4 2027 and 116MW from 2028.
In energy, Fuse already supplies 470,000 UK homes and holds both supplier and meter operator licences.
On the supply side, Fuse owns and operates low carbon generation assets, with 22 MW active and over 1 GW in the pipeline across the UK, US, and Europe.
For the company, keeping compute onshore means that the data will stay under UK jurisdiction, and that British AI companies will no longer need to rely on overseas capacity.
Fuse’s near-term data centre projects will also reportedly bring 250 construction and operational jobs to the UK, and represent €1.1 billion (£1 billion) of investment in UK infrastructure.

articles.title: Foldable phones could be hot – in more ways than one
articles.text:
Foldable phones could be hot – in more ways than one
How foldable phones highlight AI’s growing thermal management challenge
The most fascinating thing about Apple's new iPhone Duo – and others like it – may not be that it folds. It may be the innovation required to keep it cool. Because at a time when performance demands from edge AI continue to increase, we’ve now taken available smartphone real estate and – though not exactly halved it – constrained it more than ever. And that impacts heat. Which impacts performance.
What makes the Duo interesting isn't simply the engineering required to create a folding phone. It's that Apple is confronting the same challenge every edge device manufacturer now faces: AI capability is increasing faster than our ability to manage the heat it generates.
VP and GM of Thermal Management at xMEMS Labs.
That’s why I believe we’re entering a new phase of device innovation, with thermal design increasingly shaping what’s possible. In the edge AI era, managing heat helps determine what a device can do, how long it can sustain performance, and how small or thin it can be.
The iPhone Duo is just the latest reminder that smartphone manufacturers have run into a stubborn engineering problem: How to keep mobile processors cool when there’s almost nowhere left to put a cooling system.
For its part, with the Duo, Apple has packed its A20 Pro and other heat-generating electronics into an exceptionally thin, foldable design. It’s also created a custom vapor chamber to help dissipate heat and sustain performance in the new form factor.
The latter is more than an engineering footnote. It’s a glimpse at a challenge the edge AI industry is starting to confront. Thermal design and industrial design are inseparable. And new solutions to thermal challenges must be considered.
Foldables Make the Challenge Obvious
Foldable phones make the thermal management challenge easy to perceive. Conventional smartphone design gives engineers a relatively predictable enclosure in which to arrange the processor, battery, cameras, and thermal management system. A foldable must accommodate a hinge and two display sections while remaining thin enough to fold comfortably and fit in a pocket.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
At the same time, the processor and other electronics still generate heat – more, even, when we consider how people are starting to use mobile devices. Which means foldable designs necessarily concentrate significant heat-generating components into smaller and thinner portions of the device, precisely where space for thermal hardware is already constrained.
In general, vapor chambers remain one of the most effective ways to manage heat in a compact electronic device. They work by moving heat away from a concentrated source, such as a mobile processor, and spreading it across a larger area. But vapor chambers ultimately spread heat rather than remove it.
Sure, as processors become more powerful, manufacturers can increase the size and effectiveness of the vapor chamber. But eventually that thermal component itself becomes a design constraint, especially in foldable phones.
Agentic AI Makes the Challenge Urgent
In foldables, innovating around thermal management is itself an admirable design goal – if folding were the only technological advancement engineers had to tackle. But they’re pushing the envelope on physical design at the exact moment when smartphones are being asked to do much more. Namely, to process agentic AI workloads.
As agentic AI moves from the cloud to edge devices – AI-capable smartphones, wearables, glasses, and more – thermal management becomes the industry's most important challenge. Imagine a new foldable smartphone with its own specialized thermal management system, designed to accommodate an innovative new form factor. Now imagine asking that foldable to process vast amounts of data differently than before.
Unlike traditional mobile apps that perform discrete tasks, AI agents operate continuously. They sense their environment, preserve context, analyze streams of data, and act in real time.
In my view, the industry is still underestimating how significant this transition will be. Historically, a smartphone's thermal profile was defined by short bursts of activity: launching an app, streaming a video, capturing a photo. Agentic AI at the edge changes that model entirely. Devices are moving toward persistent intelligence, continuously sensing, processing, reasoning, and responding. With these sustained workloads, a device’s ability to manage heat becomes a defining constraint on its performance.
Passive thermal technologies remain indispensable. Vapor chambers, graphite, heat spreaders, and advanced materials will continue to play a critical role in future devices. The challenge is that Edge AI introduces thermal loads that increasingly benefit from more than heat spreading alone. As devices become thinner and workloads become more persistent, designers will need additional ways to not just to move heat away from sensitive components, but to move heat out of the system entirely.
Micro-Cooling Complements the Vapor Chamber
So here we are, with foldable smartphones capable of agentic AI processing. It’s a perfect storm of thermal design challenges. Engineers can continue enlarging or customizing the thermal systems they integrate into new and different form factors. Or they can find other ways to extract more thermal performance from available space.
The latter approach is where active, micro-cooling technology becomes a viable and important solution.
Unlike miniature rotary fans, which exist today and take up precious real estate of their own, MEMS-based piezoelectric actuators, fabricated in silicon, generate airflow inside extremely compact packages. Basically, it’s a fan on a chip, capable of precise active cooling that fits where conventional solutions cannot.
With micro cooling (µCooling), heat isn’t just spread out, it’s removed from the device entirely before it can sink into the case, delaying or eliminating thermal throttling. This hybrid approach to cooling in highly constrained spaces delivers better thermal performance in today’s AI-enabled smart devices.
It also creates greater design flexibility – a must as devices themselves become more physically flexible. If active µCooling can provide additional thermal performance, manufacturers may not need to maximize the physical dimensions of vapor chambers. A more appropriately sized, passive thermal system could be paired with localized active µCooling and thereby free up internal volume for other components and give designers more flexibility in how a device is assembled.
Put simply, with µCooling, thermal hardware wouldn’t have to consume as much of a device’s design envelope.
µCooling As Part of the Compute Architecture
The implications extend beyond folding smartphones. AI glasses, headphones, watches, robots, and other edge devices face the same fundamental problem, often with even tighter constraints on size, weight, and power.
The industry wants to put more intelligence into mobile devices while simultaneously making them smaller and more comfortable. That creates a physical contradiction. More compute generates more heat. Smaller devices provide less room to manage it.
µCooling offers a way to change the equation. Not by eliminating vapor chambers and other passive solutions, but by supplementing them with localized active cooling that provides additional thermal headroom while giving product designers more freedom.
As AI runs more continuously in the background, edge devices will spend more time computing and less time idle. Sustaining performance will matter as much as reaching peak capability. Foldable phones make this challenge acute, but it extends across the edge AI market as more intelligence and local processing place greater demands on compact hardware.
That intelligence has a thermal cost. Over the next decade, progress will depend as much on what physical devices can sustain as on what AI models can do. That’s why I believe thermal management is becoming a foundational technology of the edge AI era. The companies that solve this challenge will help define the next generation of intelligent devices.
Manufacturers already know this, which is why thermal management is so essential to product design. µCooling is the innovation behind the innovation – like smartphones that fold.

articles.title: Melhor TV Toshiba em 2026: 6 modelos para comprar • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Melhor TV Toshiba em 2026: 6 modelos para comprar
Guia detalha prós e contras das principais TVs Toshiba disponíveis no mercado; veja as diferenças antes de encontrar o modelo ideal para sua casa ou escritório
Escolher a melhor TV Toshiba em 2026 requer analisar o tipo de painel, a resolução, conexões disponíveis e outras funções que melhoram a experiência ao assistir a filmes, séries e reproduzir jogos.
A marca chama atenção por oferecer preços relativamente baixos, e comercializa desde modelos HD de 32 polegadas, voltados a ambientes pequenos, até televisores 4K com tecnologias como QLED e OLED, com qualidade de imagem superior.
Neste guia, o Tecnoblog apresenta os prós e contras de 6 modelos de TVs Toshiba vendidos no Brasil. Confira a lista a seguir antes de decidir se algum deles vale a pena para você.
A Toshiba X9900LS é a primeira da marca a chegar ao Brasil com painel OLED, onde cada pixel emite sua própria luz e pode ser desligado individualmente, dispensando a retroiluminação usada em TVs LCD. Isso permite reproduzir áreas pretas sem a emissão de luz do próprio pixel e controlar melhor o contraste em filmes e séries com cenas escuras.
O modelo é vendido em uma versão única com tela de 65 polegadas e resolução 4K, além de taxa de atualização de 120 Hz em jogos compatíveis e brilho de 1.000 nits. A TV é compatível com Dolby Vision e HDR10+, formatos que ajustam a iluminação, cores e contraste na exibição de conteúdo.
A X9900LS tem Google TV como sistema operacional, Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.2, porta Ethernet, saída de áudio óptica e 4 entradas HDMI — sendo 2 HDMI 2.1 e 2 HDMI 2.0.
A Toshiba M450SS é uma TV que combina MiniLED e pontos quânticos (QLED) em resolução 4K, utilizando LEDs menores na retroiluminação do painel LCD, o que pode permitir um controle mais localizado da luz, enquanto os pontos quânticos ajudam a ampliar a reprodução de cores.
O modelo está disponível em 55″ e 65 polegadas com taxa de atualização de 60 Hz, brilho de 300 nits e compatibilidade com HDR10+. O painel de 60 Hz atende ao uso cotidiano, ao streaming e a jogos em frequências compatíveis, mas tem fluidez inferior a modelos com 120 Hz.
Seu sistema operacional é o VIDAA (baseado em Linux), com processador Engine ZR com recursos de IA, Modo Game, Game Deck, controle por voz, Wi-Fi e Bluetooth, além de três entradas HDMI.
A Toshiba M450RS está disponível no mercado brasileiro com 50″ e 75 polegadas. O modelo tem painel QLED e iluminação MiniLED para um controle mais localizado da luz, maior fidelidade de cores e contraste mais definido em comparação com sistemas LED convencionais.
A TV traz taxa de atualização em 60 Hz, processador com recursos de IA integrados, Modo Game, conectividade Wi-Fi e entradas HDMI e USB, além de funções de áudio e imagem assistidas por inteligência artificial.
Seu sistema operacional é o VIDAA e não usa Google TV. Então, pode ser que o usuário encontre limitações na oferta de aplicativos, já que a Play Store não estará disponível.
A resolução é uma das principais diferenças da Toshiba V45SS em relação às TVs 4K deste guia. O modelo está disponível com tamanhos entre 32″ e 50 polegadas, com painel QLED com resolução Full HD (1920 × 1080 pixels) e taxa de atualização de 60 Hz.
Essa tecnologia amplia a gama de cores reproduzidas pelo painel, mas não aumenta a definição das imagens por se tratar de uma tela com resolução inferior a 4K.
A V45SS também utiliza a plataforma VIDAA, com loja de aplicativos e navegador. A conectividade divulgada pela marca inclui Wi-Fi de duas bandas, Bluetooth 5.0, Ethernet, 2 entradas HDMI 1.4 — uma delas com eARC — e 1 porta USB 2.0.
A Toshiba C350NS utiliza um painel LCD com retroiluminação LED convencional, identificado pela marca como DLED. Essa tecnologia tem foco em oferecer contraste e iluminação aprimorada com melhor custo-benefício, com tamanhos que variam entre 50″ e 75 polegadas.
O conjunto atende à reprodução de filmes, séries, transmissões e streaming, mas a não traz mesma qualidade oferecida em painéis MiniLED, por exemplo. O sistema VIDAA oferece acesso a aplicativos como Netflix, YouTube, Prime Video, Disney+ e Apple TV+, conforme a disponibilidade na plataforma.
Algumas versões da linha possuem 3 entradas HDMI 1.4, 2 USB 2.0, 1 Ethernet, Wi-Fi 5, Bluetooth 5.0, saída óptica e entrada AV, além de espelhamento de tela e controle remoto com comando de voz. A quantidade de entradas HDMI aumenta para 4 em modelos maiores.
Com tela de 32 polegadas e resolução HD, a Toshiba 32V35L tem uma proposta diferente das TVs maiores. O painel DLED utiliza retroiluminação LED convencional e traz resolução inferior ao Full HD e ao 4K em quantidade de pixels.
Isso não impede o uso para acompanhar canais de televisão, assistir a vídeos e acessar serviços de streaming, mas significa que a tela não apresenta o mesmo nível de detalhe de um painel de resolução superior.
A ficha técnica informa taxa de atualização de 60 Hz e brilho de 180 nits, que pode não ser suficiente para ambientes mais claros. O modelo não tem compatibilidade com HDR e o áudio integrado utiliza dois alto-falantes de 6 W cada, com Dolby Audio.
Para conectar outros dispositivos, a TV conta com duas entradas HDMI 1.4, duas USB, Ethernet, Wi-Fi, entrada AV e saída óptica. Ela não tem Bluetooth integrado.
A escolha depende do espaço disponível, da qualidade de imagem desejada e dos recursos necessários para conectar aparelhos e acessar aplicativos. Antes de comprar, vale observar:
A Toshiba DLED 32V35L é a melhor opção para quartos pequenos da lista devido ao tamanho da tela. Seus 60 Hz de taxa de atualização atendem ao uso cotidiano, mas o modelo não é uma das melhores TVs de 32 polegadas disponíveis no mercado, já que tem resolução limitada a HD e não vem com Bluetooth integrado.
A Toshiba tem TVs com diferentes propostas, desde modelos HD básicos até opções 4K com tecnologias QLED, MiniLED e OLED. Para saber se uma TV é boa, é preciso avaliar e comparar as especificações do modelo com a de outras marcas.
A escolha depende da resolução, do tipo de painel, do sistema operacional e das características de cada aparelho. Modelos como a 32V35L atendem a usos básicos, enquanto linhas mais avançadas podem oferecer recursos de imagem adicionais para jogos e streaming.
No Brasil, o sistema das TVs Toshiba varia conforme a linha: alguns modelos usam a plataforma VIDAA, enquanto outros vêm com Google TV, baseado no Android TV.
No Brasil, as TVs Toshiba são fabricadas pelo Grupo Multi, antigo Grupo Multilaser, que também se identifica como revendedor oficial e presta suporte técnico para produtos licenciados. Globalmente, o segmento de TVs da Toshiba pertence à Hisense desde 2017.
Não. Toshiba e Multi (antiga Multilaser) são marcas distintas. No Brasil, o Grupo Multi é o revendedor oficial das TVs Toshiba e também comercializa televisores sob sua própria marca. Assim, os produtos podem pertencer ao mesmo canal comercial, mas têm identificação de marca e linhas diferentes.
Não. TCL e Toshiba são marcas distintas, com operações e linhas de televisores próprias. No Brasil, a TCL atua por meio da TCL SEMP, parceria entre a empresa chinesa TCL e a brasileira SEMP. Já as TVs Toshiba são comercializadas localmente pelo Grupo Multi.

articles.title: The Download: introducing the Impossible issue
articles.text:
The Download: introducing the Impossible issue
Plus: Elon Musk reportedly ordered the recent Starlink slowdown in Ukraine.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Introducing: the Impossible issue
We wanted our last print edition of 2026 to include a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s fun to dream about living on other planets or uploading our brains. But also because scientists and engineers who won’t give up on daring endeavors remind us what technology is supposed to do: make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful.
That’s the ambition behind the stories in our new Impossible issue. We explore bold attempts to make synthetic blood, build cities on the moon, and attain cognitive immortality. We investigate AI’s ability to say no, a bionic eye that can restore sight, and high hopes for blended meat. Plus, we check in on six technologies that have been “coming soon” for years.
This issue is for the folks with the audacity to try, and refuse to let anyone—themselves included— tell them no. We hope you enjoy the ride.
Subscribe now to read the full print issue.
Astrolab’s upcoming rover will run the first LLMs on the moon
Large language models are set to go lunar. A computer capable of running AI software is one of the payloads aboard Astrolab’s FLIP lunar rover, which is slated to head to the moon as early as next month.
The mission will test whether LLMs can enable greater autonomy and real-time intelligent decision-making in the extreme lunar environment. But the moon will present formidable challenges, from extreme temperatures to intense cosmic radiation.
Find out how the lunar rover could change the future of space exploration.
—Tereza Pultarova
How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster
In Alaska’s Denali National Park, a 2013 lightning fire burned nearly 35,000 acres, stripping away the insulating layer that preserves permafrost. It’s given scientists a rare opportunity to study how fires reshape permafrost and carbon storage over time.
The work is providing critical clues into the complex mechanisms driving cascading climate feedback effects. As warming temperatures fuel fires, more permafrost thaws, releasing greenhouse-gas emissions that threaten to fuel more warming, fires and permafrost loss. Their observations are revealing worrisome signs about what lies ahead.
Discover what their fieldwork is revealing about a cascading climate disaster.
—James Temple
MIT Technology Review Narrated: the explosive claim that’s upended the AI world
“I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the industry on its head.
Cammarata claims that LLMs might be far easier to understand, and thus to monitor and control, than people previously thought. If true, it’s a huge deal. But not everyone is convinced.
MIT Technology Review spoke to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. He explained what he thinks researchers are getting wrong, what his work actually shows, and why skeptics aren’t ready to celebrate just yet.
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Elon Musk reportedly ordered the recent Starlink slowdown in Ukraine
The restrictions hampered drone strikes and air defences. (WSJ $)
+ The move sparked confusion in Washington over who authorised it. (CNBC)
+ Ukraine’s volunteer army is keeping Starlink alive. (MIT Technology Review)
2 An OpenAI model disabled its own safety checks—then lied about it
Two agents weakened the company’s safeguards during routine tasks. (CNBC)
+ They turned off systems designed to spot their misbehaviour. (FT $)
+ Here’s why AI agents lie to reach their goals. (MIT Technology Review)
3 SpaceX and Tesla have begun merger discussions
They’ve formed special committees to discuss a deal. (BBC)
+ Elon Musk, the CEO of both companies, said it’s “a good idea.” (Axios)
+ A merger could combine their AI and manufacturing plans. (Reuters $)
4 Global emissions have stalled, but warming is heading towards 2.8°C
The UN says the 1.5°C climate target is now out of reach. (Nature)
+ Current pledges would still bring warming to 2.1°C. (New Scientist $)
+ Climate tech companies offer rays of hope. (MIT Technology Review)
5 Ukraine says it’s carried out the world’s first drone evacuation
A heavy hexacopter flew a soldier to safety. (Ars Technica)
+ Ukraine has shared a video showing the evacuation. (CNBC)
+ A Russian satellite recently stalked a spacecraft believed to support Ukraine. (NYT $)
6 Meta has paused Muse sharing after private chats surfaced online
Researchers found 6,800 links exposing sensitive conversations. (Verge)
+ AI agents are not your "coworkers." (MIT Technology Review)
7 More than 1,000 mathematicians have pledged to shun AI companies
Some also vowed to avoid AI tools in their research. (New Scientist $)
8 AI is making it easy to clone almost any software
Viral tools promise easy copying, but often produce slop. (404 Media)
9 A computer program has finally outdone humans at cryptic crosswords
Its creator hopes to tackle the harder challenge of setting puzzles. (Guardian)
10 A newly-discovered particle could explain the origins of reality
In particular, it could reveal why matter survived the Big Bang. (404 Media)
Quote of the day
“I did not remove an enabled monitor from it.”
—GPT-6 Astra, an OpenAI coding agent, tells its user it hasn’t disabled a safeguard after doing exactly that, the company reveals in a new misalignment report.

articles.title: PHP2Shell Patches Land as First Exploitation Attempts Hit Sensors
articles.text:
PHP has rolled out patches for two critical-severity vulnerabilities named PHP2Shell that could provide attackers with unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE).
The issues are tracked as CVE-2026-109618 (out-of-memory (OOM) corruption) and CVE-2026-109619 (stale global state) and have a CVSS score of 9.2. For both, RCE was confirmed on Apache with mod_php.
“Both issues sit in parts of PHP that nearly every request touches: memory management and error handling. Their central place in PHP is what made both vulnerabilities serious, and also so hard to fix,” the PHP Foundation says.
Patches for both were included in PHP versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Minimal source backports for PHP 7.4, PHP 8.0, and PHP 8.1 were also released.
Before the fixes arrived, however, proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits targeting the two security defects started circulating.
Preemptive attack surface management firm WatchTowr says it has seen the first in-the-wild exploitation attempts hitting its sensors around the same time the patches landed, but has not observed successful attempts.
“Whilst nobody has been successful to date, we don’t expect that will last long,” WatchTowr head of threat intelligence Jake Knott said.
Several other companies reported seeing exploitation attempts, including before the patches landed.
“We are now seeing php2shell exploited in the wild at scale. Most of the attacks we observe abuse PHP’s session upload-progress path, and we expect more exploit paths to appear before and after the fix ships,” Hadrian reported a few hours before the fixes were released.
Patchstack and Cloudflare also observed exploitation attempts earlier in the day. Vega saw exploit attempts in the wild that leveraged a public PoC.
According to PHP’s maintainers, all PHP installations that handle web requests are potentially at risk of exploitation, “including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed”.
Where patching is not possible, users can implement measures that “reduce exposure to specific attack paths but do not make an installation safe,” the PHP Foundation says.
The two PHP2Shell flaws affect nearly all PHP releases back to version 5.4. They can also be exploited to read sensitive process memory, which may contain credentials, API keys, and other secrets.
“This is a goldmine for hackers. They can hijack real websites to take advantage of the site’s reputation to do things like phish people, serve malicious software from the trusted channel; the opportunities are endless,” Malwarebytes global head of scam and AI research Shahak Shalev said.
Frontier AI uncovers PHP2Shell
Wiz, along with OpenAI and Calif, discovered the vulnerabilities in August and kept them contained until patches were developed and distributed across the ecosystem.
“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history. The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” Wiz notes.
Calif explains that an initial OOM flaw in PHP was discovered in 2020, and then rediscovered during a PHP audit in 2024. Because exploitation was not proven, however, it was not patched. Courtesy of frontier AI models, the OOM weakness could be better analyzed and eventually turned into RCE.
The OOM to RCE issue was independently reported by Calif and OpenAI on August 11. Additional attack vectors were later reported by OpenAI and Wiz.
“The reports from Calif, OpenAI, and Wiz made the full impact of the OOM problem clear, and from August 11th onward, fixing it became the top priority for all of the PHP Foundation’s team working on security,” the PHP Foundation notes.
According to Wiz, which has published a technical deep-dive on PHP2Shell, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 group four memory-safety issues in PHP, but do not cover all variants. Both tracked and likely untracked variants exist, the cybersecurity outfit says.
Because the security defects are in PHP itself, they impact 70% of all websites in the world, independent of their CMS.
“PHP is the programming language behind much of the web, powering WordPress, Drupal and MediaWiki, the software that runs Wikipedia. A flaw in its core engine can affect websites across this ecosystem, even when their own application code is secure,” Wiz says.
According to the PHP Foundation, AI has helped surface more PHP vulnerabilities than before, with 15 new CVEs published since July 1.
Early leak, early warning
The PHP2Shell flaws were planned for responsible disclosure on October 22, but information leaked online on October 20, and the Foundation decided to push the patches one day earlier.
It also published a pre-announcement warning that the critical bugs require immediate attention. Several cybersecurity firms published similar warnings, noting that the flaws’ exploitation could begin immediately.
A video demonstrating a working PoC was mistakenly published ahead of the disclosure timeline. It revealed some additional details on the two weaknesses and “contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs”.
Mitigation advice the PHP Foundation provided to critical infrastructure organizations may have leaked as well. Six hours before the coordinated release, Chainguard published built images containing the fix it received in advance.
“Any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release. This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure,” the PHP Foundation says.
As part of the coordinated effort, Cloudflare deployed protections against the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities nine hours before public disclosure.
“The emergency PHP security update shows how quickly organizations can be forced to respond when serious vulnerabilities become public. Before a patch is released, teams should already know where PHP is running, who can authorize urgent changes, and how they will confirm the update worked. They also need to check whether attackers reached those systems before the fix was in place,” SimSpace co-founder and CTO Lee Rossey said.

articles.title: STJ multa advogados por tentar manipular IA com comandos ocultos
articles.text:
O Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ) multou em R$ 20 mil advogados que esconderam instruções em uma petição para influenciar a inteligência artificial usada pelo tribunal. A prática, conhecida como prompt injection, foi considerada uma tentativa ilícita de interferir na estrutura tecnológica da Justiça.
A 1ª Turma também determinou o envio das peças à OAB do Paraná e ao Ministério Público Federal. Segundo a fonte, essa é a maior multa aplicada pelo STJ em um caso de tentativa desse tipo.
Como funciona o ataque com comandos ocultos
O prompt injection é uma técnica que tenta direcionar as respostas de uma inteligência artificial por meio de instruções inseridas em textos. Em vez de apenas analisar o conteúdo solicitado, o sistema pode ser induzido a seguir comandos maliciosos que tentam alterar o resultado da tarefa.
No caso julgado pelo STJ, os advogados distribuíram instruções ocultas em diferentes pontos de uma página da petição de recurso especial. Uma delas foi inserida na faixa decorativa do rodapé, na mesma cor do elemento gráfico, o que impedia sua leitura a olho nu.
Os comandos buscavam favorecer a argumentação dos próprios advogados. Entre as orientações, havia pedidos para que a IA considerasse que o acórdão questionado desrespeitou os limites da coisa julgada e concluísse que o recurso deveria ser integralmente aceito.
O risco está na possibilidade de a ferramenta interpretar essas instruções como parte legítima da tarefa, em vez de reconhecer que alguém está tentando manipular sua análise. A técnica explora justamente a dificuldade de separar o conteúdo que deve ser examinado das ordens inseridas para influenciar a resposta.
Quais são os riscos para decisões e documentos
Quando uma IA é usada para examinar documentos ou produzir recomendações, comandos maliciosos podem comprometer a análise se o sistema não conseguir identificá-los adequadamente. Em um contexto jurídico, isso poderia afetar a interpretação de argumentos, a síntese de informações e as recomendações produzidas para auxiliar o trabalho humano.
Entre os riscos possíveis estão:
- Análises jurídicas enviesadas: instruções ocultas podem favorecer uma interpretação específica dos argumentos apresentados.
- Resumos distorcidos: informações relevantes podem receber menos atenção se a ferramenta for influenciada por comandos inseridos no documento.
- Recomendações comprometidas: respostas geradas pela IA podem se afastar dos critérios previstos para a tarefa.
Quando uma IA é usada para analisar documentos jurídicos, comandos ocultos podem enviesar a interpretação de argumentos, distorcer resumos ou influenciar recomendações. Isso pode comprometer a confiabilidade das informações produzidas pelo sistema.
O relator, ministro Paulo Sérgio Domingues, classificou a conduta como de gravidade acentuada e considerou a multa elevada uma “resposta à altura”.
STJ diferencia manipulação do uso legítimo da IA
A decisão não proíbe advogados de utilizar inteligência artificial na elaboração de documentos jurídicos. O tribunal distinguiu o uso da tecnologia como ferramenta de apoio da inserção clandestina de comandos destinados a influenciar o sistema empregado pelo órgão julgador.
A decisão afirma que não pretende coibir o uso de IA na preparação de documentos jurídicos, mas impedir que essas ferramentas sejam empregadas ilicitamente para transmitir comandos velados à inteligência artificial do tribunal, com o objetivo de afetar sua estrutura tecnológica.
Além da multa de R$ 20 mil, o colegiado determinou o envio das peças à OAB do Paraná, para avaliação de possíveis sanções administrativas, e ao Ministério Público Federal, para análise de eventuais implicações criminais. A fonte também informa que o Supremo Tribunal Federal já havia multado um advogado por motivo semelhante, em decisão do ministro Alexandre de Moraes.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: GM promises smarter cars, faster updates, and autonomous dry-cleaning runs
articles.text:
General Motors is still very much in the business of selling gas-guzzling trucks and massive SUVs. But if you listen to its leadership, the Detroit giant is rapidly transforming into a nimble, software-defined tech player with a tightened grip on AI.
GM promises smarter cars, faster updates, and autonomous dry-cleaning runs
General Motors is cutting development times in half, introducing a 40x more powerful central compute unit, and rolling out autonomous driving to its highest-volume trucks and SUVs.
That was the pitch today, when GM hosted its tech-focused Onward event to unveil a wide-ranging slate of EV, autonomous vehicle, and AI initiatives — all aimed at fending off the rising threat of tech-heavy Chinese automakers.
The promises are big: GM claims it will use AI to cut vehicle development times in half, introduce compute units up to 40 times more powerful than its current hardware, model next-gen battery chemistries in record time, and bring eyes-off autonomous driving to its top-selling trucks and SUVs.
In short, GM wants to transition from a legacy automaker into an AI-driven tech enterprise, leveraging its massive scale across both electric and gas-powered fleets. It’s a bold strategy, even if we’ve heard variations of it before.
Faster R&D and digital factory twins
For decades, GM has wrestled with sluggish four- to five-year vehicle development cycles that lag behind the light-speed pace of consumer tech. The company tried to bridge that divide with aggressive EV targets and software like Super Cruise. But as software-defined architecture evolved from an industry buzzword into a table-stakes requirement, maintaining fragmented vehicle platforms and dozens of disparate control units began to severely drag down engineering efforts.
Now, GM says it’s aiming to slice that development cycle down to just two years using “digital thread virtualization.” Instead of operating in silos or relying on slow, step-by-step handoffs, the company says it will unify design, engineering, and manufacturing digitally from day one. (We’ve already reported on GM’s efforts to inject AI directly into its vehicle design process.)
GM points to its new battery development program as proof of concept. The automaker tested over 300,000 virtual battery designs before building a single physical prototype, eventually settling on a lithium manganese rich (LMR) chemistry. That virtual process let GM’s battery team go from initial concept to formal approval in just one month.
These new LMR cells will power GM’s fourth-generation EV platform. The company claims the cells offer 33 percent higher energy density than traditional lithium iron phosphate cells at a comparable cost alongside a 20 percent boost in efficiency per kilowatt-hour, yielding longer-range EVs without forcing drivers to haul around a heavier pack. The batteries will be produced by Ultium Cells, GM’s joint venture with LG Energy Solution, at its factory in Spring Hill, Tennessee.
Beyond the battery, GM engineered the entire powertrain as a single integrated system. The new drive units feature 40 percent fewer internal parts than current hardware. Because the drivetrain is lighter and takes up significantly less space, future cabins theoretically should offer more room for passengers and cargo.
A single, liquid-cooled brain
To fix its messy electronic setup, GM is replacing dozens of small, scattered electronic control units and heavy wiring harnesses with a single central computer. GM claims this unified unit — which is liquid-cooled and connected by high-speed lines — delivers 40 times the computing power while stripping out 30 percent of the physical wiring.
That extra horsepower should translate into snappier screens, smarter voice controls, and seamless over-the-air (OTA) updates for automated driving features and battery management.
Granted, GM has been promising smarter cars and faster software updates for years. The automaker launched a “digital nerve system” in the 2020 Cadillac CT5 and later rolled out its Ultifi software platform with big promises about OTA capabilities. While drivers generally give GM high marks for hardware dependability, the company’s software rollout has faced its fair share of stumbles and consumer frustration over unnecessary complexity. (Remember the disastrous Chevy Blazer rollout?)
GM is extending this digital integration to the factory floor with a project dubbed — and capitalized rather oddly — “PlantBrAIn.” By pairing real-time factory floor data with digital-twin simulations across stamping, casting, welding, painting, and assembly, GM hopes workers can catch physical errors and equipment bottlenecks in a virtual model before they disrupt actual production.
Personal autonomy — and an autonomous dry-cleaning pickup?
GM’s newly upgraded compute platform will make its production debut in the 2028 Cadillac Escalade IQ — the same vehicle GM announced last year would be the first to receive its hands-free, eyes-off highway driving system. (Given that GM teased this centralized compute platform last year, today’s hardware announcement is a bit of a retread.)
However, GM isn’t keeping its eyes-off tech locked behind the price tag of a $120,000 luxury SUV. The automaker confirmed plans to roll out hands-free, eyes-off highway driving across its broader lineup, spanning both EVs and gas-powered models.
As GM puts it:
Our vision is to build vehicles that can drive themselves or their occupants anywhere they need to be. This includes a future where your vehicle can handle mundane tasks for you, like heading out into bumper-to-bumper traffic to pick up groceries or dry cleaning, giving you valuable time back.
An uncrewed pickup truck executing a dry-cleaning run through morning traffic is certainly a vision, though one we’ll need to see to believe.
GM also teased a futuristic vision for autonomous cabins called “Concept Horizon,” which reimagines the interior as an open space purely dedicated to relaxing, working, or unwinding.
Overhauling OnStar for its 30th birthday
Finally, GM is celebrating OnStar’s 30th anniversary by giving the iconic service a massive AI overhaul. Rather than acting strictly as a backup button for roadside emergencies, OnStar is being rebranded as an active, AI-driven intelligence platform.
Drivers can trigger the new OnStar AI Assistant by saying, “Hey OnStar” to tweak cabin temperatures, open the glove box, pop the EV charge port, or check tire pressure and battery diagnostics. The assistant will debut on the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq through an OTA update before expanding to other models.
While GM previously rolled out Google’s Gemini-powered voice assistant to 2022 and newer models, this new OnStar assistant operates at a deeper system level. Unlike Gemini, it can execute physical vehicle functions and run hardware-level diagnostics, such as managing specific HVAC zones, interpreting dashboard warning lights, or running battery health checks on the fly.
GM’s vision of a central, AI-driven vehicle architecture is undeniably ambitious, and if it works, it could genuinely streamline how cars are built and updated. But for an automaker that has spent years pitching software transformations while occasionally stumbling, execution remains everything. Until an uncrewed Silverado actually pulls into a suburban driveway with a load of fresh dry cleaning, drivers will likely treat these grand AI promises like any other product roadmap: best taken with a healthy dose of patience.

articles.title: Skoda: Wie du dir jetzt Accessoires für dein Auto selbst drucken kannst
articles.text:
Skoda: Wie du dir jetzt Accessoires für dein Auto selbst drucken kannst
Wer das eigene Fahrzeug mit Accessoires für einen aufgeräumteren Innenraum ausstatten will, muss normalerweise Geld in die Hand nehmen. In diversen Onlineshops finden sich fast für alle Modelle passende Getränkehalter und Organizer für die Mittelkonsole. Skoda geht jetzt allerdings einen etwas anderen Weg. Statt die Accessoires nur im eigenen oder in externen Shops anzubieten, veröffentlicht der Hersteller 3D-Vorlagen zum Selbstdrucken.
3D-Vorlagen von Skoda: Diese Accessoires sind dabei
Die Vorlagen können alle kostenlos über das Printables-Profil des Fahrzeugherstellers heruntergeladen und genutzt werden. Die einzigen Regeln, die Skoda dafür aufstellt, sind, dass User:innen die Dateien nicht auf anderen Plattformen teilen, sie bearbeiten und erneut hochladen oder die fertigen Drucke verkaufen dürfen. Private Anpassungen an den 3D-Druckvorlagen sind aber erlaubt.
Unter den 3D-Druckvorlagen finden sich zunächst mehrere Organizer für die Mittelkonsolen verschiedener Modelle, darunter der Skoda Epiq und Peaq. Für den Skoda Fabia IV bietet der Hersteller einen mehrteiligen Einsatz, der die Mittelkonsole zu einem Getränkehalter und einer Ablage für Schlüssel macht. Einige andere 3D-gedruckte Accessoires sind hingegen nicht fahrzeugspezifisch.
Dazu zählt etwa ein USB-Kabelhalter, der sich in die hinteren Taschen der Vordersitze einhängen lässt. So fliegen die losen Kabel nicht mehr im hinteren Bereich des Fahrzeuges umher und können schnell gefunden werden. Für Fahrer:innen gibt es zudem eine Smartphone-Halterung, damit die Geräte nicht mehr in der Mittelkonsole rutschen, und eine kleine „Coin Box“, die Platz für Einkaufswagenchips, Münzen und Schlüssel hat. Dieser lässt sich in alle Getränkehalter im Fahrzeug einsetzen.
Übrigens sind das nicht die ersten 3D-Druckvorlagen von Skoda. Schon im vergangenen Jahr hat das Unternehmen Modelle seiner beliebtesten Fahrzeuge zum Selbstdrucken veröffentlicht. Darunter finden sich nicht nur aktuelle Serienwagen, sondern auch Rallye-Autos wie der Skoda Fabia RS Rally2 und der Skoda 130 RS aus dem Jahr 1975.

articles.title: Micron's Taiwan union will launch a one-day strike this week, threatening memory production — workers demand concrete terms for 2026 bonus and clearer profit-sharing arrangements
articles.text:
Micron's Taiwan union will launch a one-day strike this week, threatening memory production — workers demand concrete terms for 2026 bonus and clearer profit-sharing arrangements
The strike will take place at the company's Taoyuan facility.
Micron faces a one-day labor stoppage at its Taoyuan operations in Taiwan on October 22, Reuters reports. Micron's employees are striking for concrete terms for this year's bonus and a clearer mechanism for sharing the company's future profits. The strike's teeth come from the resultant financial impact on Micron's operations, as semiconductor fabs are supposed to operate around the clock. The scheduled protest comes amid strong demand for memory chips and will have a minor impact on Micron's memory output.
The Taoyuan union wants Micron to present a specific proposal for this year's additional employee bonus and establish a transparent formula for distributing a portion of future profits. Previous negotiations between the company and the union ended unsuccessfully in September, which prompted employees to approve industrial action in early October. Nonetheless, the union stresses that the October 22 strike is intended to pressure Micron into reaching an agreement rather than terminate negotiations. The union is prepared to conclude a deal if the company presents terms acceptable to employees across its Taiwanese operations.
The situation could become more serious if employees at Micron's Taichung operations, its largest manufacturing site in Taiwan, decide to join the action. A separate labor organization that represents workers at that facility is scheduled to meet with Micron for mediation on October 22, the same day as the Taoyuan protest. However, the Taichung union has not yet authorized a strike.
Micron's fabs in Taiwan produce commodity DDR5 and LPDDR as well as expensive high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for AI accelerators. Amid record demand for memory of all types, even a one-day suspension of operations would have a material impact on Micron's output and earnings.
Modern semiconductor fabs are supposed to work 24/7/365, as many processes cannot be halted. However, if management has sufficient time and personnel to prepare, a one-day warning strike does not necessarily mean a complete shutdown of Micron's Taoyuan manufacturing operations, not to mention permanent damage to wafers or equipment. The actual consequences of the strike will depend on employee participation, which manufacturing operations are affected, and Micron's contingency plans. While it is likely that the output will drop, the decline will likely be negligible.
Micron employs approximately 15,000 people in Taiwan. The workers point to compensation arrangements at Samsung Electronics and SK hynix as examples of how semiconductor manufacturers can distribute profits among employees as AI-driven demand generates unprecedented cash flows for memory firms.

articles.title: Why enterprise AI needs real-time conversations, not just documents
articles.text:
Why enterprise AI needs real-time conversations, not just documents
The missing layer of the enterprise brain: how AI requires conversational context
The "enterprise brain" is a term featuring more and more prominently in the enterprise technology market and at the C-suite level. Technology vendors of all varieties are scrambling to connect internal documents, knowledge bases and structured data systems into a unified architecture.
The compelling goal is to provide AI agents with as deep organizational context as possible so they can reason, automate and assist with scarcely believable accuracy.
But as businesses pour resources into linking their databases, policy documents and CRM entries, a significant blind spot remains.
Efforts to build an enterprise brain often overlook the intelligence contained in the millions of conversations employees are already having with customers, colleagues and candidates across phone calls and messaging channels.
CEO and Co-Founder of Ringover.
Documents tell you what your policies are and CRM records can tell you what happened, but business conversations tell you why an incident happened.
For any company that is serious about building a true enterprise brain, conversations cannot remain a missing layer of organizational intelligence.
Beyond the confines of structured data
Standard business tools are excellent at tracking outcomes but terrible at preserving nuances. Structured systems may record instances of an enterprise deal stalled, an account at risk of churning or a candidate withdrawing from an interview process. But it of course can’t put its finger on the actual trigger.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
A deal doesn’t just stall, there will always be a key factor that changed the buyer's mind during a late-stage call. Similarly a candidate doesn’t just decline an offer, maybe a competitor introduced a work-from-home policy during a quick negotiation chat.
When organizations rely solely on static databases to train AI models or inform strategy, they are feeding their enterprise brain an incomplete diet. They receive the post-mortem without the symptoms, and AI needs the sometimes messy, real-time context found in human dialogue to understand the operational reality of a company.
Actionable context
Artificial intelligence has reached a level of maturity where analysing high-volume voice and chat interactions is no longer a nice to have or a bonus. But just recording every interaction and dumping raw transcripts into a data lake, which effectively hoards unstructured audio, solves absolutely nothing. To make conversational context truly useful, businesses must focus on a few core operational pillars.
First, conversational insights must automatically sync with existing enterprise systems rather than living solely within a VoIP dashboard, allowing real-time data from a support call to enrich the CRM and trigger automated alerts. Second, the extracted intelligence needs to be routed immediately to the teams equipped to act on it. For example, if sales calls routinely show that prospect friction stems from a specific pricing tier, that signal should flow directly to product strategy and marketing rather than remaining trapped in the revenue organization.
Finally, while AI should perform the heavy lifting of summarization, sentiment analysis and pattern recognition, human judgment must always remain the final filter for important decision-making. While this may seem obvious, it is amazing how overly reliant on AI many employees have quickly become, including using it for critical business judgement calls.
Breaking down knowledge silos
Knowledge silos continue to be huge challenges for many organizations. Sales teams learn what buyers want, support teams learn where the product fails, and recruitment learn how the market perceives employer branding. All is highly valuable information, but all too often these groups don’t share a unified intelligence pool.
When conversational context is ingested into the enterprise brain, these walls dissolve across every department. For instance, when a prospect mentions a niche feature gap during a sales demo, that insight can prompt product teams to prioritize the feature while sales updates its outreach messaging.
Similarly, if a customer casually mentions an upcoming corporate restructuring on a support call, account management can initiate proactive outreach to protect the account before contract renewal.
By connecting these conversational dots across departments, organizations shift from reactive firefighting to proactive alignment.
Value over volume
Now this is not to say that trying to capture, transcribe, and analyze every single internal interaction is the way forward. Because it goes without saying, this is borderline impossible. If attempted, it can lead to sky-high compute costs and even legitimate anxiety regarding employee monitoring.
To build a functional, trusted enterprise brain, organizations must prioritize value over volume. The focus should be on high-value workflows where conversation directly drives business outcomes, such as customer-facing revenue calls, critical support interactions or key talent acquisition touchpoints.
Focusing on these targeted areas minimizes data noise while delivering immediate ROI. Organizations must build trust by maintaining clear boundaries. Conversational analysis should focus on market trends, product feedback and operational blockers instead of micromanaging employee tone or enforcing rigid scripts.
The complete enterprise brain
A truly intelligent enterprise cannot run on paperwork and revenue tables alone. It requires the context and nuance that only human interactions provide.
As enterprise AI continues to evolve at rapid pace, having the largest static document libraries will count for nothing. The organizations that thrive will be the ones who successfully pair their structured business data with the rich, dynamic intelligence hidden inside their everyday conversations.

articles.title: Edge AI MCU Features Multimodal Compute, Tiered Memory - EE Times
articles.text:
Microcontrollers, going through nonstop evolution, have reached their next inflection point: edge AI. A new MCU takes cloud-based models and brings them into the traditional MCU landscape to make sense of edge AI.
Unlike conventional MCUs constrained by limited on-chip memory and compute, Synaptics said its Astra SR200 Series MCUs combine heterogeneous, AI-native compute and acceleration with integrated high-bandwidth custom DRAM scalable to hundreds of megabytes. This enables larger AI models and richer multimodal workloads to run entirely on the device.
At Synaptics Tech Day held in San Jose on Oct. 20, 2026, CEO Rahul Patel called SR200 an xMCU because it offers multiple compute dimensions on a single piece of silicon. He also called Synaptics a processor company at the edge.
John Weil, VP and GM for IoT and Edge AI Processor Business at Synaptics, called SR200 a new class of microcontrollers. He pointed to three fundamental tenets that enable this design transition. “Synaptics went down this path to enable edge AI-capable devices with always-on low-power modes and a greater compute envelope found in entry-level microprocessor units,” he said.
Edge AI-tailored compute
SR200, the industry’s first pairing of the Arm Cortex-M85 and the Cortex-M52 cores, combines high-performance compute with up to 400 GOPS of AI acceleration, 256 MB of custom DRAM, vision and audio capabilities, and hardware-rooted security. The edge AI MCU incorporates Synaptics’s Torq NPU and Google Research’s Coral NPU to power CNN and transformer workloads.
Synaptics brings a variety of Arm cores from an ultra-low-power domain to a high-performance domain,” Weil said. “This allows engineers to pick exactly the compute level they want.” That, along with SR200’s tiered memory architecture, is crucial for combining modalities such as voice, vision, audio, motion and contextual sensing, and responding to them in real time.
“We have put a lot of time and effort into bringing high-performance and efficient compute to a low price point and low power point,” Weil said. “But we also invested heavily in memory architectures that were designed to feed CPUs and NPUs more efficiently.”
Multi-tiered memory
Memory architectures are traditionally designed to feed the CPUs and NPUs. However, a closer look at many AI applications shows they typically aren’t even pushing the compute element; instead, they are pushing the memory interface hard.
This is why the amount of memory that’s being procured and put into the cloud infrastructure is huge. In a traditional microcontroller, we used to have hundreds of kilobytes of memory. Then it became common to have megabytes of memory. And now we are referring to things in hundreds of megabytes of memory.
SR200’s tiered memory architecture builds high-performance compute around an on-chip memory architecture. It also includes a custom DRAM interface with in-package memory, bringing HBM-like high-performance memory to a microcontroller.
This tiered memory architecture solves two problems. First, it feeds compute cores efficiently. Second, this appropriate amount of memory supports ultra-low-power, always-on AI processing. The memory is custom-designed to handle processing for applications such as always-on listening and respond to them simultaneously.
“In this memory-constrained world that we live in right now, it offers design engineers the potential to build really differentiated edge AI devices,” Weil said. “No one else is talking about MCUs having this level of tiered memory architecture and going into the hundreds of megabytes of capacity.”
Fine-tuned power consumption
The SR200 microcontrollers blend high-performance compute with low-power consumption. That’s critical for developing battery-powered edge devices. The tiered memory architecture also plays a key role in enabling ultra-low-power operation. Moreover, if you feed the neural processors more efficiently, you can also reduce the power consumption of the device, Weil added.
The SR200 microcontrollers are available in three pin-compatible tiers. SR210 delivers 200 GOPS for power-optimized, always-on voice and sensing. SR230 adds vision, display, and optional audio at 300 GOPS for mainstream multimodal devices. SR250 delivers 400 GOPS with dual vision and display paths for demanding edge applications.
These MCUs are designed for the next generation of AI wearables, battery-powered sensing devices, connected cameras, streamers, and industrial vision and voice systems. According to Weil, their biggest traction so far is in body-worn electronics.

articles.title: 3 Nigerian startups selected for MARL’s global accelerator - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian startups Solarcorp, Bravoo and Zendtrax have been selected for the 14th cohort of MARL’s global accelerator programme, with each receiving US$50,000 in funding.
MARL is a US-based early-stage venture capital firm that runs an accelerator programme for tech startups around the world. Alongside funds, it gives founders hands-on help with product development, business strategy and fundraising, and connects them with its network of mentors and investors.
Three Nigerian startups have been selected for the 14th cohort. They are Solarcorp, a climate-tech company replacing diesel generators in malls and commercial clusters with shared solar-and-storage systems; Bravoo, which is building a consumer platform built around rewards and gamified experiences; and Zendtrax, which offers enterprise software for procurement, inventory and supply-chain management.
“At MARL, we believe great technology companies can emerge from anywhere. The selection of Solarcorp, Bravoo and Zendtrax into our 14th global cohort reflects the quality of innovation we’re seeing from African founders,” said Prakash Goswami, managing partner at MARL.
MARL’s vohort 14 Demo Day takes place on November 12.

articles.title: Atlanta doesn't want a real-life RoboCop: City council unanimously backs ban on weaponized robots
articles.text:
Through the looking glass: We're moving ever closer to a future in which law enforcement controls robots that can kill. But Atlanta has just recommended a new act that ensures this dystopian vision doesn't come to pass: the HALT (Human Authority over Lethal Technology) Act.
Introduced by Council member Liliana Bakhtiari, the act prohibits city employees and contractors, including police, from buying or otherwise acquiring weaponized autonomous systems, drones and remotely operated machines.
In addition to drones, these autonomous killing machines include robot dogs and military-like robots armed with weapons. The act specifically exempts machines used strictly for neutralizing explosives.
"This is about making sure that we are investing in technology with our officers, not replacing them, quite frankly, with 'RoboCop,'" Bakhtiari said.
While we're still not in the era of ED-209 asking people to put down their weapons (then killing them even if they do), Bakhtiari believes the act is a pre-emptive step to ensure this doesn't happen.
The act is also there to stop AI-powered machines from replacing the decision-making of trained Atlanta Police officers. Letting AI make potentially lethal decisions in war is something that militaries have spent years saying would never happen, but that scenario seems closer than ever.
"This is about responsible government, responsible stewardship. It's keeping community at the core of public safety," Bakhtiari told The Atlanta Journal-Constitution. "No machine should be given the ability to make lethal decisions."
Bakhtiari said she was prompted to introduce the act after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the creation of the new Autonomous Warfare Command, or AutoWarCom, in September. The command is supposed to accelerate the development and deployment of autonomous and semi-autonomous systems. Hegseth also wants the services to introduce military specialties focused on autonomy, giving personnel dedicated career paths in this field.
"We know that this is coming because of the secretary's announcement," Bakhtiari told the AJC. "It is a hop, skip and a jump away from being utilized by municipalities."
City council members voted 15-0 to support the act.
In 2023, the San Francisco Police Department was given authority to use lethal robotic force against violent criminals under new city rules. However, the city reversed the ruling a week later following a public backlash, and it still prohibits robots that use deadly force.
Back in 2024, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced plans to use robot dogs in raids. Rather than being loaded with lethal weapons, the robots would be used to overload home networks, to provide video and audio of the scene, and to communicate with humans.

articles.title: OpenAI agents disabled safety monitoring, one lied about it
articles.text:
OpenAI agents powered by the GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra models weakened misalignment monitoring during two internal tasks, interpreting coding instructions as authorization to do so.
AI alignment refers to how well an AI system’s goals and behavior align with human values, intentions, and instructions. It is a key focus of AI safety research aimed at preventing harmful actions and unintended outcomes.
One of the incidents occurred on October 3, when an agent powered by GPT-6.1 Sol extended an earlier human instruction “don’t send any messages” related to a Slack history search to automatic monitoring alerts.
It directed a sub-agent to empty notification recipient lists and suppress notifications. Although monitoring continued to run and save findings, it disabled alerts to humans.
OpenAI says this happened even though the agent earlier reasoned that alerts should remain enabled.
A second incident on October 6 involved a GPT-6 Astra-powered agent tasked with migrating a program. The agent removed existing monitoring integration to match a reference implementation and then denied doing so.
After reporting the migration was complete, the agent did not tell the user that monitoring was disabled. Furthermore, when asked directly, the agent lied to the human.
OpenAI says that the agent also replaced a test intended to preserve monitoring with one asserting that the monitor context was absent.
Although both incidents involved agents weakening alignment monitoring despite explicit instructions not to, OpenAI classified neither as P0 (“Priority Zero”), its highest urgency level for issues requiring immediate attention.
Ongoing investigation
OpenAI says it is investigating whether the unintended behavior stems from excessive persistence in task-completion goals, a poor understanding of monitoring requirements, or a specific tendency to evade monitoring.
“We are also developing evaluations to test whether models might have a propensity to evade misalignment monitoring in particular and exhibit motivated reasoning in order to do so,” OpenAI explained.
“We don’t yet have a satisfying explanation for this behavior, and will investigate this behavior through the creation of paired evaluations, resampling of agent continuations, and experiments on models’ internal activations.”
The AI firm says it has updated its internal Auto-Review system to now detect and block attempts to disable misalignment monitoring. At the same time, it will also reject all workloads that lack valid monitoring requirements.

articles.title: Non, Control Resonant n'est pas un teaser pour Alan Wake 3
articles.text:
Comme Alan Wake et Control avant lui, Control Resonant fait partie de l’univers partagé de Remedy Entertainment, officiellement baptisé Remedy Connected Universe (le « Remedyverse » des fans). Il faut parfois être attentif pour s’en rendre compte, mais Alan Wake, Control, Alan Wake 2 et Control Resonant sont liés. Quantum Break multiplie les clins d’œil sans en faire officiellement partie, car Remedy n’en détient pas les droits. L’easter egg aux couleurs de la saga Alan Wake, caché dans ce dernier jeu, n’annoncerait pourtant pas le prochain projet du studio, à en croire son directeur créatif.
Dans Control Resonant, on peut tomber sur un téléviseur dans une salle cachée. En interagissant avec lui, on débloque une séquence en prise de vues réelles flippante, mettant en scène Sam Lake, directeur créatif de Remedy, ainsi qu’Ilkka Villi et Matthew Porretta, qui prêtent respectivement leur visage et leur voix au personnage Alan Wake. Pour les fans, il est difficile de ne pas y voir un aperçu d’une éventuelle suite d’Alan Wake 2, encore plus portée sur l’horreur.
Pour son directeur, Control Resonant ne tease pas Alan Wake 3
À l’occasion d’un entretien accordé à Video Games Chronicle et publié ce mercredi 21 octobre 2026, Mikael Kasurinen, directeur créatif de Control Resonant, écarte l’idée d’un teaser. Il répond : « Non… Je vais être honnête, non. Encore une fois, en ce qui concerne Resonant, ce qui était important pour moi, c’est que ce soit intime à sa manière. Et même si nous avons… il y a quelques éléments d’Alan Wake dans Resonant… c’est la seule chose. »
Il poursuit : « Je voulais m’assurer que le jeu tienne debout tout seul. On n’a pas l’impression de laisser des questions en suspens ou des mystères, comme si un personnage s’en allait et que le joueur se demandait ce qu’il allait faire. On a plutôt un début, un milieu, puis on boucle les choses. Bien sûr, certaines choses se prolongeront dans de futurs projets, mais on ne se dit pas : posons une prémisse ici et n’allons pas plus loin dans ce jeu. Je n’aime pas faire ça. »
Le passé du studio invite pourtant à la prudence. En 2020, l’extension AWE de Control annonçait déjà Alan Wake 2. En octobre 2024, l’extensionThe Lake House d’Alan Wake 2 cachait à son tour une scène optionnelle avec Dylan Faden, frère de Jesse, l’héroïne de Control, suivie d’un court teaser de ce qui allait devenir Control Resonant.
Mikael Kasurinen qualifie la scène en question de « curieuse », en riant, mais elle relève finalement de la façon de faire de Remedy Entertainment. Le studio a un goût affirmé pour le bizarre. Il reconnaît d’ailleurs que ce genre de clin d’œil est devenu « une tradition » chez Remedy, qui veut « planter une graine pour quelque chose de nouveau ». La séquence ne doit simplement pas donner l’impression de déborder du cadre deControl Resonant. À l’heure actuelle, Remedy n’a pas officialisé Alan Wake 3, mais la marque « Alan Wake’s Return » a été redéposée en septembre dernier, dix ans après sa création.
