articles.title: FreightTech unicorn sennder targets €1 billion in annual revenue as C.H. Robinson integration completes | EU-Startups
articles.text:
sennder, a German digital road freight forwarder, today announced that it will hit €1 billion in annual revenue for this year, as well as completing the integration of C.H. Robinson’s European operations.
The delivery scale-up has raised over €340 million in funding and is now on track to deliver IFRS EBITDA profitability for the full year of 2026. sennder now operates as one business on one platform, sennOS, moving more than 150,000 shipments a month through a network of more than 40,000 vetted carriers.
“Continued operational momentum and sustained profitability puts us in an even stronger position to invest in the digital transformation of freight,” says David Nothacker, co-founder and CEO of sennder. “We brought two large businesses onto one platform and lifted operator productivity by 45% in the process, and this milestone reinforces sennder’s role as a dependable partner for customers and carriers alike and enables us to keep raising the standard for reliability, efficiency and innovation in European road freight.”
To understand sennder’s landmark, it is important to look at the wider transport/cargo sector in Europe and the developing competition – as well as the funding being distributed in 2026.
These include Berlin-based cargo.one with nearly €17 million for multimodal freight software and Ukraine-based Cargofy with €5.2 million in primary funding for AI-powered freight operations.
In Germany, FRYTE Mobility raised €3.5 million for electric truck charging coordination and NexDash secured €2.5 million for road-freight electrification, while Belgium’s Vectrix raised €1.15 million for transport-order automation.
These announcements represent approximately €29.4 million in new company funding.
EU-Startups previously covered sennder’s €131.2 million Series D in 2021 and CEO David Nothacker’s discussion of the C.H. Robinson transaction in 2025.
Founded in 2015, sennder is a digital road freight forwarder, leveraging data and technology to increase efficiency and transparency in road logistics, with the aim of reducing empty miles and optimising transport flows.
sennder connects shippers with a broad network of carriers, with the goal of enabling low-emission, cost-effective transport while supporting carriers in navigating a traditionally fragmented industry.
Over the past 12 months, these initiatives have prevented more than 31,000 tonnes of CO2e emissions.
For sennder, today’s achievement is driven by putting profitability and revenue quality ahead of volume growth, actively optimising its customer portfolio.
Operator productivity, measured as gross profit per operator, rose 45% YoY. sennder attributes the increase to scale, the single integrated platform and its growing use of reasoning AI agents which work alongside teams, supporting them in serving customers at scale.
The AI agents reason across vast volumes of live network data to match loads with the right capacity, price shipments in real time and resolve issues before they escalate, streamlining operations further.
With profitability established, sennder will continue to invest in its platform, its AI agents and its European carrier network. The focus is profitable growth: growing volume that is sustainable and supports reliable service for customers and carriers.

articles.title: AI is an Amplifier: Scale High Performance, Not Dysfunction
articles.text:
Transcript
Nathen Harvey: For those of you that are unfamiliar with DORA, I just want to level set on which Dora we're talking about here. There are quite a few. There's the small child, Dora. She is one of my favorites. How many of you have watched that show ever, Dora the Explorer? The beautiful thing about Dora is every transformational journey she goes on, she has a map in her backpack and she completes it in three steps. Now, Swiper's always there trying to set her off course. I'm here to tell you that your AI adoption journey is going to be just like that. It's three easy steps with just a little bit of Swiper in the way. Of course, we're here in Europe, so we also have DORA, the Digital Operational Resilience Act. I do assure you that if you and your team get better at delivering and operating software and doing this in an automated fashion, that's going to make those regulators from the Digital Operational Resilience Act happy because you'll be more resilient.
Where I come from in the United States, there are a few states within the United States that have a specific set of legislation. They call it Designated Outdoor Refreshment Areas. This means that you can walk around with a beer as long as you stay within the Designated Outdoor Refreshment Area. That, I have to admit, is probably my second favorite DORA in the world. There are others, but I can't take you through all of them. What I am here to talk about is this research program, DORA, that's been running for well over a decade now. This is really research into how do teams get better at doing the technology? How do we get better at IT? How do we get better at software delivery? How do we get better not just with the technology, but as teams, as people? How do we drive our businesses forward and really serve our customers?
DORA used to be an acronym, but we've deacronymed it. DORA now stands for nothing, which doesn't quite sound right either. We have a tagline, that's what DORA stands for. It stands for get better at getting better. The interesting thing is, and we'll get to this at the end of the talk, I'm actually starting to question our tagline. I'm worried that it's not going to serve us right, right now. More on that ahead.
The 2025 DORA Research
If you know anything about DORA, you might know that we run a survey. We run a giant survey every year, and maybe you've participated in that survey. If you have, thank you for sharing your data and your insights with us. It's really helpful. Last year, we had nearly 5,000 people take our survey. We augment that with additional qualitative research. Qualitative research is basically a qualitative researcher sitting down and having interviews with practitioners, with leaders, really trying to get a little bit more context around what's actually happening.
I'm going to share some data from our most recent survey. There is a little footnote on this slide here that you'll see. This global survey was conducted between June 13th and July 21st, 2025. I'm going to tell you some things about how AI adoption is going. Do you think it's accurate? I might be lying to you. We'll leave that for you to sort out. Last year we published this report, the State of AI-Assisted Software Development. You can download the 2025 report here, dora.dev/dora-report-2025. You can grab that report there and read it. It's 140 pages long, so I'm going to summarize it for you. I am going to test you now because I'm putting up another QR code. This one, I really want you to participate in this one. I want you to answer this question for me. What is stopping you? You just generated something with an AI, or maybe one of your colleagues just generated something with an AI.
What's stopping you from shipping it to production right now? Why not go directly to production? Let's just see what we're thinking here. What's stopping you? Trust. You don't trust the solution. Governance, security, quality, uncertainty. Being fired, someone put in there. It's good. It's interesting because might you be fired if you're not using the AI also? It's interesting. You can keep throwing some answers in there. I think they're fascinating. Fear. I don't know how. We are a bank. Stop using that as an excuse, you could still do better.
AI Adoption and Use
I want to talk about AI adoption and use and what our data found. Remember, how do we collect our data? Surveys. Ninety percent of people tell the truth on surveys, 10% lie. This slide was, how many of you are using AI professionally at work? Ninety percent of our survey respondents said yes, and 10% said I'm not allowed to, so I better say no. Remember, this was June and July of last year. We're not going to ask this question again. Because, like I said, we've been doing this research for 10 years. Never once have we asked, do you use a computer at work? From this point forward, we can stop asking, do you use AI at work? Because, yes, you do. We're using it. How much do you rely on it? I think these numbers have probably changed. Reliance on something is different than just using a thing.
Like, if I rely on something and it goes away, that's problematic. What we see here is that about 35% of our respondents say I rely on it a little or not at all. A majority of our respondents are saying, yes, I rely on using that AI for that particular task or set of tasks that I'm doing. I think that's really interesting. Is it helping? We'll get to that. This one is also really fascinating to me. We asked, think back to a recent work day, about how many hours did you interact with AI? Now, stop. I get it, though. I'm falling back into these bad marital patterns. I'm sitting at home and I'm working out something with the AI and it's getting close to dinner time, and my wife is ready for me to stop working. I know like, just one more prompt. Just one more, I'll be there in a minute.
One more prompt. Please, not the 12 hours. If you're the long tail in this chart, please get up, walk away. If you're sitting here in this talk, close the laptop, stop with the AI. Just listen to me for a minute. That'll make me feel better. It will be better for your long-term health, I promise you. The interesting thing here is the median hours, median of two hours working with AI. There are other studies, not our studies and not studies that I will quote, but there are good studies, nonetheless, that ask this question about, how much time a week does a software engineer typically spend actually writing code? The ranges vary pretty wildly, but 10%, 15%, 30% at the high end. How much is two hours in an eight-hour day? It's about 30. You're probably using AI to help you write code. Also, this is, I think, a bit of a challenge for us, are like how people perceive us as software engineers. AI is coming to take your job because it's going to write all of the code for you. It's going to take away that thing that you do 10% of your time, so therefore we don't need you anymore. That math doesn't math to me either. It doesn't work.
Is it helping you? How do you feel about using this? Your perceived impact on individual productivity, it's going up. You feel more productive. I feel like I'm getting more done. I feel more engaged with the work that I'm doing. I feel like I'm spending more time on good work, valuable work, maybe less time on toil. About 5%, slightly decreased, moderately decreased, or extremely decreased my productivity. I've certainly had those days working with AI as well. I've definitely had those days. This is really interesting. We've got high levels of reliance. We're using it a lot. We feel like it's really helping us improve. What about code quality? How's the quality of the codebase that you're working with? Also, improving. With about 10% saying it's actually a little bit worse now that we're using AI. Our codebase is a little bit worse off. This is a really hard question, like, how is it impacting code quality?
What do you mean by code quality? This is one of our challenges as researchers. We don't know. We want you to tell us what do we mean by code quality. You just answer this question, we'll do the data. Here's the thing, how much do you trust the quality that AI is generating? How much trust do you have in whatever it is that it's generating? Whether it's code or that email that you're about to send off to your boss, or a prospect, or the financial plan that you've built for your family. How much do you trust that? Thirty percent trust it a little or not at all. I got to tell you, I'm on team somewhat, right there in the middle. I want to sit down and have coffee. If you were part of the 11%, that say you trust it a great deal or you trust it not at all, if you fall into either of those buckets, you're both wrong.
You should not trust it a great deal. Those are probably the ones I want to talk to most. I want to understand that. How? What are you doing? The not at all, don't you feel the FOMO? You've got to start working with these skills. That great keynote, we've got to start learning in public and leaning in to these new ideas.
If I summarize that entire 2025 report for you in three slides, I'm going to do it right now. AI's primary role in software development is that of an amplifier. The greatest returns on your investments in AI are going to come from a strategic focus on the underlying organizational system. Without that foundation, AI has a tendency to create localized pockets of productivity that are often lost to downstream chaos. I saw a post on LinkedIn, someone lamenting the fact that they can now build something in hours, and it takes six weeks still for that thing to make it into the hands of a customer, to get into production. We've accelerated part of the system, but we're not yet as an industry thinking about the entire system in a holistic manner. That's exactly what we're seeing in our data as well.
Exploring AI's Relationship to Key Outcomes
We do like to report what you're telling us with DORA, we also try to understand and make some sense of the complexity that is your organization, that is these technology tools that we're working with. What is AI's relationship with key outcomes? I promise I'm only going to do this once with one chart. I'm going to teach you how to read this chart really quickly. What we do is we collect a bunch of data, we build a little model, and this tells us the shape of the world. Then, as researchers, we have this amazing capability. We can say, here's the shape of this complex world. Let's change just one thing and see what happens. I encourage you to go back to your organizations and try to change just one thing and see what happens. Because you can't. It's impossible. You can't do that. Our data, what we do, we build up this model.
We say, let's change one thing. What thing are we going to change? We're going to change the score that you achieved for AI adoption. We're going to ramp up AI adoption, change nothing else, and then run a bunch of simulations across our model. What happens? If the score that you receive for this outcome on the vertical bar stays the same, your dot will show up on that dash line, which represents zero. To the right of the dash line, that thing increased. To the left of the dash line, it decreased. Individual effectiveness increased the most. Software delivery instability increased. Just want to be super clear. It's probably not what you wanted. Organizational performance, time spent doing valuable work, code quality, product performance, software delivery throughput, it's probably do what you want, and team performance all improved. Burnout and friction, they basically stayed at zero. Those little bars that come out from the middle of that dot, that's our certainty rate.
We call those error bars. It's not just we that call them that, that's what they're called. The wider the bar, the less certain we are about this. The tighter it is, the more certain we are about it. If you look at burnout and friction, they're both pretty close to zero, and their error bars definitely overlap zero. For burnout, this probably makes sense in June or July. I'm going to maybe counter that. Imagine, you're at work, and it sucks. You feel burnt out. You question everything that you're doing. Your manager comes over and says, here's some AI. Guess what? Work still sucks. You still hate what you're doing. Like, that's not helping your burnout at all. Just handing you a new tool isn't going to help. We see that. The positive spin on this was, it didn't hurt, it didn't make it worse. I do worry right now, today.
How many of you are managing a fleet of agents right now? Maybe a fleet sounds too many, like three or four. If you're trying to do work with three or four agents, and they're all doing very different things, you might find yourself now bouncing from task to task to task. It's ok. It's cool. Because we are all, as humans, super good at multitasking, there's research that shows this. No, wait, it's the other way around. We're all shit at multitasking. It's cool. We'll just give it all to the agents. I've certainly found myself like, I told this agent the thing that I meant to tell that agent. The cognitive overload that we're taking on, I think we don't yet understand it. I worry that in this year's research, we're going to find very different results.
When we think about some of these things. Some are getting better. Some, like software delivery instability is getting worse. In DORA, the way that we measure software delivery instability is we look at how frequently are your pushes into production resulting in what I call the, oh, expletive moment. You've all been there. Push a change to production and you or someone around you shouts out an expletive. What are we going to do? We have to act right now. Like we're going to roll that back. We're going to push forward a hot fix. That's bad. That's software delivery instability. With AI, we see that going up. In 2024, so in the previous year's research, we saw software delivery instability going up and we saw software delivery throughput going down. This year, we see that it's improving. We're seeing changes over time. A lot of these changes have to do with the J-Curve of transformation of taking on anything new.
Anytime you take on something new, your organization will likely go through this pattern. You're going to bring in a new tool. There's going to be some low-hanging fruit. You're going to go pick that fruit. You're going to eat it. Things are going to look really good. Then all the low-hanging fruit will be consumed. Now you've got to get to the hard stuff. That's when it sucks. It gets hard. Software delivery instability starts to go up. You dip into this trough. Today, I would talk about that trough as there's a couple of things. There's software delivery instability. There's the trust that you don't have. With that trust comes a lot of verification of the tools. With that verification comes maybe the changing of your job. I'm a software engineer. I write code. No, I just review it. I just read other people's code, and it's not even people that are creating it anymore.
That's going to drop you down into this dip, the instability tax, the verification tax. There is another side. We've seen this all before. DORA's been researching, as I said, for over a decade. We were there as the cloud just started taking hold. Guess what happened in every organization when they brought on the cloud? Things got a little bit better. Then they got a lot worse. Then we figured out how to use this technology. The same thing with SRE practices. We've seen this in our data modeled over time. We know that this is what's happening. What we don't yet know, because all of this is so new and because the technology is changing so fast, how do you get there? How do you get to the other side? Collectively, we're learning that right now. We're all learning that together.
Team Performance - A Look at Seven Team Profiles
With DORA, we also want to look at how are teams performing? How are you doing? We've oftentimes looked at just software delivery performance, and published benchmarks on software delivery performance, and given names to things like low performers and elite performers. How many of you show up to work to be a low performer? I didn't think so. Some of you silently raised your hands, but you're sitting next to your manager, so I get it. I see you. We're engineers. We're supposed to be low performers. Like, let the computers do the things. We looked at more than just software delivery performance. In fact, we wanted to understand how are teams doing across these eight different factors: team performance, product performance, effectiveness, friction, burnout. Remember, we found that at least 90% of the people in our survey are using AI. What we also found were that there were seven unique team profiles when looked across those eight different characteristics.
The first thing that that tells us is it's not because of AI. If everyone's using AI and we're seeing vastly different, highly variable performance levels, it's not either the AI's fault or the AI that's making that happen. What do these seven team profiles look like? First, because we had seven, we couldn't just use low, medium, high, and elite. We had to come up with way more creative names. Some of these names, just by looking at the name, you might find yourself. You might find your team. Let's look at a chart, shall we? No, let's look at seven charts. No. You can't see anything here. These things are really hard to read. We did, you could call them crimes with this spider chart or this radar chart. They don't act the way that they should. We're not going to look at these charts because you can't see them anyhow.
Let's look at two of the different groups here. Constrained by process. Teams are running on a treadmill. Despite working on stable systems, their effort is consumed by inefficient processes, leading to high burnout and low impact. How many of you feel seen right now? You can see here, burnout is high. Friction is high, or I'll tell you because it says so there. Individual effectiveness is low. The time I'm spending doing valuable work is low. My software delivery instability, actually pretty good. It's lower than everyone else's. My throughput is a little bit lower than everyone else's as well. It's not the perfect team to be on. It's not terrible. We've seen worse. We're not really delivering a whole lot of value. Let's contrast that with harmonious high achievers. Now when you go back to work, you can tell boss, we're a harmonious high achiever. Like this is what excellence looks like, we think.
We've got a virtuous cycle, stable, low-friction environment, empowered teams delivering high-quality work sustainably and without burnout. We have to think about these things. Can we deliver quality sustainably? Can we do that with low levels of friction across the organization without burning our people out? These are really important considerations. Here's the thing. If we have everyone using AI and wild variance in the levels of team performance, how do we overcome that? What are some of the signals here? I have a question for you about just that. What one thing would you need to change in your environment to confidently trust the solutions that AI generates? We just had that question about what's stopping you. Let's explore that a little bit differently. What's stopping you? What's one thing you could change right now that would unlock some of that gate? Same QR code, new answers: guardrails, tests, testing, a harness, management, competency, end-to-end test, automated testing. There's one I'm looking for in particular, validation. My manager. That's real. Observability. Education. Access to better models. Governance. This is great.
DORA AI Capabilities Model
If it's not that you're using AI, maybe it has something to do with how you're using AI. We've seen this before. When we investigated the cloud years ago, we saw some teams that were getting a lot of great value out of cloud. Some teams that were like, it's slower and more expensive. Why did we move to the cloud? It wasn't because you had the cloud or not. It was how you used it. Dr. Nicole Forsgren talks about this a lot as having a membership to the gym. How many of you have a membership to the gym? How many of you go regularly? Just having the membership isn't enough. It's not going to make you fit. You have to do the work. We investigated this. We wanted to understand, are there specific things that help some teams get more value out of AI than others? What we identified were seven capabilities that when combined together with adoption, drive better outcomes.
You've probably heard a couple of themes. There was one talk talking about AI adoption, and AI deployment, and AI value. You don't get adoption just by buying the tools. You don't get value just by having adoption. You can't have impact without adoption. Frankly, this leads us to a lot of challenges. I was talking with Blanca around measurement. How do we know that it's working? Let's go measure it. I want you to be very careful with measurement. One of the most important things with measurement is to understand what is the question that we're trying to answer. I was talking to someone else, and we were talking about what's happening in their organization. They happen to sit on the board. They go to board meetings. The people on the board are like, what are we doing with AI? Are we using AI? Are we using it? Is everybody using it?
The only question they have is adoption. Tell them that you're adopting, show them the numbers, and stop. That's not enough. It is enough to answer their question today. That's all the measurement that you need to answer that question. Next year they might ask, you all adopted all this stuff, what is our return? Now we have a different question. I can guarantee you can't get to the returns if there is no adoption. You got to start there. Measuring adoption, we all know, is not enough. It's not enough. For the love of whatever you view as good and holy, stop measuring how many lines did the AI generate. How many of you as software engineers loved being measured on how many lines of code you wrote? Why is it different for an AI? It's a stupid metric. Stop. What does matter? These seven capabilities. Having these capabilities and conditions in your team, within your organization, will help take the adoption that you're so focused on and let it drive through to real outcomes that we care about.
We've got a clear and communicated stance. If you don't make it clear how, when, where, what AI you can and can't use within your organization, this will cause all kinds of friction for your employees. If I don't know if I'm supposed to use it, one of two things will happen. I simply won't use it, and I'll be fine with that. I'll blissfully work without AI. Or I'll know the power because I've used it at home and I'm going to bring it into work and I'm going to use it anyhow. Then I'm going to worry about getting caught and getting fired for that. Make sure that your stance is clear and communicated. Next up, we have a healthy data ecosystem and access to that internal data. You want the AI to do better for you? Make sure it understands what are the policies that your organization has?
Who are your customers that you're trying to feed? Let's make sure that all of that is accessible to the AI. The next two are two that really have nothing to do with AI. Strong version control practices. The AI can go down a really crazy path if you don't have the confidence that you can roll back those changes very easily. I've talked to so many people who've said, I find myself committing to version control much more frequently. To which I say, what are you talking about? Why weren't you committing to version control every two minutes? Why is this new? It is. It's time. Learn those version control practices. All you need to know how to do really is commit and to roll back. If you can safely and confidently do those, you'll be in a better place. The next one is also super important, working in small batches.
If DORA has found nothing else, it's that if you want to improve software delivery throughput, and software delivery instability, the best way to get there is through shipping smaller changes. When you work in small batches, you can reason about what you're changing. When something goes wrong, you can reason about how to undo that, how to fix that thing. When you roll out changes, try not to roll them out to everyone all at once. Do we have progressive delivery? Can we slowly roll things out? Working in small batches is a powerful thing. Unfortunately, the bots came along, and they're like, "I see your small batches. I'm going to raise you this 50,000-line PR. Here's a small batch for you. Ship it." Even the bots do better if we give them smaller, well-defined tasks. It just makes sense.
Then two that I want to dig into a little bit further, user-centric focus and quality internal platforms. Having a user-centric focus, every piece of software that we create is made for humans. Even if the consumers of that software are bots, we're creating it for humans. The end goal is that this software makes someone's life better. That's why we're here. AI, maybe it's a forcing function for us. As software engineers, our job is not to write code. Our job is to solve problems. Our job is to understand who our users are and build the things that they need, the things that are going to improve their lives. This is fundamentally changing the work that we do. I, personally, I'm optimistic that this is helping us get closer to our users, better understand and have empathy for them, and build better solutions for them. One of the things that we found in our research, in the data, was that when you have a user-centric focus, your team performance improves.
The other thing that we found that was really interesting was when you don't have a user-centric focus, your team performance actually decreases. This is really powerful. I think when it comes to AI, there's a really fascinating thing that we can do now. Yes, AI can generate that 50,000-line PR in the time that it would have taken you to create a 10-line PR. It can do things a lot faster. What else does this do for us? This really unlocks optionality. Now I can prototype five things in less time than it took me to prototype one thing. You know what we're really bad at? Is understanding exactly what our user wants. Let's go build six things. Let's go build 10 things and try them out. Let's debate them as a team. Let's bring in some users to talk about them before we invest in actually productionalizing one of them and shipping it off to production.
Wait, but why just one? We've been building A/B test frameworks forever. Why not A-B-C-D-E-F-G? How many different things can we be actually running in production, getting real user feedback on to help us make better decisions? If you have the capability to enable your product development team to help you build higher fidelity prototypes that we can then explore lots of different options, we can converge on the best choice. We can put some of those best choices in front of users, take feedback from them, feed that back into the cycle. We're building this really tight connection with our users. This is really awesome. Let's get there.
The other thing that probably isn't a surprise that really helps is quality internal platforms help turn your AI adoption into real value for your organization. When I think about quality platforms, there's the obvious things. A platform helps us scale a capability, a technology across an organization because we centralize some of those capabilities, make them available to everyone. Another thing that if you've spent any time near platform engineering, I'm sure you've heard the phrase, treat your platform as a product. Have you heard that phrase before? One of the things about products is they have customers. Who's the customer of the platform? Before AI, who was the customer of the platform? It was other software engineers. It's other developers. I have a lot of empathy. I understand the pain that they have. I know what they're going through. Now it's changing. It's not just other developers I'm building for, I'm also building for the bots.
I need to improve my developer experience. I also need to improve the agent experience. It turns out that some of the things we do for one are good for the other. When we have better documentation, that can help our developers. It can sure help our agents. I know this because now you're all writing documentation. Everyone is writing documentation. DORA has researched it for years and said, "We see documentation is like sunshine, it unlocks all of these capabilities within an organization." Everyone's been like, yes, but writing docs sucks. How many agent files have you written or skills have you written? You are writing documentation now. What's changed? As a senior engineer, I'm not writing documentation to help a junior. I will write documentation to help a bot. Let's be honest, that's messed up. Why? Because when I write the documentation to help the junior, it takes a year or more for them to progress.
The feedback cycle on did I write good documentation or not is really long. When I write documentation for an agent, I get that feedback right away. I changed the agent and I re-ran the prompt and I saw the results from that. It's really fascinating. There was a research paper that they did a little bit of research into like, do these agents files actually help produce better output? Their finding was, no, not so much. I think the interesting thing was, as the user, do I have more confidence in the output because of the agent file? I feel like I have more control, maybe that gives me better trust. We do know, and this is true everywhere, that trust begets adoption, begets trust. The more you use something, the more you trust it. The more you trust it, the more you use it. While maybe it's not helping the bots right now, maybe it is helping me. Maybe that's good enough.
Here's the other thing about AI. We talked about internal platform. We start with developer experience. Now we have to think about agent experience. I want to go back to that very first question. What's stopping you from YOLOing that thing that the AI just generated into production? Because now everyone in your organization is a builder. We go from developer experience to agent experience to builder experience. How do I help Jane from accounting ship that application that she dreamed up last night and built with an AI? That sounds scary, doesn't it? Maybe that's the new job. Maybe that's the new platform engineering. How do we make it safe for there to be more builders across our organization? That's scary. Maybe that's what we have to do. Because otherwise what's the flip side to that? Shadow IT, shadow AI. That's always been a label, in my perception. You might not agree with this.
I feel like shadow IT is a label that we, technologists, have used to denigrate the other side of the house. Those business people, and their shadow IT. Why do you think they're doing that? So that you could stay employed. They're getting their business problems solved. Shadow IT, we should feel bad when there's shadow IT. That's a signal to us that there's a real business problem, it's so bad that they're willing to work around working with us. We need to go enable that. I think a platform team, and this idea of platform, maybe more of your engineering capacity should shift toward enabling builders, and less should go toward shipping that next feature. Just something to think about.
DORA AI Capabilities Model in Action
I want to show you the DORA AI capabilities model in action. If you go to dora.dev, you can do that or you can just watch here. I'm going to click on this little AI guy. I want to show you this capabilities model. We're going to explore it a little bit here. Let's say that you're part of the legacy bottleneck. One of the challenges that the legacy bottleneck has is product performance is low. You decide as a team, we want to improve our product performance. You can come out here to the model and you can click on product performance, and it will show you which capabilities together with AI adoption drive product performance. From this model, you can figure out like, wait, product performance? What does that even mean? How did we assess it? You can click on this how to assess button. Working in small batches, AI accessible internal data, clear and communicated stance.
What do those things mean? You can figure out how to assess them and you can learn more about them. The way that this model works though, you're doing AI adoption. You want to drive an outcome or multiple outcomes. You want to improve these things. How do you do so and make sure that the AI adoption is happening? Follow those arrows backwards with these capabilities and conditions in place. Your AI adoption is more likely to have an impact on those things on the other side, on those outcomes.
Continuous Improvement vs. Radical Change
A bad system will beat a good person every single time. That's from W. Edwards Deming. The one quote I remember to cite. Think about that. When it comes to adopting AI and changing how you work, there's two different approaches that you might take. If you're a fan of the Toyota Production System, you might know the terms Kaizen and Kaikaku. Augmenting, where we look at a current system and we try to make it a little bit better. This is continuous improvement. That's Kaizen. Then evolving. Evolving is like, maybe we throw everything out. Maybe we start from fresh and design the systems that are going to be completely different. That's Kaikaku. That's radical change. When I go back to that slide, the question that I asked you all, what's one thing you would change in order to make it safer, to trust that code that the AI generated, you could ship to production?
Not one of you said code reviews. How many of you feel like code reviews are the new bottleneck? I think it's time. I am a big proponent of Kaizen and continuous improvement, not Kaikaku, radical change. Maybe it's time code reviews go away. Maybe it's time they go away. How uncomfortable does that make you? Pretty uncomfortable. Why do we have code reviews? To validate that there are missing tests. Why else do we have code reviews? To learn. Give me one more reason why we have code reviews. Two brains think better than one. Share the knowledge. How many of you have walked up to a brand-new codebase with an LLM at your side and learned about that codebase very quickly? We can share the knowledge a lot faster. How many of you have written tests to validate that you have tests for this thing or have other ways of validating that without asking a human to look at this thing to validate that there are tests there?
How many of you sit down and do pair programming? You know what's better than asynchronous code review? Synchronous code review. Write that together. We've got four eyes looking at the code as we go. It's better. Maybe it's time to throw out code reviews. Every bit of engineering capacity that we're investing in code reviews would be better invested in better guardrails and better understanding of the intent of what we're trying to build. I know, it's radical. They don't call it radical change for no reason. I think it's time. We need to think about this as an industry. I mentioned that that 2025 report was not the latest report. This is the latest report, the DORA AI Capabilities Model Report, dora.dev/dora-aicmr. This came out in December. It goes into those seven capabilities, talks a little bit more about each one of them. How do you measure them? How do you put them in practice within your organization? All of this. I highly encourage you to download that report and check it out as well.
From Insight to Action
I want to close out with some final thoughts. The first final thought is probably the most important thing that I will say all day today. Don't believe me. Don't believe our research. The way that DORA does research is we go out and we research the world. We get as many inputs as we possibly can. None of you work for the world. Some of you, there is the world, the program, like maybe you're on that program. You don't work in the world. You work at the organization that you work at, and in its context and with its customers. Even within your organization, you don't probably work for the whole organization. You work for a business unit or an application. You've got to contextualize what we've found. Take our findings and use them as your hypothesis. DORA found that when we have a clear and communicated stance, AI adoption leads to better outcomes.
Let's go try that out. Also, you cannot do this alone. No one can improve alone. Look around you. These are your peers. We're all learning together. Also, if you join the DORA community, you can join thousands of other practitioners and leaders and researchers around the world who are taking some of these ideas and trying to figure out what does it mean when we put them into practice.

articles.title: 'How do you know what's real?': US utilities are making AI data centers prove they exist before handing over power connections — as 50% of planned buildouts are currently being delayed, stalled, or canceled
articles.text:
'How do you know what's real?': US utilities are making AI data centers prove they exist before handing over power connections — as 50% of planned buildouts are currently being delayed, stalled, or canceled
The AI boom should have been a golden age for America's electric utilities
- US data center developers have requested 1,066GW of grid connections, but Wood Mackenzie expects utilities to commit to only about 28%
- Utilities are demanding collateral, longer contracts, and study fees; Exelon's high-probability load fell from a whopping 18GW to 11GW once it insisted on the former
- Because grid costs are shared, phantom demand risks landing on household bills, and nobody knows how much of it is real yet
US utilities and grid operators are now demanding higher rates, longer contracts, collateral, and steep engineering study fees from data center developers, in an attempt to weed out what the industry calls "phantom" data centers.
Reporting from The Wall Street Journal claims the reasoning is straightforward: Grid costs are shared, so if a utility builds substations and transmission lines for a project that never shows up, everyone else on the network ends up helping to pay for them.
The numbers back up the nerves in play: developers have requested 1,066GW of grid connections for US data centers, according to a Wood Mackenzie analysis first reported by Bloomberg in August 2026, a figure equal to roughly 83% of the country's entire utility-scale generating capacity at the end of 2025.
A queue full of ghosts as collateral becomes the norm?
Wood Mackenzie expects utilities to commit to serving only about 28% of it: roughly 12% that already has firm service commitments, plus a further 17% that looks likely. The WSJ also cites a separate Wood Mackenzie measure that puts just 23% of disclosed requests in its high-confidence category.
Much of the gap is due to duplication; developers who don't yet know which utility can deliver power fastest file the same project with several of them and keep every option open until one pans out.
Others are simply speculators: commentary in POWER Magazine argued that private equity funds, land brokers and shell companies are claiming queue positions without site control or a signed customer, betting that land with a grid connection attached will find a buyer.
The phenomenon isn't new. Utility Dive was writing about phantom data centers in 2025, and TR reported in July that 67% of electricity executives surveyed by Capgemini were seeing speculative applications for capacity. The change is that utilities are now pricing the problem, and it is causing many adverse effects.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Exelon's attempts to lock down potential consumers
Exelon, which runs utilities across the Mid-Atlantic and Midwest, offers the clearest look at what happens when developers are asked to put money down.
After it began requiring transmission security agreements (TSAs), contracts that bind customers to credit obligations, committed revenue contributions, and shortfall payments, its high-probability data center load fell nearly 40%, from 18GW at the end of 2025 to about 11GW in the second quarter. Its wider pipeline of projects under study dropped from about 43GW to 25GW.
Jeanne Jones, Exelon's CFO, told the WSJ that typical requests used to be around 50MW and now often run to 1,000MW or more. The question she kept fielding, internally and externally, was "How do you know what's real?"
Exelon, however, also told analysts its $41 billion capital plan through 2029 is unchanged, so a 40% cut in expected data center load has not, so far, shrunk the spending plan.
None of this would matter much if grid capacity were cheap, but it simply isn't. PJM, the largest US grid operator, saw its capacity auction clear at the price cap for the third time in a row this summer while missing its reliability target by 6.8GW.
In September, its independent market monitor told federal regulators that 4,017MW of forecast data center load, 42% of the growth PJM had assumed, had already been canceled or delayed.
Households are feeling the cost increase; reports in July indicated that Henrico County, Virginia, asked staff and schools to cut electricity use after a 24.9% rate increase. Virginia has also moved to stop utilities passing data center costs onto everyday users, and Texas bills are rising faster than inflation. Lindsey Short of the Ohio Manufacturers' Association warned against building the grid around "the most optimistic number on somebody's spreadsheet."
Underbuilding carries its own risks, though, especially when transformers can take years to arrive, as a recent deep dive on grid bottlenecks laid out. That is why utilities are locking in the customers they do accept. Average minimum contract lengths for large customers have risen to about 10.8 years from 4.6 before 2024, according to filings aggregated by Halcyon and cited by the Journal, and a separate research brief built on Halcyon's tracker found a similar jump.
What nobody can yet say is how much of the AI power rush is real, and that poses problems for planners, stakeholders, and households alike. Until it does, utilities are doing what any lender would: asking to see the money first; households just happen to be roadkill if things don't pan out.

Rahim Amir is a UAE-based tech writer who enjoys building PCs as much as he enjoys writing about them. He has been professionally writing about PC hardware since 2023, focusing on buyer’s guides, hardware reviews, and sponsored content and features related to tech.
Having built hundreds of gaming PCs and being an avid gamer in his spare time, Rahim tends to have stronger opinions about hardware than most. This is particularly on display when he gets his way with powerful, but minimalistic RGB builds even as Small Form Factor (SFF) PCs come a close second.

articles.title: Canadian government shuts down some websites amid global cybersecurity scare | BetaKit
articles.text:
Some Canadian government websites have been taken temporarily offline “as a precaution to protect government systems and Canadians’ information,” AI and digital innovation minister Evan Solomon said on Wednesday afternoon.
“This is in response to a vulnerability identified in PHP, software used by websites around the world,” Solomon wrote in a post on X. “This is a global issue, and other governments and organizations are also taking protective measures.”
The move follows guidance from the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, Solomon said. PHP programming language developers said on Tuesday that they had found two critical security vulnerabilities and encouraged site managers to take their websites down or update them as soon as a fix was available.
The severe PHP programming language vulnerability affects content management systems, like WordPress. Roughly 70 percent of all websites run on PHP, according to online technology tracker W3techs.
According to Engadget, another major security vulnerability was also discovered Wednesday, involving TLS certificates—digital documents that help verify a website’s identity—with extremely weak encryption. This could impact everything from virtual private networks to IoT devices, where attackers could create credentials for many websites and apps. The issue is that the private keys are weak and could let attackers forge credentials for a range of websites and apps.
AI giant OpenAI has taken credit for its large-language model GPT‑5.6 Sol identifying the PHP vulnerabilities.
This is a developing story. Check back soon for more details.

articles.title: Freelander 8, así es el SUV premium del grupo Chery con cerebro de Qualcomm que llegará próximamente a las carreteras
articles.text:
El grupo Chery, y en especial su marca Freelander, sigue ampliando su catálogo de eléctricos con propuestas interesantes y diferentes. ¿El último? El Freelander 8, un nuevo modelo enorme, con opciones de hibridación y 100% eléctrico, y con la última tecnología. Y sí, cuando decimos tecnología, nos referimos al cerebro de Qualcomm que cambia completamente los sistemas inteligentes para el coche.
En este sentido, se trata de su nuevo todoterreno que llega con una impresionante longitud de 5,1 metros, tecnología electrificada con opción híbrida enchufable de 620 CV de potencia y capacidad para hasta seis ocupantes. Este nuevo Freelander 8 entra dentro de lo que el grupo Chery llama SUV premium, y razones no le faltan.
Es de los más grandes de la marca, con sus 5,1 m de longitud, 2,1 m de anchura y 1,9 m de altura, lo que se traduce en un tamaño muy interesante desde el exterior y un amplio espacio interior. De hecho, la compañía apunta a que incluso habrá versiones disponibles con llantas de hasta 22 pulgadas. Y decimos "habrá" porque se trata de un modelo actualmente en desarrollo que se irá concretando según los mercados en los que está disponible.
En este sentido, y aunque todavía faltan algunos detalles por confirmar, llegará con una variante electrificada que combina un motor híbrido de gasolina 2.0 turbo, una batería
LFP de 34 kWh y un sistema de tracción total, desarrollando una potencia máxima de 620 CV y un par máximo de 662 Nm, permitiendo acelerar de 0 a 100 km/h en 5,8 segundos. Algo increíble para su enorme tamaño.
Respecto a su autonomía, apunta a los 886 kilómetros de forma combinada, pero su apartado eléctrico permite recorrer hasta 110 kilómetros y admite carga rápida en corriente continua, con tiempos inferiores a 20 minutos para pasar del 20% al 80% de batería.
Un SUV con cerebro de Qualcomm y mucha tecnología
Y tiene un enorme despliegue tecnológico en su interior: una pantalla panorámica integrada de 46,3 pulgadas y resolución 8K que se extiende 1,2 metros a lo largo del salpicadero y una pantalla central de 15,6 pulgadas, gestionada por el procesador automotriz Qualcomm SA8295P. En la parte de atrás incluye una pantalla suspendida de 17,3 pulgadas destinada a las plazas traseras, aunque no en todas las configuraciones.
Este sistema integrado ofrece información de conducción, navegación, ayudas a la conducción, monitorización del entorno, entretenimiento y funciones específicas para la conducción todoterreno. Lo complementa un sistema de audio Harman Kardon con hasta 23 altavoces.
Además, el Freelander 8 incluye sistemas avanzados de asistencia a la conducción, incluyendo funciones de conducción autónoma nivel L2+ y más de 30 asistentes de ayuda al conductor, además de incorporar el sistema SIVP (Super Intelligent Valet Parking), que permite que el coche realice de forma autónoma determinadas maniobras para buscar plaza de aparcamiento, y el i-ATS (Intelligent All-Terrain System) ofrecerá hasta nueve modos de funcionamiento, incluyendo programas específicos para diferentes superficies y escenarios de conducción.
Sobre su disponibilidad y precio, todavía es pronto, pero Freelander confirma que sabremos más en los próximos meses.

articles.title: Interspecies communication
articles.text:
Interspecies communication
Decoding how animals communicate could reveal the inner lives of other species—and give humans a window onto how they see the world.
Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us. Decoding how animals communicate with one another could offer a window into the inner lives of other species and help humans realize that “animals are sentient creatures who think, who have hopes and dreams of their own,” says Con Slobodchikoff, the founder of Zoolingua, a company working on dog-to-human speech.
The sticking points
Teasing all this out is complex. To decipher howls, squeaks, and clicks, researchers must match the creatures making sounds with what’s happening around them. Prairie dogs, for example, utter a different series of yips when a coyote approaches than when a hawk is nearby. It’s painstaking work, especially for difficult-to-observe species, like deep-diving whales or subterranean mole rats.
There are other hurdles. Many animals communicate not just through sound but through visual cues, touch, pheromones, or a combination of signals, some of which might be difficult for us to perceive. And without a multispecies Rosetta stone, it’s hard to know if translations are accurate.
The progress
Over the past 50 years, a growing arsenal of devices has made it easier to observe the sophisticated ways animals communicate. Hydrophones at the bottom of the ocean can capture humpback whale song, and tiny wearable “biologgers” can record a bat’s every squeak.
In the last decade, advances in AI have leveled up our ability to make sense of it all. The technology can detect different calls, distinguish which sounds belong to which animal, and spot patterns. Researchers at the Earth Species Project (ESP), a nonprofit founded in 2018 to decode animal communication, recently used machine learning to detect vocalizations of carrion crows and determine which bird made which call.
They suspect that more advanced AI could translate critters’ chatter. Large language models like Claude and ChatGPT excel at finding relationships between words, explains Sara Keen, one of ESP’s behavioral ecologists. ESP hopes its own NatureLM—trained on human speech, music, and animal sounds—will be able to interpret the vocalizations of a variety of species.
That promise, however, is still theoretical. Yossi Yovel, a neuroecologist at Tel Aviv University, worries that these models will put too much emphasis on acoustic similarities and make mistakes—like lumping together similar sounds that have different meanings.
As for a two-way convo? It’s not clear when—or whether—that will happen. Still, “a lot of animals have an evolutionary structure that is similar enough that we should be able to understand what they’re saying,” Slobodchikoff says.
Progress meter ............ 4
Researchers have amassed heaps of data on animal communication, but they’re still trying to figure out how to decipher it all.

articles.title: Wegen geleakter KI-Gespräche: Meta stoppt vorübergehend die Freigabefunktion in seinem KI-Agent Muse
articles.text:
Meta Muse: Tausende private KI-Gespräche waren per Suchanfrage auffindbar
Nutzer:innen von Metas KI-Agent Muse hatten die Möglichkeit, Inhalte wie Suchanfragen, Unterhaltungen oder Bilder direkt aus der App heraus mit anderen zu teilen. Diese Freigabefunktion hat der Tech-Konzern jetzt vorübergehend ausgesetzt. Der Grund: Der KI-Agent konnte sensible Informationen offenlegen, wenn Nutzer:innen Inhalte über Weblinks teilten. Das hat eine Analyse des Sicherheitsunternehmens Claroc ergeben. Ars Technica bat den Tech-Konzern daraufhin um eine Stellungnahme. Dieser gab an, den Datenschutz der Funktion zu überprüfen und gegebenenfalls Änderungen vorzunehmen.
Muse-Gespräche waren online leicht auffindbar
Auch viele andere Apps bieten Freigabefunktionen. In der Regel klicken Nutzer:innen hierfür auf eine Option, um eine URL zu erstellen, über die jede:r die Inhalte aufrufen kann. Um zu verhindern, dass Unbefugte an sensible Informationen gelangen, enthalten diese URLs typischerweise eine lange, schwer zu erratende Textfolge. Laut Meta-CEO Mark Zuckerberg wurde auch Muse „von Grund auf für Datenschutz und Sicherheit entwickelt“ – mit einem Haken. Denn eine zentrale Designentscheidung bei der Erstellung der URLs hat die Links offenbar leicht auffindbar gemacht.
Forscher:innen von Claroc fanden rund 6.800 Links, die Muse-Nutzer:innen zum Teilen von Unterhaltungen erstellt hatten. Dabei stießen sie auf Informationen, die eindeutig nicht für die Öffentlichkeit bestimmt waren. Darunter befanden sich Notizen für ein Vorstellungsgespräch samt Kontaktperson und Termin sowie der gesamte Urlaubskalender eines Unternehmens, in dem die Abwesenheiten aller Mitarbeiter:innen vermerkt waren. „Es genügte eine einzige Abfrage“, so die Forscher:innen in einem Beitrag auf dem Blog des Unternehmens. „Was die von Muse geteilten Inhalte leicht auffindbar macht, ist der Titel, der in der Webadresse enthalten ist und in öffentlichen DNS-Einträgen für alle suchbar ist.“
Mangelnder Datenschutz beschädigt Vertrauen
Die Forscher:innen fanden die Muse-Freigabelinks, weil sie alle den Domainnamen cf.metaaiusercontent.com verwenden. Zusätzlich fügt Muse den Namen der Konversation samt langer Textzeichenfolge in die URL ein, was die Entdeckung laut den Forscher:innen zusätzlich erleichtert hat. Gegenüber Ars Technica erklärte Meta, das Bug-Bounty-Programm solle Forscher:innen eine Möglichkeit bieten, genau solche Szenarien zu melden und so dabei zu helfen, den KI-Agenten zu verbessern. Asaf Aprozper, Mitbegründer und CTO von Claroc, gab gegenüber Ars Technica allerdings an, er habe die Erkenntnisse gemeldet – und keine Antwort erhalten.
Da Meta die Freigabefunktion ausgesetzt hat, laufen Muse-Nutzer:innen vorerst nicht mehr Gefahr, sensible Informationen online auffindbar zu machen. Der Vorfall könnte dem Image von KI-Agenten, deren Risiken derzeit im Fokus der Debatte stehen, allerdings weiter schaden. Mangelnder Datenschutz gilt in Deutschland als eine der größten Hürden für den Einsatz von KI. Knapp 90 Prozent der Menschen hierzulande halten den Schutz personenbezogener Daten für wichtig und 73 Prozent gaben an, intransparente KI-Produkte zu meiden. Das ergab eine repräsentative Civey-Umfrage unter rund 2.500 Personen, die im Auftrag des Bundesverbandes Digitale Wirtschaft durchgeführt wurde.

Get gaming at 1080p and 1440p with this affordable rig from Newegg
Right now, the best way to pick up a gaming PC is to buy a pre-built, with hardware prices shooting through the roof. If you took these specs and tried to build a matching PC yourself, you'd struggle to beat this price. With the Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 Ti at your disposal, you're getting one of Nvidia’s latest-generation mid-tier graphics cards. It has 4,608 CUDA cores and a boost clock speed of 2,527MHz. Unlike the more power-hungry top-end RTX 50-series cards, you only need one eight-pin PCIe connector to deliver power here, so you can banish those worries about burning GPU cables.
Our RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB review makes clear how good the performance is with this Blackwell GPU for gamers, especially at 1080p and 1440p. The charts you'll see below show that, especially with ray tracing in the mix, compared to rival cards at this level. Full DLSS support is included, too, so you can add multi-frame generation as a backstop. That'll give you a nice frame rate boost in the most resource-heavy games if you're pushing up to the highest resolutions.

For the CPU, you're getting the Intel Core i7-14700F. This continues to be a popular CPU option for gaming, despite being a little older. articles.title: Samsung’s latest 55-inch Frame TV is down to its lowest price yet
articles.text:
If you want a TV but prefer something that won’t clash with your room’s decor, Samsung’s The Frame is a standout option that’s designed to look like a piece of framed art instead of a black, monolithic rectangle mounted to your wall. You can buy the latest version of the 55-inch Samsung Frame TV on sale for around $897.99 ($402 off) at Amazon, which marks a new low price. Larger sizes are on sale, too, including the new 98-inch model, which is down to $3,749.99 ($1,252 off).
Samsung’s latest 55-inch Frame TV is down to its lowest price yet
The slim, wall-mounted TV can display paintings and photographs when you’re not watching your favorite shows.
The 2026 model is largely the same as its predecessor; The biggest hardware change is that this size of the TV features built-in ports instead of using Samsung’s One Connect Box. Like previous models, it has a matte, canvas-like display that more closely resembles an actual painting better than a glossy TV screen. Its built-in motion sensor detects when someone enters the room and can automatically display artwork, even adjusting its brightness and colors based on ambient lighting. It supports Samsung’s Art Store, which offers access to more than 5,000 works ranging from world-famous galleries to lesser known, independent artists. A full subscription costs $49.99 annually, though you can also enjoy 30 new free, rotating artworks every month. Samsung includes a wall mount and a black bezel in the box, with additional magnetic frame styles available separately to better match your space or taste.
In terms of performance, the Frame prioritizes style over image quality, so it’s not necessarily the best choice for cinephiles who may be willing to pay more for a brighter picture, deeper blacks, and more lifelike colors. Still it offers a refresh rate of up to 144Hz with variable refresh rate support for smoother gaming, along with HDR10 Plus and Dolby Atmos support for a more immersive audio/visual experience.

articles.title: iPhone Duo nicht vorbestellt? Was ihr jetzt vor dem Kauf wissen müsst
articles.text:
iPhone Duo ohne Vorbestellung kaufen? Was ihr vorab wissen müsst
Foldables stecken nach wie vor in der Nische. Nur etwa 1,6 Prozent der verkauften Smartphones weltweit sind faltbar. Mit dem Verkaufsstart des iPhone Duo könnte sich das ändern. Schließlich hat das Gerät zur Vorstellung immense mediale Aufmerksamkeit erfahren – auch dank einer cleveren Animation beim Öffnen und Schließen. Wie bei vielen neuen iPhones werden vor allem Early Adopter früh dabei sein wollen, um zu zeigen, dass sie die begehrte Neuheit schon am ersten Tag in der Tasche haben. Entsprechend schlecht stehen offenbar die Chancen, ohne Vorbestellung an ein Gerät zu kommen.
Kann ich das iPhone Duo einfach so kaufen?
Der Vorbestellungszeitraum startete am 16. Oktober. Eine Woche später, am 23. Oktober, werden die Bestellungen ausgeliefert. Vorausgesetzt, man war wirklich fix mit der Vorbestellung. Denn schon nach wenigen Minuten hat sich das Lieferdatum nach hinten verschoben. Wer heute (Stand: 21. Oktober) ein iPhone Duo bei Apple bestellen will, muss sich schon bis Ende Januar 2027, bis das Paket mit dem Foldable nach Hause kommt. Bei Händlern wie Mediamarkt oder Saturn sieht das nicht viel anders aus.
Dabei geht es allerdings um den Online-Versand des Smartphones. Wie sieht es also vor Ort aus? Wie MacRumors berichtet, sollen zumindest manche Mitarbeiter:innen der Apple-Stores dazu angewiesen worden sein, Kund:innen ohne Vorbestellung davon abzuhalten, in die Geschäfte zu kommen. Sie sollen stattdessen darauf hinweisen, dass sie auf der Suche nach dem Gerät wahrscheinlich enttäuscht werden. Ob die Vorgabe weltweit gelte, sei allerdings unklar. So oder so: Die Chancen, ein iPhone Duo ohne Reservierung an Tag eins zu ergattern, scheinen schlecht zu stehen.
Einen Funken Hoffnung gibt es noch für den Tag danach. Denn Informationen zum sogenannten Walk-in-Purchase, also der Abholung einer Bestellung im Laden, will Apple ab dem 24. Oktober teilen – auch in Deutschland. Das alleine garantiert aber natürlich noch nicht, dass ausreichend oder überhaupt Geräte vor Ort zur Verfügung stehen.
Brauche ich Apple Care für das iPhone Duo?
Eine Streitfrage bei jedem iPhone-Neukauf: Lohnt sich die Investition in Apple Care Plus? Schließlich kostet die Zusatzversicherung fürs iPhone 20,99 Euro im Monat oder 209,99 Euro im Jahr. Trotz des ohnehin schon hohen Startpreises von 2.299 Euro ist es aber eine Überlegung wert, Apple Care Plus abzuschließen. Denn Foldables gelten nach wie vor als empfindlich und weniger robust als „normale“ Smartphones.
Deswegen solltet ihr zunächst einen Blick auf die Reparaturkosten werfen, die anstehen, wenn das iPhone Duo Schaden nimmt. Der Austausch der Displayschutzfolie des faltbaren Bildschirms ist mit 49 Euro noch einigermaßen erschwinglich. Nimmt das Display aber ernsthaft Schaden, wird es teuer. 1.149 Euro kostet euch die Reparatur ohne Apple Care Plus. Mit dem Zusatzservice sind die Reparaturen zwar nicht gratis, aber wie 9to5Mac berichtet, sinken die Kosten für die Reparatur des inneren Displays auf 99 US-Dollar. Deutsche Preise lassen sich bislang nicht nachvollziehen.
Was ändert sich an der Software?
Auf dem iPhone Duo läuft iOS 27, aber mit ein paar kleineren Änderungen. So befindet sich das Dock nicht mehr unten am Bildschirmrand, sondern rechts an der Seite. Das soll die einhändige Bedienung erleichtern. Außerdem unterstützt das Gerät Multitasking. Wie auf dem iPad ist es möglich, sich auf dem großen Bildschirm zwei Apps im Splitscreen anzeigen zu lassen. Erweiterte Funktionen wie Stage Manager oder den Fenstermodus gibt es allerdings nicht.
Auf der Keynote im September 2027 zeigte das Unternehmen außerdem bereits angepasste Apps wie Netflix oder Slack, die das äußere und das innere Display clever nutzen. Ob das zum Start bei jeder bekannten App so funktionieren wird, bleibt abzuwarten. Entwickler müssen ihre Anwendungen erst an die neuen Formate und dynamischen Größen anpassen. Der Wechsel von der vorherigen auf die neue Liquid-Glass-Designsprache hat gezeigt, dass nicht Anbieter von Tag 1 dabei ist.
Verzichten müsst ihr, wie bei anderen iPhones auch, zunächst auf Siri AI. Apple bringt die KI‑Assistenz vorerst nicht in die EU. Das Duo ist hier kein Sonderfall.
Brauche ich eine Schutzhülle für das iPhone Duo?
Wie gesagt: Foldables sind empfindliche Geräte, auf die es gut achtzugeben gilt. Eine Schutzhülle kann da von Vorteil sein. Es muss ja nicht gleich die 150-Euro-Hülle mit eingebautem Kickstand von Apple sein. Auf den etablierten Plattformen bieten bereits mehrere Hersteller Modelle für um die 30 Euro an.
Wie ihr das Foldable darüber hinaus bestmöglich schützt, könnt ihr zudem in diesem Ratgeber nachlesen.
Was muss ich sonst noch über das iPhone Duo wissen?
Anders als bei anderen Smartphone ist das innere Display beim iPhone nicht glänzend, sondern matt. Das reduziert nicht nur Spiegeleffekte, es soll auch dafür sorgen, dass die Bildschirmfalte nicht so gut sichtbar ist.
Außerdem hat das Gerät keinen Schacht für Sim-Karten. Ihr braucht für die Nutzung im Mobilfunknetz also eine E-Sim. Die sollte euch euer Provider in der Regel kostenlos zur Verfügung stellen.

Fintech
MNT-Halan rises 6.6% on Egypt trading debut
One of Africa’s most closely watched initial public offerings (IPOs) has finally happened. MNT-Halan, Egypt’s fintech unicorn, ended its first day on the Egyptian Exchange (EGX) 6.6% above its IPO price, after jumping as much as 18% earlier in the session.
The debut follows a heavily oversubscribed offering that raised about EGP 7.84 billion ($150 million) from selling a 20% stake in its local Egyptian business. Retail investors had demanded far more shares than were available, while the institutional tranche was also oversubscribed several times over.
Why does the first day matter? Oversubscription tells you investors wanted shares at the offer price. Trading tells you what they are willing to pay once the IPO allocation disappears and buyers have to meet sellers in the open market. MNT-Halan closing higher suggests the EGP24.50 ($0.47) offer price left enough room for new investors to make money without giving away too much value.
There is an important wrinkle, though. The IPO itself was a secondary sale; existing shareholder MNT Investments sold the shares and received the proceeds. MNT-Halan did not raise fresh capital directly from the listing. Its shareholder has separately said it plans to inject up to EGP4 billion ($76 million) into the Egyptian business.
Between the lines: MNT-Halan’s debut is also bigger than MNT-Halan. Last week, some Egyptian fund managers sold existing stocks to free up cash for this IPO and others behind it. A strong first day gives them a reason to keep going.
Banque du Caire, Egypt’s sixth-largest commercial bank, is next, and its planned offering could be much larger. MNT-Halan has now given Egypt’s IPO pipeline something every market needs before the next big sale: a buyer who made money.
Happy customer service week.
Your success and ours are the same story. Happy Customer Service Week. This year’s theme is The Extra Mile, and it’s the only way we know how to do this. Visit: fincra.com.
Streaming
Netflix lays off Africa content boss in global shake-up
Netflix, the global streaming platform, spent the past decade building a local content library in Africa. One month after celebrating ten years in South Africa, one of the executives who helped build it is out.
The company has laid off Ben Amadasun, its vice president of content for the Middle East and Africa. He joined in 2019 to lead African content acquisitions and co-productions, and eventually rose to oversee content across the Middle East and Africa. Kaye Ann Williams, Netflix’s director of scripted content for sub-Saharan Africa, will now lead its content strategy. Netflix’s current investment in African content is reportedly unchanged.
Explain like I’m new here: Netflix has become unusually important to Africa’s film industry. Amazon Prime Video stopped commissioning African originals in 2024, while Showmax shut down as a standalone streaming service earlier this year. Netflix is now one of the few global platforms still regularly commissioning African productions at scale.
South Africa shows how large that role has become. Netflix said it has worked with more than 30 local production companies, supported over 8,000 jobs, and carried more than 300 South African titles since 2016. In October, Williams said Netflix now commissions 15 to 20 South African titles annually, up from eight to 12.
In September, Netflix announced another large South African slate, and local productions can still travel. The Polygamist, a South African Netflix original, reached Top 10 in 62 countries on the streaming platform.
Between the lines: Content budgets are ultimately allocation decisions. Losing a senior executive who represented Africa matters most when those budgets are being fought over. Netflix is cutting about 1,000 jobs globally, has replaced its chief content officer, and Ted Sarandos, the company’s chief executive officer, has explicitly said he sees room to strengthen the slate in the United States and Canada.
What to watch: Watch the commissions. If Netflix keeps ordering 15 to 20 South African titles a year, funds more productions elsewhere on the continent and maintains production budgets, the Africa strategy is intact. If those numbers start shrinking, Amadasun’s departure will certainly look more consequential
Ten years of telling African tech stories.
Class of 2016, stand up! Meet the storytellers behind a decade of storytelling for African tech. 230+ startups, VCs, and more. From first cheques to unicorns. Have a story to tell? Let’s make it count. #TheWimbarts
Banking
Nedbank now owns NCBA. But its shares are temporarily off the NSE
We’re nearing the tail end of South African lender Nedbank’s takeover of NCBA Group, one of East Africa’s largest banking groups. The deal was first announced in January.
Almost 80% of NCBA shareholders accepted the offer, giving Nedbank more than enough support to take its planned 66% controlling stake in the Kenyan bank. Now, NCBA’s shares are taking a short break from the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE) while the paperwork catches up with the deal.
What happened? NCBA shares will be suspended from NSE trading after market close on 21 October. Trading will resume on November 2.
Explain like I’m new here: NCBA shareholders tendered 79.9% of the bank to Nedbank, more than what they asked for.Now that the deal has cleared its final conditions, it’s time to transfer the shares and settle payments. The suspension is meant to freeze trading in NCBA shares; the shareholder register can be finalised without new purchases or sales muddying the numbers.
NCBA is not in trouble. The suspension also gives NCBA and the NSE time to pay shareholders who have accepted the offer and prepare the transfer of the shares. On November 3, about 1.087 billion NCBA shares will be transferred to Nedbank.
Shareholders will get paid that day in newly issued Nedbank shares and cash, depending on the offer’s terms. Nedbank expects to announce the final transaction results on November 5.
What happens after that? If everything goes to plan, Nedbank will take control of a 66% stake in NCBA; the remaining 34% stays with minority shareholders. NCBA retains its name, Nairobi headquarters, and local leadership. Nedbank will gain a deeper foothold in East Africa, including Uganda and Tanzania, and expand its digital banking operations in Ghana, Côte d’Ivoire, and Ethiopia, where NCBA already operates.

Spiro enters Ghana with 100 electric motorcycles
Spiro, Africa’s most-funded e-mobility company, has launched its first 100 bikes in Accra, Ghana. The company announced on Tuesday that it is introducing the Ekon 450 M1 v3 motorcycle and a battery-swapping system.
Spiro is the latest electric motorcycle company to expand into a new market, after ARC Mobility, the Kenyan-focused e-bike maker, entered South Africa in September.
Explain like I’m new here: Spiro’s expansion push is coming amid its fundraising haul. Since the start of 2026, it has raised over $300 million and turned its focus to a battery-swapping network as a moat. With large networks, Spiro makes money from subscriptions, helping it lock in riders.
To support its manufacturing ambitions, it acquired UK-based engineering firm Coexlion in May to bring production in-house. This helps it control inventory costs, offering it a predictable way to assess risks for its asset-financing business.
Ghana’s motorcycle market is opening up: Ghana is becoming a more interesting market for commercial two-wheelers. The country spent years prohibiting commercial passenger transport by motorcycle under its old road traffic rules.
The Road Traffic (Amendment) Act, 2025, and Road Traffic Regulations, 2026, have created a legal framework for commercial motorcycle operations, subject to requirements including a valid commercial rider’s licence. However, Spiro will face competition. Ghanaian electric mobility firm Kofa already operates a battery-swapping network, while Wahu Mobility offers e-bikes and services aimed at working riders.

articles.title: Memory Bugs Account for Most of Chrome’s 353 New Security Fixes
articles.text:
Google on Tuesday announced the promotion of Chrome 156 to the stable channel with patches for 353 vulnerabilities.
Most of the resolved security defects were memory safety flaws, including 163 memory corruption bugs, 125 use-after-free issues, and 17 out-of-bounds reads. Of the remaining weaknesses, 36 are improper input validations.
The browser refresh resolves six critical-severity vulnerabilities: five memory corruption defects and one use-after-free bug.
Chrome 156 also resolves 61 high-severity security issues, 197 medium-severity flaws, and 89 low-severity weaknesses.
Google makes no mention of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild.
Per the internet giant’s advisory, no bug bounty reward will be paid for 285 vulnerabilities. They were either found by Google (266), Xinyang Ge (Anthropic – assisted by Claude), or OpenAI Codex Security.
Google says it handed out $50,000 in bug bounties for 24 of the vulnerabilities, but the final amount will likely be much higher, as the company has not disclosed the amounts paid for 44 of the flaws.
Quyen Son at VinFast received the highest reward, of $10,000, for a high-severity use-after-free issue in Site Isolation.
The latest Chrome iteration is now rolling out as versions 156.0.8078.47/.48 for Windows and macOS, and as version 156.0.8078.47 for Linux.

articles.title: Première mondiale en Ukraine : un drone géant évacue un soldat blessé directement depuis la ligne de front
articles.text:
Bloqué depuis près de 500 jours dans une position de première ligne sous la menace constante des tirs ennemis, un combattant de la 30e brigade mécanisée a pu être exfiltré grâce à un hexacoptère lourd « Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 », conçu par le fabricant Gurzuf Defense. Alors que les méthodes traditionnelles d’évacuation par le sol étaient rendues impossibles par les mines et l’activité des drones russes, les forces ukrainiennes ont mis en place cette mission d’urgence pour sauver le soldat retranché.
Une mission d’extraction par drone sous haute tension
L’opération a nécessité une coordination importante entre plusieurs brigades et le fabricant pour acheminer d’abord du matériel spécifique avec des mousquetons vers le blessé. Le soldat a ensuite pu s’attacher lui-même à un système de treuil fixé sous le drone, piloté à distance par des opérateurs restés en liaison avec lui. Le vol a duré exactement 1 heure, 14 minutes et 36 secondes, couvrant une distance de 62 kilomètres sous surveillance de l’espace aérien et avec protection.
Le cofondateur de Gurzuf Defense, Pavlo Feldblium, précise que cette technique d’évacuation par les airs comporte des risques pour le blessé et doit rester un dernier recours lorsque toutes les autres solutions échouent. Le modèle Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 pèse environ 98 kilos, possède une autonomie de vol jusqu’à 25 kilomètres avec une capacité de charge de 70 à 90 kilos, et évolue à une altitude opérationnelle comprise entre 150 et 300 mètres.
Des innovations face à l’impasse des terrains minés
Cette première intervention réussie ouvre la voie à une nouvelle manière de gérer des blessés sur les théâtres d’opérations où la surveillance constante par drone complique les secours « traditionnels ». Les véhicules robotisés terrestres risquent en effet d’être la cible de tirs et peinent à traverser des terrains accidentés, ce qui laisse souvent les soldats bloqués pendant des jours.
D’autres initiatives industrielles sont également en développement, à l’image du drone StarGate conçu par SkyFall (que vous pouvez voir dans la vidéo ci-dessus), qui intègre un conteneur civière et des fonctions d’autonomie basées sur l’intelligence artificielle pour faire face aux situations de brouillage GPS. La systématisation de ces évacuations aériennes exigera dans tous les cas un travail rigoureux de planification pour chaque mission en fonction des conditions sur le terrain à l’instant T.
