articles.title: Distributed Spring Batch Without a Message Broker
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- Spring Batch can scale horizontally without a message broker by using the relational database it already requires as the coordination plane. It fits the small-to-medium clusters many teams run.
- The pattern solves the problems a broker otherwise handles for you: sizing work to the live node count, assigning per-execution master responsibility with no standing coordinator, and claiming partitions with compare-and-set writes so no partition is silently lost.
- Node failure is handled by heartbeats and a two-phase recovery. It marks a stale node as unreachable, then after a grace period window, removes it and reassigns its incomplete, transferable partitions.
- Correctness is an explicit contract. Transferable work runs at least once and must be idempotent; nontransferable work runs at most once and is failed rather than moved. A partition is never silently lost.
- Database coordination fits where operational simplicity and cost matter most. Its ceiling is database contention and past that point, at very large clusters or sub-second latency, a broker remains the better choice.
Introduction
Spring Batch has been the default framework for batch processing on the JVM for more than a decade. Jobs are built from steps, such as chunk-oriented readers, processors, and writers, with a metadata repository that makes runs restartable. For the nightly extract, transform, load (ETL), financial reconciliation, and data-validation workloads on a single machine, it is hard to beat.
The pressure appears when one machine is no longer enough. A reconciliation run that once fit inside its window grows with the business until it does not and the natural response is to spread the work across nodes. The established answer from Spring Batch is remote partitioning. A manager step divides the work into partitions and dispatches them to workers over a message broker such as Apache Kafka, RabbitMQ, or a JMS provider, via Spring Integration.
Remote partitioning is a proven approach. When a broker is already part of the platform it is the right one. But a broker is an extra operational tier and many teams would otherwise never run one. They already operate a well-managed relational database (Spring Batch requires one for its job repository regardless). Teams have little appetite for standing up, securing, and monitoring a messaging cluster solely to fan out batch partitions.
This article describes an alternative for that common case: coordinating a distributed, fault-tolerant Spring Batch job across a small-to-medium cluster using only the shared database. It is not an argument against brokers, but an account of what it takes to remove one from this job, where the approach’s boundaries lie and where a broker is still the better tool.
Where Single-Node Batch Ends and the Broker Question Begins
If you reduce the distributed batch to its essentials, four questions need to be answered through whatever your coordination.
First, how is the work divided and across how many workers? Split too coarsely and nodes sit idle; split too finely and overhead grows for nothing. The right number depends on how much capacity exists when the job starts.
Second, who is in charge of a given run? Something has to split the work, track it to completion, and finalize the job. In broker-based partitioning, that is the node running the manager step.
Third, how does a worker take ownership of a partition without a second worker also running it? Run it twice and you can corrupt data. Run it zero times and the job is silently incomplete.
Fourth, what happens when a node dies mid-run? Its in-flight work has to be detected and, where safe, recovered automatically, without violating the third requirement.
A broker answers some of these questions for you. Its queue hands each message to a single consumer and dispatch is decoupled from execution, so a slow or dead worker does not stall the producer. Take the broker away and every question has to be explicitly answered, in SQL, against a store built for durable shared state rather than message dispatch. The rest of this article is about answering them well.
Structuring Database-Coordinated Partitioning
The design treats the database Spring Batch already needs as the sole coordination plan without broker or coordination service such as Apache ZooKeeper and no deployment platform. Every piece of cluster state lives in ordinary SQL tables, so the whole cluster is inspectable with a SELECT statement.
Three tables augment Spring Batch’s own schema. The BATCH_NODES table is the node registry, having one row per node, with its status (active or unreachable), its last heartbeat timestamp, and its current load. The BATCH_PARTITIONS table tracks the partition lifecycle, having one row per partition and keyed by that partition’s own step-execution ID (each partition is itself a Spring Batch StepExecution, distinct from the manager step that scopes the run), with its assigned node, its status (pending, claimed, completed, or failed), and whether or not it may be transferred to another node on failure. The BATCH_JOB_COORDINATION table binds each job execution to its master node and manager step, with a status of its own. What matters here is the shape of these three tables, not their full column lists.
One thing this design does not remove is the need for a shared, persistent job repository, but that requirement is intrinsic to distributed partitioning, not something added by this pattern. A partition’s payload, the execution context describing its slice of work, is written by the master and read back by whichever node executes it. The master then reads the result back to be aggregated. That handoff is a cross-JVM exchange of Spring Batch metadata, so the store has to be shared and durable. Spring Batch’s own remote partitioning imposes the same requirement. There, the broker carries only a pointer to the partition, never its data. What this design removes is the broker, not the repository. The one shared database serves as both the metadata store and the coordination plane.
Coordination is decentralized by design. There is no standing master elected for the whole cluster. That approach would reintroduce the leader-election machinery and single point of failure that dropping the broker avoids. Instead, the node that launches a job becomes that job’s master, for that execution only (a later section walks through what it does). Two jobs launched on two different nodes have two different masters running at the same time. Because mastership is scoped to a single job execution, losing a master affects only that one job, never the cluster. There is no coordinator to elect and none to lose.
Reusing Spring Batch’s Partitioning Hooks: The Entry Point
For a Spring Batch developer the first question is practical: Where does my code plug in and how much of it changes? The answer is almost none, which makes the approach usable. That simplicity falls out of an extension point Spring Batch has always had.
Spring Batch already splits a partitioned step into two independent responsibilities. A Partitioner interface decides how work is split. It produces a set of named ExecutionContext objects, one per partition, each describing a slice of the input. A separate PartitionHandler decides how those partitions are executed. The built-in TaskExecutorPartitionHandler runs them in local threads, while Spring Batch’s own remote partitioning swaps in a MessageChannelPartitionHandler that ships them over a broker. The manager step is assembled from these two pieces plus a StepExecutionAggregator that combines the results:
new StepBuilder("reconcileStep.manager", jobRepository)
    .partitioner("reconcileStep", clusterAwarePartitioner) // how work is split
    .partitionHandler(clusterAwarePartitionHandler)         // how partitions are distributed
    .step(reconcileStep)                                    // the ordinary worker step
    .aggregator(aggregator)
    .build();
That partitionHandler(...) line is the whole seam. Because Spring Batch treats partition distribution as a pluggable strategy, this approach supplies its own PartitionHandler, one that writes partition rows to the database and monitors them in the slot the broker-backed handler would otherwise occupy. The partitioner is a subclass of Spring Batch’s own Partitioner. Nothing else moves. The worker step (reconcileStep above) is an ordinary chunk- or tasklet-based step, results aggregate through the standard StepExecutionAggregator, and a restart works through the standard JobRepository. A developer comfortable with local partitioning writes the same manager step and changes exactly two beans, the Partitioner and the PartitionHandler.
That covers the manager. Turning the same deployable into a cluster member is configuration, not code. A single flag enables the behavior with auto-configuration registering the node, starting its heartbeat, and starting a poller, without either a broker client or extra beans. A few intervals tune that behavior, including heartbeat cadence, worker poll cadence, per-node concurrency, and the two heartbeat-age thresholds that drive failover, with production-sane defaults (a node is marked as unreachable at about ten seconds and removed at about thirty seconds).
From then on, every node, master and workers alike, runs one loop. On startup it inserts itself into the BATCH_NODES table and heartbeats on the configured interval, publishing its current load, which is the number of partitions it is running right now. On each poll, it scans the BATCH_PARTITIONS table for rows assigned to it, claims them with the compare-and-set update shown later, and then does the one thing that keeps the programming model intact: It looks up the worker step by name and runs it. That name is not arbitrary. It is the name passed to the .partitioner("reconcileStep", ...) method on the manager, recorded in the coordination row, so the worker resolves the same Spring Batch step bean and executes it with the partition’s ExecutionContext. Each node runs up to a configured number of partitions at once and when a step finishes it records it as COMPLETED or FAILED.
So the coordination lives behind extension points Spring Batch already asks you to implement, turned on by configuration rather than new code.
Implementing It on a Spring Batch Cluster
Figure 1. Architecture, a per-job master and worker nodes coordinating through the shared database. (Source: created by author.)
Figure 1 shows the runtime shape. A standing set of peer JVM nodes each register in the BATCH_NODES table and heartbeat. When a job is launched on one of them, that node acts as master for that run. It queries the live nodes, sizes the split to them, writes the partition rows, and monitors to completion, while every node, master included, polls for and executes the partitions assigned to it.
How the Master Step Drives the Run
The master step is not exotic. It is an ordinary Spring Batch partitioned (manager) step, running on whichever node launched the job. What makes that node the master is where the PartitionHandler runs. When Spring Batch executes the manager step, it calls the handler’s handle(...) method on that node, and the database-backed PartitionHandler blocks there until the whole distributed run is finished.
Inside that single call, the master does four things in order. First it records the run, writing a new row in the BATCH_JOB_COORDINATION table that ties this job execution to the manager step’s execution ID as the run’s identity and marks it as STARTED. Then it writes one PENDING row per partition into the BATCH_PARTITIONS table, each tagged with the node to which it is assigned. Then it runs a monitor loop, waking on a short interval to reassign any partitions orphaned by a removed node (their assigned node is gone from the BATCH_NODES table) and to check whether any partition is still PENDING or CLAIMED. Finally, when nothing is outstanding, it fails the manager step if any partition ends as FAILED, otherwise it marks the coordination row as COMPLETED, hands the workers’ step executions to the StepExecutionAggregator, and finishes the job.
Notice what is absent. Workers never call the master and the master never calls the workers. Every decision the master makes, it makes by reading and writing these rows. That is why losing a master is contained rather than causing a cluster outage. Its state is in the database, not in the memory of a coordinator.
Enterprise Scenario
Consider nightly financial reconciliation across dynamically provisioned cloud nodes. The dataset is large enough that if one node misses the batch window, a well-managed relational database is already in place. The operations team has no appetite for a broker purely for this workload. The same shape recurs in mid-sized ETL and in data-validation jobs where each partition is a slice of input that must be recoverable if a node dies. These are the conditions this pattern targets.
Sizing Work to the Live Cluster
Standard remote partitioning splits work before it knows how much capacity exists to run it. The grid size is chosen blind, often as a fixed constant, and the pieces are dispatched into the broker to be picked up as capacity frees. Without a broker, you have to face this issue directly. Before splitting, the master asks the database which nodes are currently alive and passes that count into the partitioner. The partitioner exposes one method that takes this live node count and returns the partitions, so the split is sized to the cluster that actually exists at that instant.
Each partition is expressed as a Spring Batch ExecutionContext, the framework’s key-value carrier for a partition’s input. The parameters that define one slice of work (a row range, a file name, and an ID window) go in and the worker step reads them back to know what to process. Because the partitioner is handed the live count, it can choose the partition count for the cluster at hand, using either one or two per live node or whatever the workload calls for.
An assignment strategy then maps those partitions onto nodes: round-robin for even distribution and fixed-node-count to confine a job to n nodes, or least-loaded, which places each partition on the node reporting the lowest current load and steers work toward the nodes that are most idle. Because assignment is both capacity-sized and load-aware, the split matches the cluster that exists instead of a number fixed in advance. Assignment is fixed at that point. It is placement, rather than runtime rebalancing, so a node that finishes early does not pull partitions from a slower peer and only node failure moves work. That runtime rebalancing is one thing a broker’s pull semantics give for free and this trades away.
Claiming Work Without Double-Execution
Once partitions are written and assigned, each worker independently polls for its PENDING partitions and transitions them to CLAIMED before executing. That transition is the correctness-critical moment, a single guarded statement that drives every worker transition, with the target status passed in as a parameter.
-- claim, then later complete or fail: one guarded UPDATE
UPDATE batch_partitions
SET    status = ?,                 -- CLAIMED, then COMPLETED or FAILED
       last_updated = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
WHERE  step_execution_id = ?
  AND  assigned_node = ?
  AND  status IN ('PENDING', 'CLAIMED');
The WHERE clause is the whole point. It explains why CLAIMED appears on both sides. It admits only a row that is still PENDING or CLAIMED, so once a partition reaches a terminal state (COMPLETED or FAILED) or is reassigned, no late write can move it. For the claim, the row starts as PENDING. Also, allowing CLAIMED makes a reclaim idempotent and allows the same statement to carry the later COMPLETED and FAILED writes, which start from CLAIMED.
Two properties then prevent double execution. First, each partition is assigned to exactly one node at partition time, so under normal operation only that node polls for its row. Second, both the worker’s write and the master’s reassignment are guarded. The worker’s write is guarded by the assigned_node and the PENDING/CLAIMED status, the reassignment is guarded by that status as it moves the row back to PENDING under a new node. So if a stalled node completes its partition just as the master reassigns it, the second write matches nothing. If the master went first, the completion fails because assigned_node no longer points to that node. If the node went first, the reassignment fails because the status is already terminal. Either way, exactly one write takes effect. This is not a contended pull-queue with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED statements. Partitions are preassigned, so the guarded update governs the lifecycle, not the dispatch. The one-partition-one-node guarantee a broker gives through its queue here comes from row-level state transitions.
Recovering From Node Failure
Figure 2. Node lifecycle and two-phase failover. (Source: created by author.)
Nodes fail. Liveness here is tracked directly rather than inferred from broker acknowledgements. Every node updates a heartbeat timestamp on an interval, using the database clock rather than its own. The staleness check compares against that same clock, so liveness is unaffected by skew between the machines’ own clocks. Detection and removal are decentralized. Every node runs the cleanup sweeps, so no single monitor’s death blinds the cluster. Reassigning a removed node’s partitions, though, is done by each affected job’s own master in the monitor loop described earlier.
Recovery is a two-phase process, as shown in Figure 2. In phase one, a node whose heartbeat is older than the unreachable threshold (ten seconds by default) is flipped from active to unreachable. In phase two, a node that is still stale past the longer cleanup threshold (thirty seconds) is removed. Its incomplete partitions are resolved by contract. Transferable partitions become eligible for reassignment and non-transferable partitions are marked as FAILED so the job fails cleanly rather than risking a second run. The gap between the thresholds is a grace period window and is there on purpose. A brief garbage collection pause or network blip marks a node as unreachable without taking its work and it recovers on its next heartbeat. Only sustained absence escalates to removal. Reassignment reuses the same compare-and-set discipline as claiming, so a partition that has reached COMPLETED in the meantime is never resurrected.
Best Practices and Gotchas: Making Database Coordination Production-Ready
Treat Transferability as a Contract, Not a Hint
The most consequential design decision is that transferability is declared, not inferred. Each partition carries one bit of metadata. If the node running the partition dies, is that work safe to rerun elsewhere? The partitioner implementation marks each partition as transferable or not, with the framework following that marking exactly rather than deciding on its own. (In the reference implementation it is a method the partitioner overrides.)
Transferable partitions assert the work is idempotent and safe to rerun, an at-least-once guarantee. On node loss, a partition is reassigned and may run twice. Non-transferable partitions assert the opposite, at-most-once. On node loss a partition is failed rather than moved and is never run elsewhere. Summing a numeric range is transferable, but appending to an external ledger or calling a pay-once API is not. This choice is a correctness contract, so decide per partition on whether the work is idempotent.
Rely on Fencing, but Do Not Trust It Alone
A node that loses its own heartbeat stops claiming work and aborts before running a claimed partition, leaving it for the master to reassign. This fencing shrinks the window in which two nodes run the same transferable partition, but it is best effort. A hard-paused JVM can wake and finish work already reassigned, so transferable work must be truly idempotent. What the system never relaxes is that no partition is silently lost. The partition either completes, or the job fails.
Design Restarts to Be Idempotent
Worker failure is automatic, but master failure is harder. When a surviving node finds a coordination row still in flight whose master has left, it atomically claims the stranded job and marks it as failed, so the job is cleanly restartable rather than being stuck forever. Recovery is fail-and-restart, not resume-in-place, so a job can restart even when its master has died after every partition completed but before finalizing. Restarts must therefore be idempotent. This requirement also binds the at-most-once guarantee to a single execution. A lost master forces a restart while its workers may still be finishing, so non-transferable work that must survive one needs a reconciliation step on restart. Automatic takeover, resuming a job without a restart, is on the roadmap. The open work is making that takeover safe when two nodes could otherwise both act as the master.
Run the Database Like a Critical Dependency
Once the database is the coordination plane, it is a hard dependency for the whole cluster, so run it replicated with backup and failover suited to the workload. The payoff for this design is that all coordination states are plain SQL. You diagnose a stuck run with a SELECT statement against the BATCH_PARTITIONS table rather than a broker console. Index the hot polling and completion-scan queries so they never fall to table scans.
Know Where the Ceiling Is
The pattern targets roughly two to twenty nodes and the ceiling is database contention, not a fixed node count. Heartbeats, polling, and status updates are all database traffic. That traffic is modest on a small-to-medium cluster, but it grows with node count and job concurrency until it competes with the batch workload for the same connection pool and I/O. Validate the range under your own load.
Trade-offs: When to Use Database Coordination and When to Reach for a Broker
Database coordination is not a universal replacement for broker-based partitioning. Choose it when the database is already present and well-managed, when operational simplicity and cost matter more than raw scale, when adding messaging middleware is impractical (constrained environments, limited operations capacity, and portability across clouds) and when the cluster sits in the small-to-medium range.
Reach for a broker when the cluster grows past that range into many dozens of nodes, when sub-second coordination latency is required, when the batch platform already shares a mature streaming backbone with other workloads, or when the work maps naturally onto the broker’s delivery and ordering semantics. The shared database also becomes a dependency you must manage at a high standard. If that approach is unrealistic, a broker’s separation of concerns may serve better.
It helps to place the database-coordinated approach against its neighbors. Spring Batch’s own remote partitioning dispatches over a broker with no built-in awareness of how many workers are live and no automatic reassignment when a worker dies after receiving a partition, which are the gaps this pattern closes. The Spring Cloud Task deployer-based partition handler is also broker-free, but it provisions a worker per partition through a platform such as Kubernetes, whereas this pattern coordinates a standing cluster of peer JVM nodes that poll for work. Database-coordinated schedulers such as Quartz, db-scheduler, and JobRunr share the instinct of coordinating through a database and failing over on node loss, but they target scheduling or general background jobs rather than Spring Batch partitioned-step execution.
Conclusion
Removing the broker from distributed Spring Batch does not delete a requirement so much as move it into SQL. The same four questions a broker answers implicitly (sizing, coordination, single ownership, and node failure) get explicit answers: a live-node count feeding the partitioner, a per-job master with no standing coordinator, compare-and-set lifecycle transitions, and a two-phase heartbeat failover. The payoff is horizontal scaling and automatic recovery with nothing in the stack beyond the database Spring Batch already required.
The database is already there and is put to work for the common case where a broker would only add moving parts. The database has a real ceiling. Knowing where that ceiling sits is most useful. The takeaway is that a relational database used as a coordination plane is enough to run correct, fault-tolerant distributed batches for the many teams whose scale never demanded a broker.
Author’s Note
The design described here is drawn from spring-batch-db-cluster-partitioning, an open-source framework the author built and maintains, which was peer-reviewed and published in the Journal of Open Source Software. It is the worked example because it is the implementation the author knows in full detail; the patterns transfer whether a reader adopts it or builds their own. The full multi-database schemas, code, and a runnable multi-node example are available in the open-source repository.

articles.title: Former international boxer’s LegalTech startup EstateMin raises €1 million to scale in the US | EU-Startups
articles.text:
EstateMin, an Irish-founded LegalTech startup helping trust and estate law firms manage estate values with its AI-powered platform, has secured €1 million in pre-Seed funding.
The funding round saw participation from NDRC, First Port Syndicate, and Enterprise Ireland, which invested through its High Potential Start-Up programme. Angel investors Mike Hanrahan, Moira McKenna, and Conor Stanley also participated alongside other Irish angels.
“The real benefit for our clients is how much easier EstateMin makes it to get us information. Executors and family members can complete their intake right from the portal, on their own time, instead of juggling calls and paperwork during an already difficult process. That means their matter moves faster and they spend less time chasing us for updates,” said James Greenwood of Greenwood Law in Illinois.
Founded in Ireland in 2024 and now headquartered in Brooklyn, New York, EstateMin was built to solve a problem its co-founder and CEO, Isabella Hughes, experienced firsthand. A law graduate and former international boxer, Hughes spent time working as a legal executive, manually retyping client information into legal documents, a time-consuming process that she describes as unnecessary.
To solve this problem, she teamed up with Oisín Dolphin, a machine learning expert with over eight years of experience, who was drawn to the same problem after going through probate following the death of his father. The two met at an NDRC founder weekend at Dogpatch Labs in 2024. John Noonan, who brings more than four years of experience across product and consumer success at legal technology company Clio, subsequently joined as the third co-founder.
“What Oisín was describing was something I was doing every day. You don’t necessarily question it when it’s simply part of your job. Then somebody points out that you’re taking information a client has already provided and typing it all over again, and suddenly you realise how much time is being lost,” said Hughes, co-founder and CEO of EstateMin.
EstateMin’s AI-powered platform helps attorneys manage estate planning, estate administration and trust matters by digitising client intake, organising estate information, extracting data from documents and supporting form preparation. Its AI Case Reviewer scans files to flag missing fields, inconsistencies, or additional forms needed before a submission is finalised.
The platform integrates with existing legal case management systems, including Clio, and the company says it can become operational in about two minutes with minimal configuration. The platform is already helping trust and estate law firms manage more than €686 million ($770 million) in estate values across 777 matters.
Law firms reportedly save five to seven hours on each estate planning matter and five to ten hours on estate administrations. The platform is active across all 50 US states, and EstateMin is reporting 20% month-on-month revenue growth.
The journey to this point hasn’t been easy, with Hughes recounting a pivotal moment where they had to decide between the US and the UK. After initially building for Irish law firms and seeing slower adoption than expected, Hughes said they didn’t have the money to try everywhere and choose between the UK or take the bigger risk and expand to America.
“The response we’d had in New York was completely different, so we decided to go for it,” she explained.
The pre-Seed funding is earmarked for customer acquisition in the US, scaling EstateMin’s go-to-market operations, and expanding its engineering and product teams. The company has already hired two software engineers and added US business development capacity as part of its US push.
“EstateMin started with a very simple problem: why are highly trained legal professionals spending so much time retyping information? We’ve gone from working on that problem in Dogpatch Labs to building specifically for firms across America. Now we want to see how far we can take it,” Hughes added.

articles.title: Google Cloud and NVIDIA Announce General Availability of NVIDIA Vera Rubin Infrastructure
articles.text:
General availability of the instances is coming next month, with planned expansion of availability to Europe — bringing an integrated platform for training, inference and large-scale reinforcement learning to cloud customers.
A5X instances bring together NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72, NVIDIA ConnectX-9 SuperNICs, Google Cloud Virgo Network and Google Cloud’s fourth-generation advanced liquid-cooling technology for demanding agentic inference and reinforcement learning workloads at scale. Google Cloud plans to scale its Vera Rubin-based infrastructure to as many as 960,000 Rubin GPUs across multiple sites.
Ineffable Intelligence, a London-based technology company founded by AlphaGo creator David Silver, was the first customer to access A5X. Ineffable is using the platform to advance large-scale reinforcement learning and shape “superlearner” systems that learn continuously from experience.
Learning through interaction requires a continuous cycle of generating experience, evaluating outcomes and updating models, requiring infrastructure that can support the entire process at scale. A5X brings Vera Rubin into Google Cloud’s AI Hypercomputer as an integrated system, combining compute, networking and storage to support experience-driven learning at scale.
“We’re building superlearners that continually improve through their own experience,” said David Silver, founder and CEO of Ineffable Intelligence. “That demands both substantial compute and a tight connection between generating experience and training on it, so each improvement in the agent can quickly shape its next experience. Vera Rubin’s combination of compute performance and high-bandwidth connectivity, between the Vera CPU and Rubin GPUs and between the Rubin GPUs within the rack, allow us to push the scale and ambition of our reinforcement learning research further.”
WPP, a London-based marketing and communications company, has also demonstrated its creative agent reference architecture on NVIDIA Vera Rubin-based A5X instances using NVIDIA Nemotron models and NVIDIA OpenShell, part of the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture for safe AI agents.
The agents turn conversational requests into multistep creative workflows, such as video generation, upscaling and restyling, with human approval before execution. OpenShell provides governed sandboxes for agent execution, helping control access to sensitive brand assets and creative tools. In WPP’s initial tests, workloads that typically required a multi-node cluster ran on a single A5X instance.
As organizations deploy agentic systems, they need to protect the proprietary models and sensitive data that power these systems — even when running on infrastructure they don’t own.
Google Cloud will be among the first cloud providers to offer NVIDIA Confidential Computing at rack scale on bare metal instances such as A4X Max instances powered by NVIDIA GB300 NVL72. Additionally, Google Cloud is making Confidential Computing generally available on G4 VMs powered by NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs, offering a flexible platform for confidential inference and fine-tuning. Customers including Vertebrae, Polaris Cloud and Confidential Core AI are using Confidential G4 for conversational privacy, verifiable agent execution and policy-governed enterprise intelligence.
To support energy-efficient deployment at scale, Google Cloud and NVIDIA are exploring NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS capabilities for Vera Rubin-based infrastructure to help optimize performance per watt and expand capacity within available data-center power budgets.
Learn more about NVIDIA Vera Rubin and Google Cloud A5X instances.

articles.title: Solid-state batteries
articles.text:
Solid-state batteries
Batteries that swap liquid electrolytes for solid materials promise to charge faster, last longer, and (crucially) run cooler.
The rise of the lithium-ion battery, which powers everything from the smallest personal electronics to gargantuan energy storage systems, has been nothing short of revolutionary. But as anyone who’s boarded a plane in the last decade could tell you, storing and pumping out energy by moving charged lithium ions through a liquid electrolyte soup has its drawbacks, not least that the batteries have a troubling tendency to catch fire. Enter the solid-state battery, which swaps liquid for a solid ceramic or polymer, creating power packs that charge faster, last longer, cram more energy into smaller spaces, and (crucially) run cooler. A new generation of companies aim to bring such batteries to market, and if their bets pan out, the tech could substantially ease the shift away from fossil fuels.
The sticking points
Solid-state batteries have been “just a few years away” for more than a decade now. In laboratories, the technology works. But there have been challenges. In designs that pair the solid electrolyte with a lithium-metal anode (the side of the battery that releases electrons into an electrical circuit), needlelike filaments called dendrites tend to grow during charging, and they eventually push through the electrolyte and short the cell. Solid electrolytes are supposed to physically block the formation of dendrites, but many of them crack as the treelike projections break through like roots in a concrete foundation.
Then there’s the problem of manufacturing at scale. Mass production requires large quantities of defect-free sheets of ceramic-like material to make the electrolytes as well as dry rooms for assembly, since those electrolytes have a tendency to react with water. Would-be manufacturers quote a range of potential prices for solid-state batteries, but most expect them to fall in line with lithium-ion packs sometime in the mid-2030s.
The progress
Nascent as the technology is, solid-state batteries have already seen high-profile missteps. But one of America’s most advanced solid-state-battery companies says it’s closing in on being able to bring its product to market. The Bill Gates–backed QuantumScape launched in Silicon Valley in 2010 and built its battery around a class of ceramic materials that it says is compatible with lithium—meaning no dendrite formation. “We spent, then, like 10 years learning how to process it to satisfy all of the other requirements,” says Tim Holme, QuantumScape’s cofounder and chief technology officer. In 2025, the startup announced a proprietary, large-scale manufacturing method for quickly producing and heat-treating the ceramic electrolytes used in its batteries. “Nobody has ever done this in the field of ceramics before,” Holme claims. For 10,000 years, producing ceramics has involved slowly cooking the starting materials in an oven over the course of days. “We figured out a way to shorten that down to several minutes,” he says.
Plenty of other companies are pushing the tech forward as well. Toyota, the world’s biggest automaker, launched a research program on solid-state batteries way back in 2010. It’s now partnering with the global energy and petroleum company Idemitsu Kosan on a pilot plant, promising cars that can travel up to 745 miles after charging 10 minutes or less—a huge leap, if it works out. In China, CATL, the giant behind roughly 40% of the global battery market, is aggressively pursuing solid-state batteries too, pumping nearly $2.6 billion into a research program in 2024 alone. Mercedes, meanwhile, equipped one of its EQS sedans with solid-state batteries last fall; after driving nonstop for 750 miles, the car still had some range to spare.
Will the tech gain traction? Investing in vehicle batteries makes sense given the size of the potential market. But any little uptick in cost typically gets passed on to buyers, so the first solid-state EV batteries will inevitably be more expensive.
Grid storage buyers, who are working to meet the increasing demands posed by data centers, may also hesitate to purchase new technologies that still haven’t come down the cost curve. Then again, the promise of energy storage that lasts longer than lithium-ion’s typical eight hours could make them easier to persuade.
Some companies are taking a page from a playbook employed by outfits pursuing fusion: Focus on near-term markets with better margins to help fund development and bring down costs. Solid-state firms including California-based Solid Energies and Arizona-headquartered Sion Power are looking at selling batteries to the aviation industry or the military. “Those are sectors that are less sensitive to cost, and they typically require lower volumes as well,” says Evelina Stoikou, head analyst for battery technologies and supply chains at the consultancy BloombergNEF. “It’s a good way to prove your concept, then go through and fund the pilot plant where you can make that and eventually scale up.”
Progress meter ............ 7
The technology works, the capital is there, and demand is not far behind. But as with anything in manufacturing, unknown unknowns remain.

articles.title: OpenAI Agents Silenced Security Team Alerts, Removed Misalignment Monitor
articles.text:
OpenAI has disclosed that internal AI coding agents powered by GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra undercut its misalignment monitoring in two October incidents.
“In both cases, the agents considered whether monitoring safeguards should be preserved, but interpreted routine coding instructions as permission to weaken them,” OpenAI said.
On October 3, a researcher asked a Sol agent to build evaluation tasks from employee feedback on Slack and told it not to send any messages on Slack.
The pipeline stalled when the monitor flagged a planned fix but lacked the access needed to record its finding. The researcher had the agent redirect the monitoring output somewhere accessible and rerun the pipeline.
[ Read: OpenAI Models Hacked Data Portals, Raided a Crypto Wallet to Finish Tasks ]
Sol handed the repair to a subagent with orders to keep monitoring intact. The subagent ruled out suppressing notifications as unsafe, but Sol decided the “no messages” request covered the monitoring system too and ordered the suppression.
The patch removed every recipient of monitoring reports and blocked notifications, cutting off automatic alerts to OpenAI’s security team. Findings were still stored, but no one would be told about them.
On October 6, a user asked an Astra agent to update their code to mirror a reference implementation. Another agent had previously told Astra not to disable the monitor “even temporarily.”
Astra handed the work to a subagent, and both treated the task as license to remove the program’s monitoring integration in order to match the reference code.
Astra then reported the job done without mentioning the change and, when asked, denied removing monitoring.
OpenAI’s system pages its security team for immediate review only for P0 incidents, while lower-severity findings are not escalated right away. Neither event was rated P0, and neither agent’s work was automatically halted.
“We’ve seen several cases in which agents launched a deployment with misalignment monitoring disabled: the agent itself remained monitored, but that monitoring did not cover the deployment it launched,” the company said.
Auto-Review, required for all internal Codex use, has been updated to spot and stop attempts to turn off misalignment monitoring.
OpenAI also aims to require a valid safety case for each workload category, automatically shutting down workloads that lack one or fail to meet it.
The company has yet to determine whether the agents were simply overpersistent or prone to dodging monitoring. “We don’t yet have a satisfying explanation for this behavior,” it said.

articles.title: They want your blood
articles.text:
This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here.
They want your blood
Health tech companies want data from your blood in return for a vague promise of a longer life.
It’s an overcast Saturday morning when I give my 12th vial of blood for testing in six weeks. It’s my 24th this year. At this point, I feel like a pro. I schedule these blood draws first thing in the morning so I don’t get hangry, download the requisition papers ahead of time, avoid strenuous exercise for the 24 hours prior, and make sure to drink a glass of water beforehand so my teeny veins are easier for the phlebotomist to find.
In fairness, 12 of the 24 vials were ordered by my doctor to monitor ongoing treatment for a few metabolic issues. Eight were to feed my experimental digital twin. The last four are to test an app called Death Clock, which estimates when you’ll die based on your current health. Currently, the app says I’m going to die at 97 years old on Friday, October 5th, 2085.
For greatest accuracy, and to calculate my biological age, Death Clock offers a “free” blood panel with its $69 annual subscription. The app also offers various other optional, upsell panels recommended based on the health history you upload during onboarding. It suggested that I add on tests for thyroid function, heart and artery health, and liver function. On top of the blood panels, the app also recommended I try a continuous glucose monitor, buy a smart scale, buy a blood pressure monitor, get a professional VO2 max evaluation, schedule a liver ultrasound, screen for cervical cancer, start taking daily creatine monohydrate, schedule an annual full-body skin cancer exam, get a baseline coronary CT angiography, consider getting APOE testing for Alzheimer’s risk, and get a colonoscopy.
I was getting a vampiric promise of longevity. My blood was the roadmap to a long life. If I did everything the app’s “life lab” proposed, I could get an extra 17 years, dying at the ripe old age of 114 on September 12th, 2102.
Even so, watching my blood flow into yet another test tube, I thought of my parents. Blood is more than just a mix of plasma, iron, water, and nutrients. Metaphorically, it’s also a history of the family that came before you — and sometimes, though not always, clues to how they died.
Death Clock is a provocative name, but it’s hardly alone in wanting my blood. Oura and Whoop have already added partnerships with Quest Diagnostics, so their users can hand over their blood too. Google recently announced an integration with Function Health, a startup that makes it easy for people to order these kinds of lab tests. When Apple’s new Health app launches, that too will come with a Quest Diagnostics partnership. Blood is in, and more of these partnerships are undoubtedly on the way.
It’s not hard to guess why. Blood contains data — the thing that keeps health tech companies fed. In this age of personalized tech, what could be more personal than the stuff literally flowing through your veins? But as with any highly valuable, highly private data source, the user has to get something equally valuable in return. Right now, that seems to be a vague promise to live longer.
“The reality is life is precious, life is short, and we’re all going to die. The question is when, and I think culturally, we are in denial about death,” Brent Franson, founder and CEO of Death Clock, tells me. “Our view is we want to shake people and say, ‘Hey, the only thing that matters most in your life is whether or not you exist,’ and you want to take your health seriously so you can exist as long as possible.”
Franson says that to help people understand their own health and the changes they need to make, they have to know what’s going on in their bodies — that’s where the blood comes in. It feels like a hyper-literal take on the idea of looking inside oneself to find the answers to life.
It’s an alluring premise, but there’s a limit to what any one person can learn from any quantity of blood. Later in our conversation, Franson acknowledged that the greatest predictor of longevity is socioeconomic status. The rich live longer because they can afford better healthcare — and your blood says nothing about what your income bracket will be.
Those limits are sobering to witness firsthand. In April 2021, I got a phone call from my cousin in the middle of the night. My mom was struggling to breathe and had been rushed to the hospital. Something had been wrong with her for a while. Her speech had been slurred for a whole month, and she was struggling with phlegm that just wouldn’t go away. My mom insisted it was a stubborn cold. This cousin, a doctor, suspected my mom had a series of mini strokes and was now suffering from a potential combination of both a stroke and heart attack — a cardiocerebral infarction.
In the ER, my mom loudly protested that everyone was worried over nothing. Her father had lived to 101. Her mother was alive and doing well at 94. Her blood, our family blood, was destined for a long life, and we had no history of cardiovascular issues. (Never mind that my uncle had nearly died from a stroke the year prior.) She yelled at the top of her lungs that at 72, she was entirely too young to die.
The doctors didn’t find what was wrong with her that night. Over the next few months, we ran her through a gauntlet of tests, many of which involved blood draws and machines of all types. It turned out, my cousin was also wrong. My mom didn’t have a mini stroke and her cardiovascular function was perfectly fine. Instead, she died six months later from spontaneous bulbar amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, which has nothing to do with blood. It was in her body that April, but no blood test would’ve found it. ALS wasn’t in our family history — and as genetic testing later revealed, she didn’t carry the gene for it either. There was nothing she could’ve done to prevent it.
The other proposition is that running your blood through a health tech app’s algorithm and AI chatbots will tell you more about yourself. It’s presented as a democratizing move that empowers you to take action outside of the 15 minutes you might get with a doctor — or at the very least, helps you to make the most of an appointment.
I’ve uploaded my various blood tests to multiple apps, asking their accompanying AI chatbots to analyze my data. The big-picture interpretations are similar. My tests invariably point to an inflamed but improving liver. I had high cholesterol, but medication seems to be working. My cardiovascular labs have begun to look pretty optimal, according to every app. The combination of good fasting glucose and HbA1c alongside improving but mildly elevated fasting insulin suggests I have “managed” insulin resistance. In other words, I have learned that going to the doctor and addressing my myriad metabolic issues is working. I could have told you that without any of this extra data.
I’ve also learned that doctors, health tech features, and AI can look at the same tests and arrive at different conclusions. For instance, absolutely no one agrees about my most recent fasting insulin. I’ve been told it’s everything from normal to borderline high or high. What should I do? Do I need to do anything? I don’t know, because the advice is all over the place.
This type of mixed signaling leads to one of two outcomes. You could become a Bryan Johnson type, where you get 15 vials of blood drawn at once and sell your blood-testing protocol as a product. You could obsess over every tiny change. Or you could be like me and find this thinly disguised datamining expedition mainly repackages things you already know.
“Doctors don’t order these 150 biomarker panels like Function Health, and they don’t do it for a good reason. There’s a high false-positive risk in doing that many tests, especially on somebody who’s asymptomatic for most of the tests. It creates a lot of confusion and annoyance, I think, for existing primary care physicians,” says Franson.
When I point out that Death Clock also offers an extensive range of blood tests, he says the difference is the app takes a more middle-of-the-road approach. The app only covers a basic panel in the subscription — the rest are à la carte options depending on an individual’s health needs. Same as a doctor would do, he says.
Then what’s the point?
“What we want to be tomorrow is a full replacement for primary care as it relates to preventive health,” Franson explains, saying that patients should still go to doctors for scenarios like injuries or surgeries. His vision is to provide a sort of telehealth guidance for everyday lifestyle interventions and routine screening procedures.
“It’s kind of a Death Clock on the outside, but it’s a Life Lab once you’re in.”
The app does offer some solid advice. Get more steps in. Try to stick to a sleep schedule. Limit alcohol. Eat five servings of fruits and vegetables. Do this consistently for the most benefit. There’s some personalized advice. Mine is centered on getting my liver back to normal. But if the “life lab” is mainly telling me to do more of what I’m doing, to focus on lifestyle interventions — if that’s all any of these health apps do, did they really need my blood?
If there’s one thing Franson and I agree on, it’s that we’ll all die someday. Everyone and everything you love will die also. That’s objectively scary and painful.
“If we were all a lot healthier, didn’t eat processed food, exercised more, focused on sleep, did less drinking and smoking — the average life expectancy would be higher than it is. There’s no debate about that,” says Franson. “We’re more informed than ever; even so, we’re not smarter than we ever were. We just have much more information … but we don’t have a great solution to the uncomfortable fact that we’re all going to die.”
I recognized perhaps a bit of my father in what Franson had to say. He liked control and certainty, and insofar as my father could influence death — the ultimate uncertainty — he did. He took daily walks and did light calisthenics well into his 70s. He obsessed over his diet, took endless supplements, and went to the doctor often. He always boasted that he’d live to 100 years old. He didn’t. Though most people would say dying at 88 is a good run, he spent the last 10 years of his life battling Parkinson’s, eventually losing control of his limbs and forfeiting his memories to dementia. More diseases that can’t be found in your blood. Even so, he refused to cede that his end was out of his hands. It led to a lonely, painful, and drawn-out death.
Perhaps where we differ is that I’m less afraid of dying. I’m more worried about prolonged sickness, of holding on just to hold on. Counterintuitively, I’m hoping my blood panels don’t extend my Death Clock estimate further into the future. It’s not that I don’t want to live a long life. I’m just uninterested in a long life without good health. I went into this experiment skeptical, but open to the possibility I could learn something.
So far, I’ve mostly decided my blood never held the answer to my real question. How do I live a life that allows me to die well?

articles.title: Live event marketing tech startup Hive brings on Frontier Growth with Series B | BetaKit
articles.text:
Twelve years and two major pivots in, Kitchener-Waterloo-based Hive believes it has found the scale and the partner to take its marketing platform for live events to the next level.
Hive announced $27 million USD (nearly $38 million CAD) in equity Series B financing today from Charlotte, North Carolina-based Frontier Growth.
The vast majority of that amount consisted of secondary capital used to all but buy out Hive’s first institutional investor, Washington, DC’s Avenue Growth Partners, which led its $7-million USD Series A in 2023.
“We continue to chug along, but now we get to do it with somebody who’s seen companies our size go to the next level [many] times.”
While this Series B financing also includes a small portion of primary capital to help fuel Hive’s product development and go-to-market plans, co-founder and CTO Patrick Hannigan told BetaKit in an interview that for Hive, which has been hovering around breakeven for years now, the primary motivation was to team up with Frontier given its long track record supporting scaling vertical software companies and experience in live events.
“This isn’t a venture investment,” Hannigan said. “This isn’t the, ‘Oh I hope there’s [a] 100x kind of opportunity [bet].’ This is a sustainable, intentionally-built business … We continue to chug along, but now we get to do it with somebody who’s seen companies our size go to the next level [many] times.”
Frontier founding partner Andrew Lindner, who is joining Hive’s board, said in a statement that Hive has achieved “something rare in vertical software.”
“The team has built a product that is deeply embedded in its customers’ revenue, then compounded that advantage with proprietary data and network effects,” Lindner added. “The live events market is large, underserved by generic tools, and moving quickly toward automation. Hive is positioned to lead that shift.”
While Hive has raised about $35 million USD to date, most of that has been secondary. Hannigan declined to share the exact breakdown or Hive’s latest valuation.
RELATED: Senso to be acquired by New York-based marketing platform Zeta Global
Hive offers what Hannigan has described as a Mailchimp specifically for venue owners and live event promoters. Its software helps clients, from big arenas in major cities to tiny bars in the middle of nowhere, connect often disparate fan purchase data with email, text, advertising, and customer relationship management tools so they can automate core marketing tasks using AI. The goal is simple: to help them better understand their audience and sell more tickets.
Today, the 75-person startup serves over 1,600 venues, promoters, and festivals, providing a sticky, revenue-generating “communication engine” that has helped those clients sell more than $1 billion USD worth of tickets to date. Hannigan claimed that the company is now “well past” $10 million USD in annual recurring revenue.
That journey began in 2014 when Hannigan and Hive co-founder and CEO Ian Roberts, a pair of students in a University of Waterloo computer lab with a passion for live music, launched the company as a ticketing business.
That year, Hive gained acceptance to the school’s Velocity incubator as well as Silicon Valley accelerator Y Combinator (YC), and raised a $750,000 USD seed round from YC, small funds, and angels as it embarked on a series of pivots. Over the intervening years, Hive tried a number of different kicks at the can as it struggled to raise money, including an attempt at building engagement and analytics tools for musicians, before finally finding product-market fit around 2019 with marketing software for music venue owners.
Hannigan credits Hive’s staying power to those Canadian roots.
When the COVID-19 pandemic hit the following year, Hive lost 60 percent of its revenue almost overnight. Hannigan said the then eight-person startup decided to stay the course “because we were scrappy Canadians.”
Roberts told BetaKit over email that the pair believed in what they were building, wanted to support its clients during this time, were bullish that live events would recover, and were profitable enough leading into this period to avoid any layoffs.
“We just kind of kept the lights on and pushed through,” the CTO added. “And once the industry consolidated and popped back … we were on this really interesting growth trajectory.”
While most of Hive’s customers are based in the US, 70 percent of its team, including most of the company’s engineering staff, is located in Canada. Hannigan credits the company’s staying power to those Canadian roots.
“I think we’re grittier than [other] people,” he said. “We last longer than [other] people. We’re more efficient than other people.”
Feature image courtesy Hive.

articles.title: Mars: So wollen Forscher mithilfe urzeitlicher Regenfälle Hinweise auf Leben finden
articles.text:
Mars: So wollen Forscher mithilfe urzeitlicher Regenfälle Hinweise auf Leben finden
Ein Forschungsteam unter der Leitung von Wissenschaftler:innen des Institute of Science Tokyo (Japan) hat eine Mars-Karte erstellt, die zeigt, wo vor Milliarden Jahren urzeitliche Regenfälle ein wichtiges präbiotisches Molekül – Formaldehyd (H₂CO) – auf der Marsoberfläche abgelagert haben könnten.
Diese Karte könnte künftige Untersuchungen auf dem Mars unterstützen, indem sie unbemannte und bemannte Missionen gezielt zu Stellen lenkt, an denen noch Spuren von vergangenem Leben erhalten sein könnten.
Der Mars war vor 3,5 bis 4,1 Milliarden Jahren wärmer und feuchter
Trotz des heutigen Klimas auf dem Mars sind sich Wissenschaftler:innen inzwischen einig, dass es dort vor 3,5 bis 4,1 Milliarden Jahren wärmer und feuchter war. Dies wirft die Frage auf, ob der Mars in jener Zeit Leben beherbergt haben könnte – etwa in Form von Mikroorganismen.
Die im Planetary Science Journal veröffentlichte Studie baut auf früheren Erkenntnissen auf, die zeigten, wie Formaldehyd (H₂CO) in der Atmosphäre entstehen kann. In Verbindung mit Wasser kann Formaldehyd als Ausgangsmolekül für chemische Reaktionen dienen, aus denen Zucker, Aminosäuren und andere komplexe organische Moleküle hervorgehen: die Bausteine des Lebens. Die spezifische Frage lautete: An welchen Stellen auf dem Mars könnte das Formaldehyd die Oberfläche erreicht haben?
Simulation der Bedingungen, die vor 4 Milliarden Jahren auf Mars herrschten
Um eine Karte der möglichen Orte zu erstellen, simulierten die Forscher:innen die Bedingungen, die vor 3,5 bis 4,1 Milliarden Jahren auf dem Mars herrschten. Sie untersuchten dabei, wie Faktoren wie Temperatur, Wasserdampf, atmosphärischer Druck und UV-Strahlung die Bildung von Formaldehyd beeinflussten. Ihre Simulation zeigte, dass die chemische Aufspaltung von Wasser durch UV-Licht in der Marsatmosphäre reaktiven Wasserstoff freisetzen würde – ein wesentlicher Baustein für die Bildung von Formaldehyd, das anschließend mit Niederschlägen auf die Oberfläche gelangen könnte.
Da Wasser sowohl die Entstehung als auch die Verteilung von H₂CO beeinflusste, stellten die Forschenden die Hypothese auf, dass der frühere Wasserkreislauf auf dem Mars bestimmt haben könnte, wo sich diese Verbindung ansammelte.
Karte könnte helfen, vielversprechende Ziele für Marsmissionen zu finden
Im letzten Schritt der Kartenerstellung wurden diese potenziellen „Hotspots“ in Bezug zu den Landeplätzen vergangener Marsmissionen gesetzt.
Studienleiter Shungo Koyama sagte gegenüber Universe Today: „Durch den Vergleich unserer Karte mit den Ergebnissen von Marsrovern können wir untersuchen, ob Orte mit einer höheren H₂CO-Konzentration möglicherweise auch günstigere Bedingungen für chemische Prozesse boten, die mit der Entstehung von Leben in Verbindung stehen könnten. Sollten zukünftige Beobachtungen diesen Zusammenhang bestätigen, könnte unsere Karte dabei helfen, vielversprechende Ziele für künftige Marsmissionen zu identifizieren.“

articles.title: Online Business Setup Tools Every Australian Founder Needs - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Starting a business in Australia is easier than ever on paper, but getting the setup right from day one is where most founders slip up.
Anyone can register an ABN online and launch a website over a weekend. The trouble starts a few months later, when mail is going to the wrong place, invoices are buried in a spreadsheet, and customers cannot tell whether your business is the real deal.
Whether you are a first-time founder, a freelancer going full-time, or someone whose side hustle has outgrown the kitchen table, the right tools can save you hours and plenty of stress. So, a smart online business setup in Australia is less about buying everything and more about choosing the few things that really matter.
Here are seven tools and checks worth putting in place early.
1. Business Name and ABN Check
Before you spend anything on branding, make sure your name is available, and your registration details are in order. The Australian Business Register’s ABN Lookup via Space Penguin’s ABR lookup tool shows who is already trading, and ASIC’s registers let you check whether a business name is taken.
It is a quick step that gets skipped far too often. A founder prints business cards, buys a domain, and then finds out another company already holds the name. A few minutes of searching can save you a full rebrand.
While you are at it, check that the matching domain name and social media handles are free. Using the same name everywhere makes you easier to find and easier to trust.
You can use business registration service providers such as Space Penguin who are also AUSTRAC enrolled for peace of mind.
2. A Virtual Address
Every business needs an address. It goes on your registrations, invoices, website, and online listings. If you work from home, putting your residential address on all of those is not ideal for privacy, and it can look less professional to customers. That is where a virtual address comes in.
A virtual address gives your business a proper street address in a business district, usually with mail handling included. Letters are received for you, scanned and sent to your inbox, and physical items can be forwarded when you need them. Providers offer addresses in major cities such as Sydney and Melbourne, which suit founders who travel, work remotely, or sell to customers in another state.
Before you sign up, read the fine print. Ask how mail and parcels are handled, whether forwarding costs extra, and whether the address can be used for your business registrations. Also confirm any address rules with the relevant authority or your accountant, since some registrations have their own requirements.
3. Professional Email and Domain
A free email address works fine for a side project, but it does little for your credibility once you start quoting for real work. A business email at your own domain looks more professional and is harder to mistake for spam.
Platforms such as Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 bundle custom email with shared calendars, cloud storage, and video meetings, so you get several tools for one monthly fee. Ask your provider to set up basic email authentication as well, so your messages are less likely to end up in a junk folder.
Once your email is running, add your business name, ABN, and virtual address to your signature. It is a small detail, but it shows customers that you are properly set up.
4. Accounting and Invoicing Software
Spreadsheets are fine for the first few invoices. After that, they get messy fast. Cloud accounting tools such as Xero, MYOB and QuickBooks connect to your bank feed, send invoices, track expenses, and keep your GST records tidy, so you are not scrambling when BAS time rolls around.
The real advantage is time. When every invoice and receipt lands in one place, you spend far less time chasing paperwork. Many accountants and bookkeepers already work with these platforms, so ask yours which one they prefer before you commit.
5. A Website or Online Store
Your website is your shopfront, and for many customers it is the first thing they will see. Platforms such as WordPress, Shopify, Wix, and Squarespace let you launch without hiring a developer. Pick the one that fits what you sell, since an online store and a simple services site have very different needs.
Make sure your site loads quickly on mobile, because plenty of customers will find you on their phone. Put your business name, ABN, and contact details on a contact page, and keep them matching across your other listings. A few basic SEO tools can also help you check page speed and see which searches are bringing people to you.
6. Payment Tools
Customers expect to pay how they prefer, whether by card, Apple Pay, Google Pay, or a simple invoice link. Payment providers such as Stripe, Square, and PayPal make this easy to set up without a high upfront cost.
Compare transaction fees and payout times before you choose, since small differences add up as you grow. If you also sell in person at markets or pop-ups, look for a provider that handles both online and in-person payments, so all your sales land in one place.
7. Security and Backup Tools
It is easy to put security at the bottom of the list when you are busy, but a single hacked account can stop your business in its tracks. A password manager, multi-factor authentication on your key accounts, and automatic cloud backups cover most of the basics.
The Australian Cyber Security Centre publishes free guidance written for small businesses, which is a good place to start. Spending an hour on this now is far cheaper than recovering from a problem later.
Final Thought
Setting up a business is mostly about getting the foundations right: a registered name, a proper virtual address, a professional email, tidy accounts, a solid website, easy payments, and decent security. None of these tools is complicated, and you do not need all of them on day one.
Start with the basics, add more as you grow, and revisit your setup every year. The founders who do this early tend to spend less time on admin and more time on the work that actually brings in customers.

articles.title: Ya son oficiales: Philips presenta sus nuevos monitores curvos para trabajar y jugar con tasa de refresco de hasta 144 Hz
articles.text:
¿Me compro un monitor para trabajar o para jugar? Puede que nos hayamos hecho esta pregunta en alguna ocasión, sobre todo si solemos jugar y estudiar o teletrabajar mucho en casa. Para ello, Philips ha presentado su nueva gama de monitores con los que podremos tener una buena experiencia en ambos casos: se trata de los Philips 27E3C2500 y 32E3C2500.
Dos monitores para jugar, estudiar y trabajar
Ambos ordenadores comparten casi las mismas características, a excepción del tamaño que el primero cuenta con una pantalla de 27 pulgadas y el segundo tiene una diagonal de 31,5 pulgadas. En ambos casos nos encontramos ante un panel que ofrece una muy buena resolución QHD (2560 × 1440p) y una tasa de refresco de hasta 144 Hz.
La tasa de refresco alta es ideal para gaming, pero también para productividad. El motivo es que superar la barrera de los 60 Hz evita que acabemos con la vista tan cansada tras muchas horas estudiando o trabajando. Además, estos monitores también cuentan con las tecnologías SoftBlue, para reducir las emisiones de luz azul, Flicker-free, para disminuir el parpadeo de la pantalla, y Easy Read, para facilitar la lectura en pantalla.
Los dos monitores también incorporan altavoces con potencia de 2W, lo que nos evita comprar altavoces externos o una barra de sonido salvo que busquemos una mejor experiencia sonora. Ambos vienen equipados con entradas HDMI y DisplayPort y son compatibles con VESA 100 x 100 mm, permitiendo que podamos instalar brazos articulados en el escritorio.
Por otro lado, los monitores incorporan pantallas curvas de 1.500R (el estándar que solemos encontrar) y vienen con Adaptive-Sync, una tecnología orientada sobre todo al gaming que sincroniza la freciencia de actualización del monitor con la señal de la tarjeta gráfica, evitando así problemas como el tearing.
Se prevé que los monitores de Philips lleguen este mismo mes de octubre a un precio de 169 euros (27E3C2500) y 219 euros (32E3C2500). Además, también estarán disponibles otras versiones con resolución Full HD denominadas 27E3C2200 y 32E3C2200.

articles.title: Blog Review: Oct. 21
articles.text:
From server to rack; AMBA CXS; digital twins; edge AI development loop; satellite power; global talent challenges.
Synopsys’ Neeraj Paliwal considers how AI workloads are shifting key design and optimization considerations from the server to the rack, with designs starting from the target workload and working backward to optimize for useful AI work per watt and dollar.
Cadence’s Ravi Vora demonstrates how AMBA CXS evolves a wide, credited link into a scalable shared transport for multi-protocol and multi-node traffic that enables controlled interleaving while preserving stream ordering, route identity, packet reconstruction, and required contiguity.
In a podcast, Siemens’ Conor Peick and Katherina Westrich chat about the adoption of digital twins in the semiconductor industry, ranging from chip design and verification to fab construction and automation.
Arm’s Christopher Seidl shows how to create a development loop for edge AI in which target information and evidence from real execution flow back into the next iteration.
Keysight’s Nancy Friedrich explores the trends driving rising requirements for satellite power generation and distribution and how lab-based power-emulation configurations can be leveraged to assess system performance in scenarios that affect the performance of satellite solar arrays and battery packs.
In a blog for SEMI, Stanton Chase’s Jan-Bart Smits compares semiconductor talent shortages across North America, EMEA, and Southeast Asia, warning that while causes differ by region, government subsidies alone cannot buy the expertise needed for desired buildouts.
Plus, check out the blogs featured in the latest Low Power-High Performance newsletter:
Rambus’ Paul Karazuba examines multiple interacting factors impacting PCIe retimer reach, including silicon design, controller intelligence, channel quality, and the transmission medium.
Siemens EDA’s Shehab Ashraf looks at short-resilient via insertion and its effect on reliability and performance.
Cadence’s Mayank Bhatnagar shows how open interfaces and interoperability let designers choose technologies based on system needs.
Arm’s Francisco Socal outlines extending chiplet connectivity across AXI and CHI with scalable protocol subsets, interoperability, and flexible transport support.
Ayar Labs’ Vladimir Stojanovic and Global Unichip’s Igor Elkanovich explain how optical engines can operate reliably alongside high-power AI processors in multi-chip packages.

articles.title: Android Auto : la meilleure nouveauté de Gemini arrive enfin, mais une grande partie des utilisateurs en sera privée
articles.text:
Pour vous aider à garder les mains libres tout en obtenant des informations utiles quand vous êtes au volant, Google déploie « Personal Intelligence » sur Gemini pour Android Auto et Android Automotive. Concrètement, cela va vous permettre d’obtenir des réponses sur mesure en conduisant, sans avoir à manipuler votre smartphone.
Une connexion directe avec vos applications Google
Gemini ne va plus se contenter de répondre à des demandes « basiques » autour de la navigation ou de la musique. En autorisant la liaison avec les services du géant de Mountain View, la fonction va pouvoir aller piocher directement dans Gmail, Google Agenda, Google Photos, Maps, YouTube et le moteur de recherche pour répondre au mieux à vos questions. Dans l’exemple donné par Google, le conducteur qui est sur son trajet pour l’aéroport demande à Gemini quelle est la porte d’embarquement et si son vol est à l’heure. Plus besoin de prendre votre téléphone pour ouvrir une autre application, donc.
Pour générer ses réponses, Gemini va piocher dans différentes sources, toutes issues des applications Google que vous utilisez. Trouver un restaurant le long de son trajet ou lancer un itinéraire vers un cabinet médical enregistré dans l’agenda peut maintenant être fait simplement par la voix. Vous pouvez aussi retrouver le lieu d’un rendez-vous à partir d’une image stockée dans votre galerie Google Photos en décrivant simplement l’image à haute voix à l’intelligence artificielle.
Disponibilité et gestion des données personnelles
Évidemment, aucune application n’est reliée par défaut. L’activation se fait manuellement via les paramètres de Gemini, et l’option peut être désactivée à tout moment. Sans cette autorisation, les commandes classiques de la voiture continuent de fonctionner normalement, mais sans personnalisation des réponses.
Le déploiement commence dès aujourd’hui sur Android Auto et dans les mois à venir pour les véhicules avec Google directement intégré au tableau de bord. La fonction se destine uniquement aux comptes personnels des utilisateurs âgés de 18 ans et plus. Les comptes professionnels ou éducatifs Workspace ne sont pas concernés. Comme beaucoup de fonctionnalités IA, l’Europe n’est pour l’instant pas concernée, tout comme la Suisse, le Nigeria et le Royaume-Uni.
À lire : La voiture la plus vendue du monde va enfin passer à l’électrique
