articles.title: Europe’s Industrial Leaders Reinvent Engineering and Manufacturing With NVIDIA
articles.text:
To increase productivity, accelerate innovation and create new opportunities for economic growth, Europe’s industrial leaders are tapping NVIDIA CUDA-X and Omniverse libraries, as well as NVIDIA Cosmos and Nemotron open models, across the engineering and manufacturing lifecycle.
Bringing those capabilities together on the factory floor, the NVIDIA Factory Operations Blueprint (FOX) is now available in early access on GitHub, providing a path for developers to build and deploy always-on factory manager agents that coordinate work across machines, and specialist agents focused on use cases such as visual inspection, root cause analysis, report generation and fleet management.
These agents can connect to frontier models, including NVIDIA Cosmos and Nemotron, and foundational knowledge including computer-aided design, product lifecycle management, simulation software, and IT and operational technology systems.
Building on the FOX blueprint enables the ecosystem to build industrial agents that monitor factory operations in real time, correlate visual findings and machine logs to investigate problems, and coordinate responses. With Cosmos in-context learning, these agents can adapt using examples and documentation, without fine-tuning.
Siemens is integrating agents built using FOX into Intelligence Center X, its agentic enterprise system, to help identify root causes and coordinate factory operations, for estimated cost savings of 20%. Siemens’ Process Preparation X agents use NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory tools and skills to generate defect images for circuit-board inspection. At its Erlangen electronics factory, Siemens used this approach to reduce calibration time of inspection processes by 40%.
Accelerating Engineering From the First Design
NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries accelerate simulation, giving engineers faster feedback to explore design alternatives before committing to physical prototypes. At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA is releasing cuDSS for general availability, accelerating the demanding calculations behind the complex simulations of structural stress, fluid flow, electromagnetic fields and semiconductor device behavior.
Mercedes-Benz uses Siemens’ Simcenter STAR-CCM+ running on NVIDIA GPUs to compare vehicle designs through faster aerodynamic simulations. In factories, the company applies NVIDIA Cosmos 3 and the Metropolis VSS blueprint to build agents for vehicle inspection and windshield assembly verification, detecting deviations and ensuring consistently high quality.
Cadence is benchmarking automotive fluid-dynamics workloads on NVIDIA GPUs to assess opportunities for faster design iteration, while Autodesk brings the NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo and Warp frameworks into NavPack, integrated with Autodesk Alias, to help designers like those at Bentley’s predict vehicle performance and iterate faster using simulation-trained AI.
imec and Infineon are accelerating semiconductor simulation with Synopsys software and NVIDIA accelerated computing. Benchmarks of S-Litho on imec’s model show up to 40x speedup, while Infineon uses Sentaurus Device with NVIDIA CUDA libraries to achieve a 12x speedup in 3D breakdown simulation for next-generation power devices.
Leonardo is working with Neural Concept on AI-driven aircraft design, tapping NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to bring aircraft geometry and aerodynamic simulation results together.
Car manufacturers use Dassault Systèmes’ LEO & AURA Virtual Companions, powered by NVIDIA Nemotron, and orchestrating CATIA AI Agents & SIMULIA AI Agents with SIMULIA solvers, accelerated by NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, to rapidly design and virtually test vehicle doors before building physical prototypes.
UniversalAGI is working with Saab to protect sailors from life-threatending wave impacts at sea, using UniversalAGI’s Latent Interaction Field Transformer physics AI foundation models with accelerated processing by NVIDIA Warp to evaluate thousands of wave conditions and headings in real time instead of days. These capabilities enable vessels to anticipate dangerous motion and autonomously select safer routes to avoid putting sailors at risk, while NVIDIA Omniverse libraries help visualize vessel behavior at sea.
PhysicsX is working with GB1, Britain’s America’s Cup team, on AI-powered yacht design, using NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to visualize hull geometry and pressure fields, while Fermioniq’s Sofia agent helps Deltares and Dutch ministries model river flow by translating natural-language requests into simulation solvers built on NVIDIA Warp.
Mistral plans to use CUDA-X, Warp and Omniverse libraries to accelerate physics simulation and generate training data for engineering AI models.
Testing Factories and Robots Virtually
NVIDIA Omniverse and Isaac libraries enable digital twins and robotics simulation, helping manufacturers evaluate production systems and robot behavior before making changes on the factory floor.
Audi uses a battery-production digital twin built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to test production concepts before physical equipment is available. The company is also working with Dassault Systèmes and Agile Robots to simulate and validate mobile humanoid robots and logistics processes in DELMIA virtual twins built with Omniverse libraries.
Schaeffler is integrating digital twins of its humanoid actuators — components that move robot joints — with NVIDIA Isaac simulation frameworks, helping its robotics partners evaluate component behavior in simulation and reduce physical testing.
At Volkswagen Sachsen’s Transparent Factory, Wandelbots uses NOVA with Isaac Sim, built on Omniverse and OpenUSD, to validate assembly workflows digitally and prepare applications for physical robots.
Falkor, a KONGSBERG company, is integrating agents and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries into its platform. With Microsoft Azure NCv6 virtual machines powered by NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs, agents with spatial intelligence combine engineering data, operating information and 3D equipment geometry to see, simulate and reason over industrial facilities, supporting inspection and maintenance use cases across the process and energy industries.
The same simulation approach extends to AI infrastructure. Schneider Electric, together with AVEVA, is developing an AI factory digital twin built for Nscale with Omniverse libraries to help engineers compare power, cooling and equipment configurations before making physical changes.

articles.title: Jensen Huang Nvidia GTC keynote disrupted by Greenpeace protest over chips in Russian drones — 'What are you doing about that?' heckler demands before being thrown out
articles.text:
Jensen Huang Nvidia GTC keynote disrupted by Greenpeace protest over chips in Russian drones — 'What are you doing about that?' heckler demands before being thrown out
"What are you doing about the environmental destruction?"
Protesters disrupted Jensen Huang's Nvidia GTC keynote in Berlin on Wednesday morning. Just minutes into the CEO's customary address, the broadcast was interrupted by a heckler from the crowd demanding the CEO answer claims that the company's chips were found inside Russian drones, and charges of environmental destruction more broadly. While the incident wasn't fully picked up by Nvidia's livestream, footage filmed by attendees shows protestors standing on chairs with a large banner that reads "Nvidia, clean up your dirty business!"
Multiple videos and images shared to X show protestors brandishing a large banner with a Greenpeace logo. "Jensen, what about the technology that was found in Russian drones? Those were Nvidia chips. What are you doing about that?" one of the protestors called out across the auditorium. "What are you doing about that? What are you doing about the environmental destruction?" the heckler demanded.
Huang can be heard on the broadcast and in the video stating, "It's okay, go easy," as security rushed to escort the protesters out of the hall. "I'll talk to you later," Huang stated as the individuals were removed from the premises.
The complaint raised by the protester appears to relate to recent reports that Nvidia Jetson chips have been found in Russian cruise missiles used against Ukraine, as well as in AI drones. Reports indicate Russia's S-71 'Monochrome' weapon has autonomous targeting capability powered by Nvidia's consumer-grade Jetson Orin chip. "Our Jetson Orin modules are consumer-grade products sold to students, developers, and startups for a wide range of beneficial applications," Nvidia told Tom's Hardware at the time. The company reiterated that the chips are not available in Russia and are not designed for military purposes, but admitted it cannot track the resale of pre-owned Jetson chips after they are sold.
A report in August claimed that a Russian AI drone killed three civilians in Ukraine, the first documented case of civilian deaths caused by a Russian drone using fully autonomous targeting. Images of the recovered drones confirmed they contained Jetson Orin modules. "All important issues, but let me get through my keynote," Huang quipped before continuing his presentation.
Huang is in Berlin for Nvidia's three-day GTC event, taking place from October 20-22. The customary keynote, given this morning, also includes fireside chats and talks for developers and business leaders.

articles.title: So hat es sich angefühlt, im Jahr 2026 nochmal mit Windows 7 zu arbeiten
articles.text:
Vier Dinge, die Windows 7 bis heute besser löst als Windows 11
Es begab sich also, dass ich im Jahr 2026 für einige Zeit wieder Windows 7 genutzt habe, um damit zu arbeiten. Grund dafür war ein alter Laptop, den ich mir auf Ebay für wenig Geld ersteigert habe, um damit weniger abgelenkt arbeiten zu können. Wie genau das abgelaufen ist, könnt ihr hier nachlesen. Auf diesem Laptop war noch Windows 7 installiert.
Also dachte ich mir: Wieso nicht schauen, wie sich dieses Betriebssystem aus dem Jahr 2009 heute anfühlt. Dabei ging es mir aber nicht darum, wie performant Windows 7 heute noch ist. Denn natürlich laufen viele moderne Programme nicht mehr auf diesem OS. Aber gibt es Features oder grundlegende Strukturen, die anders als heute sind – und vielleicht sogar besser?
Dabei sind mir vor allem vier Dinge aufgefallen, die in Windows 7 meiner Meinung nach noch deutlich angenehmer waren, als es heute bei Windows 11 der Fall ist.
Windows 7 sollte heute nicht mehr einfach so genutzt werden, denn das Betriebssystem erhält seit Jahren keine Sicherheitsupdates mehr. Schwachstellen bleiben also ungepatcht, weshalb das System ein leichtes Ziel für Schadsoftware und Angreifer im Netz ist. Zudem haben aktuelle Browser den Support eingestellt, was das Surfen riskant macht. Wir haben Windows 7 auf einem Rechner genutzt, der nicht mit dem Internet verbunden war.
Es geht auch ohne Microsoft-Account
Einen der größten Unterschiede bemerke ich direkt schon beim Start. In Windows 7 konnte man noch ein lokales Benutzerkonto anlegen. Es war also nicht nötig, ein Microsoft-Konto zu haben und sich damit anzumelden. Oder mit anderen Worten: Es war nicht erforderlich, Teil des Microsoft-Ökosystems zu sein.
Ein lokales Profil existiert isoliert auf dem Rechner: Zugangsdaten, persönliche Angaben und Dateien bleiben physisch auf der Festplatte, ohne mit den Servern von Microsoft synchronisiert zu werden. Für die Inbetriebnahme von Windows 7 war weder eine E-Mail-Adresse noch eine bestehende Internetverbindung erforderlich.
Bei den neueren Versionen von Windows (und bei Apples sowieso) ist Microsoft sehr darauf bedacht, nicht nur ein Betriebssystem zu verkaufen, sondern die User direkt an ihre Plattform zu binden. Oftmals zulasten von Privatsphäre, Offline-Fähigkeiten und der Kontrolle über die eigene Hardware.
Ein Betriebssystem, kein Vertriebskanal
Freilich war es schon immer so, dass Microsoft ein großes Interesse daran hatte, den Windows-Usern auch ihre andere Software zu verkaufen. Bei Windows 7 war das aber noch verhältnismäßig dezent. Nach dem Start finde ich da ein eher reduziertes System vor. Paint, der Editor, Windows Media Player, das Snipping Tool oder Minesweeper wecken in mir heute beinahe nostalgische Gefühle – und ich kann sie auch einfach ignorieren, wenn ich möchte. Selbst Standardprogramme wie Windows Mail sind damals noch optional und mussten erst mit dem „Windows Live Essentials“-Paket, manuell heruntergeladen werden.
Heute sind zahlreiche Microsoft-Dienste fest im System verankert: Onedrive startet automatisch und synchronisiert ungefragt Nutzerordner. Microsoft Teams soll das Standard-Tool für Kommunikation sein. Edge will nicht nur mein Browser sein, sondern auch jedes PDF öffnen – und schiebt sich auch sonst ständig ungefragt in den Vordergrund. Dazu kommen noch die Web-Apps von Microsoft 365, die Xbox-App oder der inzwischen auch allgegenwärtige Copilot. Kurzum: Das Betriebssystem fungiert heute als Vertriebskanal für Microsofts Cloud-Ökosystem.
Keine ständigen „Empfehlungen“
Was mir in Windows 7 nicht an jeder Ecke begegnet: Reklame, die als „Tipps“ oder „Empfehlungen“ getarnt ist. Das Startmenü listet nur das auf, was tatsächlich auf meiner Festplatte installiert ist. Weder gibt es Pop-ups, die für andere Produkte werben, noch muss ich mich erst durch die Datenschutzeinstellungen klicken, um Banner abzuschalten.
In Windows 11 tauchen hingegen im Startmenü Vorschläge für Apps und Abonnements auf, der Sperrbildschirm bewirbt Games oder Microsoft-Produkte, die Widget-Leiste ist vom MSN-Newsfeed dominiert, der wiederum auch Werbung ausspielt. Selbst in der Einstellungen-App finden sich Banner, die zum Kauf von Onedrive-Speicher oder Microsoft 365 bewegen wollen.
Windows 7 fühlt sich noch deutlich mehr wie ein Werkzeug an, das mich in Ruhe arbeiten lässt, anstatt den Desktop als fortlaufende Werbefläche zu monetarisieren.
Die Taskleiste ist in Windows 7 noch wirklich flexibel: Sie lässt sich einfach entsperren und an jeden Bildschirmrand verschieben. Ich kann die Schaltflächen selbst beschriften, gruppieren oder einzeln anzeigen lassen. Auch Drag-and-Drop funktioniert nahtlos: Ich kann eine Datei einfach auf ein Programm-Icon in der Leiste ziehen, um das Fenster in den Vordergrund zu holen oder die Datei direkt darin zu öffnen. Außerdem reicht ein kurzer Rechtsklick, um schnell auf zuletzt geöffnete Dokumente oder angeheftete Favoriten zuzugreifen.
Auch das Kontextmenü funktioniert einfach. Ein Rechtsklick auf eine Datei zeigt direkt alle verfügbaren Einstellungen und Befehle in einer einzigen, nachvollziehbar gegliederten Liste. In Windows 11 ist das ein zweistufiges Menü, das viele gängige Optionen wie Packprogramme, Text-Editoren oder Druckbefehle hinter dem Punkt „Weitere Optionen anzeigen“ versteckt. Häufig benötigte Aktionen wie Kopieren oder Löschen wurden zu kleinen, unbeschrifteten Icons am Menürand.
Was in Windows 7 oft ein einziger Klick ist, braucht in Windows 11 oft zwei Schritte oder den Griff zur Tastenkombination „Shift + F10“. Das Design mag zwar moderner und aufgeräumter aussehen, opfert dafür aber die praktische Direktheit von Windows 7.
Alternativen für Windows 7
Wer Optik und Funktionen von Windows 7 vermisst, für den können einige Linux-Distributionen eine gute Alternative sein. Denn eines ist klar: Im Jahr 2026 sollte niemand mehr mit einem veralteten Betriebssystem, das diverse Sicherheitslücken hat, durch das Internet surfen. Wie ihr Linux einfach installieren könnt, erklären wir euch hier.
Linux Mint ist für viele das Betriebssystem, das Windows 7 am ähnlichsten ist, etwa durch das klassische Startmenü links unten, oder die anpassbare Taskleiste. Beim Wechsel von Windows 7 auf Linux Mint fühlt sich vieles intuitiv und vertraut an. Ähnlich einsteigerfreundlich ist Zorin OS, das extra für Wechsler entwickelt wurde und per Knopfdruck ein Windows-typisches Layout bietet, inklusive praktischer Hilfen zur Ausführung von Windows-Programmen.
Für User, die Wert auf große Flexibilität und transparente Aero-Glass-Effekte wie bei Windows 7 legen, empfiehlt sich Kubuntu. Diese Distribution arbeitet mit einem rein lokalen Benutzerkonto, erzwingt keine Cloud-Anbindung und überlässt den Usern die Kontrolle über ihre Updates.

articles.title: Apple Music has a new logo
articles.text:
Apple is officially launching a rebrand of Apple Music. Following the appearance of a redesigned wordmark in a video and an updated app icon in an iOS 27.2 beta, Apple introduced the new “identity” for Apple Music today. There’s a new logo, the updated wordmark, and a new sound composed by British producer Fred Again and Nest Acoustics.
Apple Music has a new logo
Apple is giving Apple Music a rebrand, including a new sound composed by British producer Fred Again and Nest Acoustics.
In a video, Apple says that for the rebrand, the company “wanted sound to create the visuals,” showing the music note logo and the wordmark underwater and how that water responded to sound. It’s a pretty cool video, honestly, and I like seeing how the water morphs the logo and wordmark. The video is also one of the most Apple things I’ve ever seen, but I still think it’s cool.
The new look is expected to roll out across platforms “this week,” according to Wallpaper. I’m guessing that means it will show up in the final iOS 27.2 release, following the release candidate version of the update that launched this week.

articles.title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
articles.text:
Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.
The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.
Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.
OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”
Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].
“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”
The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.
The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.
According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.
“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”
The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages.
This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

articles.title: Are the Kindle Scribe e-readers as good as they sound? Here's what you need to know before you buy one
articles.text:
Should I buy a Kindle Scribe or a Kindle Scribe Colorsoft? Here's what you need to know
These e-readers also let you scribble down notes — but are they worth the extra spend?
Kindles aren't just for reading — Amazon also makes a couple of Kindles that you can scribble notes on. The Kindle Scribe and Kindle Scribe Colorsoft both have a generous, glare-free e-ink screen you can use for reading or writing; they're billed as streamlined, minimalist productivity tools that help you stay focused.
We've been impressed with both e-readers — the Kindle Scribe holds a coveted spot in our best e-readers ranking. However, there are some compromises involved in choosing one of these models rather than a reading-only option. If you're not sure which one to buy, or whether a different Kindle altogether might fit your needs more closely, you're in the right place.
In this guide, I'll provide a handy overview of the Kindle Scribe and Scribe Colorsoft, including how the specs match up and any major downsides for each model, as well as how they compare to the wider Kindle lineup. I'll also round up the different iterations so you can see your options and what they cost. Let's get started...
Kindle Scribe — Overview
The Kindle Scribe is Amazon's black-and-white e-reader with writing support included. We're on our third generation, released in the US in late 2025 and in other territories in early 2026. We awarded it an impressive 4.5 stars in our Kindle Scribe (2025) review.
Probably because it had already had a relatively recent update, the Kindle Scribe wasn't included in the big refresh the rest of the range enjoyed in October 2026 (we now have a classic Kindle 2026, a Kindle Paperwhite 2026 and a Kindle Colorsoft 2026).
The Scribe is basically a Kindle, except that if you want to take notes, you can grab the stylus and scribble down your thoughts. That's probably simplifying it a bit too much — there are a number of writing features to explore, including an adjustable-size Quick Notes pad, various workspace templates, AI-powered handwriting conversion and summary creation tools, and the ability to add notes onto a book (with text wrapping around it) or in a margin column. The newest version also includes Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive connectivity.

The Kindle Scribe is not just a Kindle Paperwhite with writing functionality, though — it diverges in both design and specs from the reading-only models. For a start, it's much bigger. The screen is 11 inches diagonally, while reading Kindles have a 6-inch or 7-inch screen. It's also heavier, clocking in at around double the weight of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft models (with 7-inch screens). Like the cheapest base model, it isn't waterproof, so it's not good for reading or note-taking in the bath.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
In reading mode, the battery life is among the longest on any Kindle, but switch to note-taking, and it drops considerably. Amazon estimates around 3 weeks of writing before you'll need to recharge — still a lot longer than your average tablet, mind you. You can choose from different storage capacities, but keep in mind that all the writing features eat up quite a bit of space.
In some territories, you can choose between a model with a frontlight and one without. If you want to read or write in any lighting conditions, you'll need to stump up for the frontlight version. Assuming you have, you'll be able to choose from a range of color temperatures (from blue-toned to yellow-toned) and there's a sensor that'll adjust brightness automatically depending on your surroundings.
Kindle Scribe Colorsoft — Overview
The Kindle Scribe Colorsoft is essentially a Kindle Scribe, but with color display support. Most of what I've described in the previous section is also relevant here: there's an 11-inch screen (although the overall proportions are slightly different), no waterproofing, a range of storage capacities, and warm or cool backlighting options (you can't opt out of a backlight here).
Due to the color screen, the battery life has taken a further hit: you can expect around eight weeks of reading or two weeks of writing per charge.
View Original

View Original
This is the first-generation model, and it launched at the end of 2025. We awarded it four stars in our Kindle Scribe Colorsoft review, but there are some caveats to be aware of if you're thinking of buying one.
First, you can't use the writing and color capabilities in tandem — so you couldn't take notes on a graphic novel, for instance. Our resident e-reader expert believes that color e-ink just isn't quite there yet, which could be a deal-breaker if you're buying it specifically to enjoy graphic novels.
At this price (high), an iPad or Android tablet is a viable alternative and could deliver better value for money if you're seeking an all-round productivity tool with a colorful screen.

articles.title: Inside NVIDIA Sentry: Secure AI Agents at Runtime | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
An AI agent can complete its assignment and still cross a security boundary. Recent incidents show that agents can circumvent security controls while using tools, credentials, and services to pursue their assigned goals. Monitoring and enforcement need to operate outside the agent’s reach so that it can’t alter or disable them.
NVIDIA Sentry is a security software framework that monitors AI agents and enforces policies governing their access to models, tools, and data. Part of the NVIDIA OpenShell reference architecture announced at GTC Berlin, it’s built on NVIDIA DOCA, runs on NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs, and provides host-isolated runtime protection for AI agents. NVIDIA Sentry validates that an agent operates according to its designed intent and within its defined operational boundaries.
Trusted even when host resources can’t be trusted, it controls the agent’s only path to the model, providing tamper-evident traceability of agent activity while enforcing granular security controls on agent access in silicon. In addition to inspecting agent communications, NVIDIA Sentry uses out-of-band observability to establish real-time situational awareness, continuously evaluating agents’ runtime security and behavior to validate their security and integrity.
This post explains how NVIDIA Sentry evaluates agent requests, detects threats, and enforces security policies independently of host software.
An independent security layer for agent runtime protection
An earlier agentic AI security post described how NVIDIA BlueField runs security services in a hardware trust domain independent from the host.
NVIDIA Sentry builds on that foundation to continuously monitor AI agent behavior and enforce access policies independently of host software, establishing a strict security boundary in a separate hardware trust domain outside the agent’s reach to keep agents operating within their designed intent.
Software runtime boundaries remain essential. NVIDIA OpenShell is a secure runtime for autonomous agents that governs what an agent can do. OpenShell separates policy enforcement from the agent workload, so a compromised agent can’t change its own restrictions. NVIDIA Sentry adds an independent hardware safeguard out of band, running on BlueField-4, beyond the agent’s reach and knowledge.
In the OpenShell reference architecture, agents execute on NVIDIA Vera CPUs, while BlueField-4 sits on the node’s only path to the model. NVIDIA Sentry inspects agent-to-model communications and enforces access policies without relying on the agent to report its own behavior. Memory introspection adds context about the agent’s execution environment, such as a container or microVM, to help detect external threats and agent misbehavior.
Governing agent communications
DOCA Tower is NVIDIA Sentry’s AI security gateway. Built on Envoy, the open source edge and service proxy, it operates as a transparent proxy for agent traffic, placing a bidirectional inspection layer between an agent and the external environment.
Agent network traffic reaches BlueField-4 through a direct network I/O path that bypasses host OS/hypervisor packet processing. All of the agent’s network communications are governed by NVIDIA Sentry as BlueField-4 sits on the only path to the model and to the outside world.
An agent’s network access boundary is controlled using DOCA Flow and DOCA Tower, which work in concert to restrict agent access to approved resources. DOCA Flow is used to implement a layer-4 firewall for each agent, accelerated in silicon on BlueField-4. The firewall blocks connections to unauthorized destinations and forwards permitted traffic to DOCA Tower for layer-7 (application layer) inspection, authorization, and additional security checks.
DOCA Tower acts as a transparent proxy, performing Transport Layer Security (TLS) termination using built-in, in-silicon TLS acceleration. For connections configured for inspection, it decrypts the agent traffic permitted by the layer-4 firewall to inspect and control agent communications.
NVIDIA Sentry uses the Open Policy Agent (OPA), an open source policy engine, to evaluate access requests against defined policies. OPA uses Rego, a declarative domain-specific language designed to evaluate complex hierarchical data structures. OPA runs locally in memory and can evaluate requests in under a millisecond, depending on policy complexity and configuration.
DOCA Tower is compatible with OpenShell policies, using OPA to extend network access policies and runtime controls into BlueField-4 and to the infrastructure.
Enforcing agent access policies with runtime context
An agent’s network communications provide only part of the information needed to assess its security and integrity. Visibility into the agent’s execution environment adds context for evaluating access requests that go beyond a traditional resource access policy.
DOCA Argus provides real-time visibility into an agent’s execution environment and operational state, giving NVIDIA Sentry additional context about agent access requests.
It uses live memory introspection to analyze selected regions of volatile host memory and obtain independent evidence of the system’s operational state.
DOCA Argus runs independently of the host, analyzing host memory on BlueField-4 without host-resident agents. This agentless design provides independent runtime visibility while preserving host compute resources. By operating outside the host in its own isolated trust domain, DOCA Argus remains beyond the reach of host software even if the host is compromised.
DOCA Argus maps the execution environment in real time—for example, containers to their respective pods and sandboxes to microVMs—and identifies the running processes and their properties within each environment. It also maps relationships between processes and threads, file access, network connections, loaded libraries, CPUs, GPUs, memory, and other system resources. DOCA Argus tracks containers, processes, and loaded libraries using their associated hashes.
This runtime context enables NVIDIA Sentry to connect agent access requests to the processes and execution environments behind them, enforcing policies that consider both the requested action and the security and integrity of the agent making it.
Using runtime context to evaluate agent access
NVIDIA Sentry correlates network connection information from DOCA Tower with runtime context from DOCA Argus to evaluate access requests. NVIDIA Sentry uses this context to enforce policies based on additional attributes and assertions provided by DOCA Argus. It also enriches tamper-evident records of agent activity with runtime context, reducing the need for downstream correlation.
Figure 1 shows how these checks work. DOCA Tower uses its policy engine to correlate a network connection with the agent’s process that initiated it, its properties, and the container it belongs to. A network access policy can, for example, require that the container’s hash match a list of approved container hashes. It can also require that the initiating process, identified by its hash, appear in the container software bill of materials (SBOM), have permission to initiate network connections, and use an approved execution path and command-line arguments. DOCA Tower then checks whether policy permits the requested access—for example, access to an API and permission to perform the requested action.
NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Argus real-time observations and alerts to continuously evaluate agent security. Potential warning signs include executing unapproved tools; using ptrace to attack another process or spawn a process that attacks the agent; excessive outbound traffic suggesting data leakage; unauthorized file access or changes; CPU spikes; excessive writes to temporary folders; and large-scale file deletion. When NVIDIA Sentry detects any deviation, it can request millisecond-scale in-silicon containment.
Extending controls to agent interactions
Agent security policies need to govern both what leaves the sandbox and what comes back. Requests can expose sensitive information or initiate unauthorized operations. Responses can introduce malicious instructions or other content that redirects an agent from its assigned goals.
NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Tower’s extensible inspection capabilities to apply controls to requests and responses. These controls can:
- Apply IP-, URL-, and protocol-level restrictions to agent communications.
- Capture tamper-evident records of agent requests, responses, and data flows for behavioral analysis and investigation.
- Govern agent-to-agent (A2A) and Model Context Protocol (MCP) traffic.
- Detect and redact personally identifiable information and secrets, including API keys, tokens, and passwords.
- Identify and block content prohibited by policy.
NVIDIA Sentry evaluates inspected requests and responses throughout an agent’s session, applying policy as the agent accesses models, tools, APIs, and services.
Evaluating agent behavior using specialized models
NVIDIA Sentry integrates with specialized AI models to analyze agent communications and classify agent behavior using tool calls and available reasoning traces. These models run locally or remotely on dedicated GPU-accelerated systems. The classifiers assess whether an agent’s behavior remains consistent with an agent’s designed intent or indicates behavioral drift.
The models can classify agent communications inline or out of band. Inline classification can trigger blocking before potentially harmful content reaches its destination. Out-of-band classification can trigger a response action after detecting agent misbehavior.
Tamper-evident activity records and detection results provide forensic evidence for further incident investigations.
Agent communications require continuous classification to detect misbehavior. DOCA Argus complements this classification with ongoing analysis of the agent’s operational environment to evaluate runtime security and behavior.
NVIDIA Sentry can contain and quarantine agents within milliseconds using BlueField-4 in-silicon enforcement capabilities without the cooperation of the agent or the host software.
These independent controls matter when software boundaries fail. Even if an agent escapes its sandbox, NVIDIA Sentry retains its monitoring and enforcement capabilities as it operates from BlueField-4’s isolated trust domain.
Enterprise security platforms can also use NVIDIA Sentry telemetry to correlate detections and request response actions. The protected record preserves the observed activity and policy context that led to enforcement for subsequent review.
Using agent identity in access decisions
Security controls must connect an agent’s identity with its permissions and requested action. NVIDIA Sentry uses this identity context in application-layer policy evaluation. DOCA Tower integrates with SPIFFE/SPIRE to support verifiable workload identity and supports integration with partner identity systems.
Identity establishes who is making a request. Authorization policies determine which resources an identity may access and which operations are permitted. Runtime evidence adds context about the execution environment associated with the request.
This approach connects identity and runtime security. If an agent’s behavior or integrity changes, NVIDIA Sentry can use that context when evaluating subsequent access requests, applying the organization’s defined policies.
Preserving a trusted record of agent activity
Security teams need evidence for incident investigations, even when an agent has escaped its sandbox or altered host-based logs.
NVIDIA Sentry produces attested telemetry and tamper-evident records using BlueField-4’s independent trust domain. DOCA Tower records inspected communications and policy decisions outside the reach of the agent and host software, while DOCA Argus contributes independently observed runtime signals.
An agent that changes a log inside its own environment cannot make the same change to the protected record maintained on BlueField-4.
Attestation provides verifiable evidence of telemetry’s source and integrity. Security teams can use these records to reconstruct observed interactions, review enforcement decisions, and support audits.
NVIDIA Sentry can supply this telemetry to enterprise security platforms, such as XDR and SIEM platforms and security data lakes, connecting agent activity with broader threat intelligence, detection logic, and incident-response workflows.
Extending NVIDIA Sentry with enterprise security capabilities
NVIDIA Sentry enables developers and cybersecurity providers to extend monitoring, governance, and enforcement through DOCA libraries and microservices.
DOCA Tower uses Envoy’s extensibility, enabling partners to adapt existing plugins or develop new ones to run on BlueField. This provides a familiar foundation for integrating access controls, content inspection, telemetry, and specialized detection logic into the application-layer path.
NVIDIA plans to publish core plugins to accelerate development, including a plugin that exposes agent communications for further analysis of available reasoning traces.
Partners can combine these capabilities with their identity services, AI classifiers, threat intelligence, and security operations platforms. NVIDIA Sentry contributes independent runtime visibility and infrastructure enforcement, while connected platforms add enterprise context and coordinate investigation and response.
Building layered protection for AI agents
Scaling agentic AI requires continuous visibility into and control over what agents can access and do throughout execution. NVIDIA Sentry brings that control into an independent infrastructure domain, combining application-layer inspection through DOCA Tower with runtime evidence and visibility from DOCA Argus and in-silicon enforcement on BlueField-4.
Alongside NVIDIA OpenShell, NVIDIA Sentry extends protection from software execution boundaries to a hardware-isolated safeguard. It enables security teams to evaluate agent identity, authority, interactions, and runtime integrity together—and act when behavior crosses defined boundaries.
Developers and cybersecurity teams can begin exploring these foundations with NVIDIA DOCA. Available libraries and microservices, including DOCA Argus, DOCA Flow, and OVS-DOCA, provide a starting point for experimenting with out-of-band observability and infrastructure enforcement ahead of NVIDIA Sentry’s planned availability early next year.

articles.title: Laser says its new ChargeCore semi-solid state powerbanks are the safest you can buy - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Australian consumer electronics company Laser says it next generation of ChargeCore powerbanks with next-generation semi-solid-state battery technology are the safest you can buy today.
The new Laser ChargeCore battery range include models with three capacities and deliver safety and stability thanks to the onboard semi-solid-state technology.
They are available in 10,000mAh, 20,000mAh, and 27,000mAh capacities with progressively more powerful 20W and 35W USB-C PD (Power Delivery) fast charging options.
Semi-solid-state battery technology is an evolution in battery chemistry and the biggest advantage is improved thermal stability while still offering stronger and faster charging performance.
The advancements in the battery technology can now be implemented in consumer products, including power banks that store and deliver more power in a compact design while remaining stable even under demanding conditions.
The batteries have a gel-like core, which helps reduce overheating and fire risk.
Its enhanced safety reduces heat, which means the battery has a longer life and can last through more charges and will not catch fire.
Laser put the new ChargeCore semi-solid state batteries through rigorous testing and even when the battery was pierced, hammered, and sliced, it still worked and didn’t catch fire.
Laser is celebrating its 40th anniversary 2027 and has made a name for itself as delivering affordable yet high-quality tech to Australian customers.
Has sold power banks to Australians for the last 15 years and it prides itself as being on the cutting edge of battery technology.
Laser launched Australia’s first range of LiFePO4 battery technology in 2025 and is now among the first to move to semi-solid-state technology with this latest range.
“We’ve been closely following semi solid state battery development for some time, since first visiting an EV factory several years ago, and advancements since that time mean that it can now move into smaller, more compact options,” says Chris Lau, Laser Managing Director.
“Simply put, I believe that semi-solid state chemistry makes this the safest powerbank technology available in Australia today.
“We are focused on safety and peace of mind, and we know that it is a huge concern for Australian consumers these days when buying powerbanks,”
“I’ve personally had the opportunity to see first-hand the testing that goes into the manufacturing of these semi solid state powerbanks, including the stress testing placed on the battery technology.
“It gives you an appreciation for just how much engineering, testing and development sits behind something consumers simply put in their bag and use every day.”
The Laser ChargeCore semi-solid state batteries include easy-to-read digital displays which the battery’s remaining capacity.
And they also have built-in protection against overcharging, overcurrent, short circuits and overheating.
Each battery has three ports: two USB-A and one USB-C while the 27,000mAh battery has two USB-Cs and one USB-A – so you can charge three devices at the same time.
Each battery also comes with a 60W-rated cable and a built-in heat sensor.
The batteries will be able to charge an iPhone 17 to 50% in about 30 minutes.
The batteries will be able to charge smartphones, tablets, portable gaming devices, earphones, cameras, drones and much more.
The ChargeCore 27,000mAh semi-solid-state power bank has a higher capacity output and can charge laptops, including the MacBook Air, Chromebooks and Surface devices.
The new series is available in Black, Galactica, Grey, and Dark Cherry.
Pricing and availability
ChargeCore Everyday Semi Solid State Series at Harvey Norman and Laser Online
– 10,000mAh with 20W USB-C PD – $49.95 (Black available now, Galactica, Grey, and Dark Cherry coming soon)
– 20,000mAh with 20W USB-C PD – $69.95 (Black available now, Galactica, and Dark Cherry coming soon)
– 27,000mAh with 35W USB-C PD – $99.95 (Black, available now)

articles.title: Nouvelle cyberattaque en France : les données de propriétaires de chiens et chats ont encore été volées
articles.text:
Il y a quelques jours, un pirate qui se fait appeler ChimeraZ a revendiqué un nouveau vol de données d’envergure sur un forum. Le hacker a mis en vente plusieurs bases de données sur une plateforme criminelle. Ces annonces ont été rapidement repérées par le site spécialisé FrenchBreaches.
 🔴 Alerté par FrenchBreaches, le LOOF confirme une cyberattaque et le vol de données ! Noms, adresses, e-mails, identifiants de chats et dates de naissance potentiellement exposés. L’organisme annonce avoir identifié l’origine de l’attaque et suspendu certains services. https://t.co/jqATim9kWd
— FrenchBreaches (@Frenchbreaches) October 20, 2026
Le répertoire le plus volumineux appartient à l’I-CAD, le fichier national d’identification des chiens, chats et furets. Selon le hacker, 2,9 millions de propriétaires et 50 000 vétérinaires sont concernés par cette fuite. Le pirate revendique aussi le piratage des données de 1,4 million de personnes recensées dans la Société Centrale Canine (SCC), l’organisme de référence pour les chiens de race. Enfin, le hacker prétend également avoir compromis le Livre officiel des origines félines (LOOF), l’organisme qui gère les pedigrees des chats de race. Environ 654 000 enregistrements ainsi que plus de 90 000 documents (48 Go) ont été volés. Au total, ce sont plus de 4 millions de personnes qui auraient été touchées.
Dans les échantillons analysés par le média spécialisé, on trouve des noms et prénoms, des coordonnées, des numéros de puce électronique, des noms d’animaux, voire des pedigrees et des tests ADN. Il y a suffisamment d’informations pour relier précisément un animal à son maître, ce qui ouvre la porte à toutes les dérives et abus. Avec le nom d’un animal, sa race ou son numéro de puce, un escroc peut rendre un faux message très crédible. Il peut notamment se faire passer pour un vétérinaire ou un organisme officiel afin de réclamer un paiement. Les éleveurs, dont les coordonnées professionnelles ont été volées, sont particulièrement visés.
À lire aussi : Cyberattaques en France : les dernières fuites de données et entreprises touchées
Le LOOF confirme rapidement la cyberattaque
La fuite a été rapidement confirmée par le LOOF. Dès le 20 octobre, l’organisme a confirmé avoir été victime d’une cyberattaque. Selon le communiqué, des individus se sont introduits dans le système informatique pour récupérer des données. L’organisme confirme que des noms, prénoms, adresses postales et e-mail, noms et numéros d’identification des chats, et dates de naissance, ont été subtilisés. Le Livre officiel des origines félines précise par contre n’avoir identifié « aucune donnée sensible » ayant été compromise. Par précaution, le LOOF a coupé l’accès à plusieurs de ses services. Ensuite, l’origine de l’attaque a été découverte, et la brèche a été colmatée.
Entre les lignes, l’organisme confirme qu’une même entité s’est attaquée à l’I-CAD et à la SCC. D’autres structures ont été ciblées par des attaques du même type. Celles-ci ont été revendiquées par « le ou les mêmes individus », indique le LOOF. Ce n’est pas la première fois que les données de l’I-CAD se retrouvent entre les mains de cybercriminels. Cet été, des pirates étaient déjà parvenus à pénétrer dans le système d’Ingenium animalis, la société qui gère le fichier I-CAD. Les intrus avaient volé les adresses e-mail de millions de propriétaires de chats et de chiens. Ces attaques s’inscrivent évidemment dans l’explosion des fuites de données en France. Pays le plus touché d’Europe, la France recense plus de 40 millions de comptes piratés en six mois.

articles.title: NVIDIA cuDSS Now Generally Available to Accelerate Engineering and Scientific Simulations
articles.text:
NVIDIA cuDSS, launched today in general availability, is an NVIDIA CUDA-X library that shifts a critical part of engineering and scientific simulations onto GPUs.
Complex engineering feats — from advanced chips to aircraft to industrial systems —– depend on simulation to predict how designs will perform before they’re built. As designs become more complex, simulations take longer to run, increasing computing demands and limiting the number of ideas teams can test.
NVIDIA cuDSS accelerates solving large sparse systems — the math-heavy step that repeats throughout engineering and scientific simulations and often limits how many designs a team can test — by tapping into GPUs. This lets applications reduce time to results and increase simulation throughput, enabling end users to explore larger more realistic models, more accurate representations and a wider design space at a reduced cost.
Industry leaders are already integrating NVIDIA cuDSS into their tools to transform workflows for their end customers:
- Applied Materials: With cuDSS, Applied Materials accelerated sparse solves in Ginestra, its physics-based, defect-centric simulation platform, by up to 10x versus CPU-only approaches, speeding exploration of semiconductor materials and device reliability.
- COMSOL: Using COMSOL Multiphysics with NVIDIA cuDSS on NVIDIA accelerated computing, ZEISS SMT achieved a measured 4x speedup in an EUV lithography plasma simulation benchmark, completing the full simulation in six days and 14 hours.
- Cadence: Uses cuDSS in its Celsius software to accelerate simulations of heat, structural stress and warpage in advanced chips and 3D chip designs, helping customers including Nokia analyze complex designs faster.
- Dassault Systèmes: Dassault Systèmes reports an 8-10x speedup using cuDSS within its Abaqus structural and computer simulation technology electromagnetic solvers for performance-critical simulations across industries.
- Siemens: Siemens uses cuDSS in Simcenter STAR-CCM+ to accelerate simulations of structures in fluid-structure interaction workflows.
- Synopsys: Synopsys uses cuDSS in its Sentaurus Device simulator tool to accelerate simulations of advanced logic, memory and power chips, helping Infineon model increasingly complex devices faster.
Accelerated Simulation at Scale
As simulation workloads grow in size and complexity, cuDSS can scale out of the box from individual workstations to large computing clusters.
Developers can integrate cuDSS into existing engineering, scientific and optimization software offerings, bringing GPU acceleration to tools already used by engineers and researchers. They can use cuDSS through C, C++, Python and Fortran interfaces.
Learn more about cuDSS by visiting the NVIDIA demo booth and Dassault Systèmes booth at GTC Berlin.
Featured image courtesy of Dassault Systèmes.

articles.title: Microsoft Previews dotnetup: Toolchain Manager for .NET SDKs and Runtimes
articles.text:
Microsoft has released a public preview of dotnetup, a cross-platform toolchain manager that installs, updates, and removes .NET SDKs and runtimes inside the user's account rather than a system-managed directory. As reported on the .NET Blog, the tool was announced on October 15 by Chet Husk, program manager for the .NET SDK, and follows the model of rustup and nvm.
According to the documentation, commands and behavior may change between preview releases, and production machines should keep using the installers, package managers, or Visual Studio.
The design, as described in the announcement, tracks intent instead of versions. A developer asks for a channel such as latest, lts, preview, daily, a major like 10, a minor like 10.0, or a feature band like 10.0.1xx, and dotnetup resolves it to a release. Exact versions, as the post notes, stay pinned during updates.
Several requirements can share one managed installation, and the tool reads the nearest global.json so team builds stay deterministic. Furthermore, according to the docs, files live under the user's local data directory on Windows, macOS, and Linux, and dotnetup never writes to Program Files\dotnet or /usr/share/dotnet.
Installation uses a bootstrap script fetched from aka.ms with curl or irm. As described in the docs, it places the binary in ~/.dotnetup after checking its SHA-512 checksum, and dotnetup init then installs the latest stable SDK and configures the shell. The docs list three access modes: none runs .NET through dotnetup dotnet without touching the environment, shell edits the shell profile, and everywhere, the Windows-only default, changes the system PATH and needs elevation.
The docs also warn that everywhere mode takes precedence over machine-wide copies, including the one Visual Studio installs, so projects needing an SDK dotnetup has not installed fail to build. To avoid that, setup reportedly offers to migrate existing machine-wide installs.
As reported, monthly servicing becomes a single dotnetup update, which re-resolves every tracked channel and installs the newest matching versions. Individual runtimes can be targeted, for example dotnetup runtime install aspnetcore@10.0, and the docs list the SDK, .NET runtime, ASP.NET Core runtime, and Windows Desktop runtime as supported components. After an update, as stated in the post, dotnetup removes any component no remaining requirement needs, and sdk uninstall or runtime uninstall trigger the same cleanup.
Moreover, preview and daily builds install side by side through dotnetup sdk install preview or dotnetup runtime install daily, although the docs note that daily builds are not code-signed. dotnetup self update refreshes the tool itself. Over the dotnet-install scripts, the post claims tracking of installed components, signature and checksum validation, faster multi-version installs, and one CLI surface on every platform. The stated roadmap includes admin-level installs on Windows, replacing the script-based parts of the GitHub Actions and Azure DevOps tasks, and agent skills so AI assistants reach for the tool by default.
Meanwhile, on r/dotnet, one developer with months of use praised the simpler Linux setup, but the top comment asked why anyone would pick dotnetup over mise, which several already use.
Others criticized the curl-to-shell bootstrap, asked for winget, apt, or Homebrew packages, noted that Visual Studio does not see dotnetup installs, and wanted dotnet-ef and other CLI tools managed too. In reply on the blog, Husk stated that packages are planned after user validation.
For interested readers, full documentation, including the command reference and telemetry details, is available on Microsoft Learn, and feedback goes to the dotnetup category of the dotnet/sdk GitHub discussions.

articles.title: Scaling CPO Testing Beyond A Single Die
articles.text:
Fiber alignment, connector durability, and simultaneous optical and electrical testing pose challenges for high-volume manufacturing.
Key Takeaways:
Experts At The Table: The industry is forging a path from single-site to multi-site testing while system architectures and connector types continue to evolve. Semiconductor Engineering sat down with Matt Griffin, senior product manager for optoelectronics test at Teradyne; Ira Leventhal, vice president of research and venture at Advantest America; Dave Armstrong, fellow at ISE Labs, a subsidiary of ASE Group; and Kazuo Yamaguchi, silicon photonics researcher and engineer at Keysight Technologies. What follows are excerpts of that conversation. To view part one, click here.
Fig. 1: (L-R): Teradyne’s Griffin; Keysight’s Yamaguchi; ISE Labs’ Armstrong; Advantest’s Leventhal.
SE: Is it true that you can only test one die at a time today?
Armstrong: I would hope some insertions will go away over time, but right now there are more things being added than being subtracted. It’s a hard one. In terms of testing one die, that depends on the die. If an 8 kW GPU is your main ASIC, and you have multiple connectors around multiple sides of the part from a tester resource standpoint, and the amount of power a tester can deliver and take out of the part, it’s pretty challenging to get beyond one die. But if you look down the NPO-versus-CPO path, NPO is typically a single connector device. You’re going to have to be able to go to multi-site to scale that to high volume. Insertions two and three are the fertile ground for multi-site. Those are longer more complex test insertions. PIC wafer testing tends to be single-site today. From my experience, there is some hope on the horizon to bring it up a little bit higher with some capabilities in the probe card area, notably from Technoprobe.
Griffin: I agree with Dave. Most production solutions today are single-site, and when you talk about the optical engine, the main bottleneck is fiber alignment. Many companies are working on multi-site solutions, and I hope they succeed and take off because that only helps the whole industry ramp faster. But we’ve got a little bit longer to go there.
SE: For these alignment ports, can you repeatedly test at that site?
Griffin: Ideally, you’re able to repeatedly test almost infinitely because you should never be contacting the device with the optical probe or the fiber array unit (FAU). When you’re bringing up a new test solution, you do sometimes crash FAUs on first systems. In reality, the bigger concern is contamination on the FAU, so cleaning is needed. On the connector side, at the module level or for optical engines with receptacles attached, the optical connector lifecycle is where we need more effort, because the device-side connector is designed to be attached once and, hopefully, never disconnected. And every new connector generation changes both the connector recipe and the automation recipe.
Leventhal: In a sense, this is nothing new. For instance, with BGAs, if you socket at the device too many times, then you start worrying about damaging the balls on the BGA. It’s a similar problem and the industry will gravitate toward connector designs that are more robust. Matt made a really important point about how your test side connector needs to be some sort of a hardened connector that doesn’t wear out easily after 20 to 50 insertions. It needs to last for tens of thousands or 100,000 insertions. So you’ve got to go to a hardened metal, and then you’ve got a hardened metal going against the receptacle on the device, which is not going to be that hardened metal. If you’re not careful, you could damage that connector sooner than the spec lifetime. So as the industry evolves to the winning connector designs, robustness on the device side is going to be a really important part of that.
SE: What are the challenges with making simultaneous electrical and optical connections?
Armstrong: It’s just a question of time.
Yamaguchi: Beyond DC and optical probing, the harder part of simultaneous electrical and optical connection is characterizing electro-optic devices in RF. Modulator and photodetector performance is ultimately validated through S-parameters, so you need optical and high-frequency RF contact at the same time. Probe cards can only fit a limited number of RF lines, and their bandwidth is also limited, while today’s devices are characterized beyond 200 GHz. At wafer and die insertions, simultaneous connection is really an RF probing challenge.
Leventhal: Warpage is going to create additional challenges on top of just trying to solve the problem in an ideal case. You need to be able to align in multiple axes. And the BGA has a crazy amount of pins that you have to make reliable contact with, so that problem is getting more challenging. Adding to that is being able to do the right level of alignment, either coming from the top or coming from the side. It’s significantly challenging. I agree with Dave, it’s a question of time in multiple senses. Each insertion takes time, although there are ways of minimizing that by integrating certain operations together. But also, it’s going to take time for all of this to mature to the point that it’s going to be easier to test at scale.
Griffin: At its core, there’s an optical and an electrical interface to the device at every insertion, and sometimes those interfaces are on the top side of the device, sometimes the bottom side, and sometimes both. And then when you talk about module level, they’re on two to four sides of the package across some number of optical engines. So if you look at optical alignment on its own, it’s not that big of a challenge. But when you start combining it with all the different, I’ll say, flavors of architecture that we’re seeing, and trying to design a scalable test system that can handle as many of those flavors as possible for your customers, that’s really where some of the fun challenges are.
Armstrong: I also chair the IPSR test roadmap for photonics, and in our latest report we highlight a test methodology for AC testing. AC testing, bit error rate testing, will be one of the bigger time sinks. If we had good DFT, we could just do loopback on the optical side and loopback on the electrical side at the same time. And technically, there’s no reason you couldn’t combine those two tests. But today, most people are saying, “Okay, I’ll do loopback on one side or the other side, and a bit error rate test of some nature on the other side, so that becomes a very expensive setup that doubles the effective test time. The more DFT and concurrent testing we do, the better off we’ll be in the long run.
Griffin: The automation challenge is still there, but I agree with Dave’s point. Most customers going to volume will have some sort of loopback capability — electrical, optical, or a combination — but it remains to be seen what wins out there.
SE: Which measurements dominate production test — optical power, insertion loss, or bit error rate?
Armstrong: In terms of test time, it seems like a lot of people are very concerned with insertion loss just because of how often it’s done, but I don’t think that should be number one. Eye quality would be number one, and high-quality receiver sensitivity would also be high on the list, and bit error rate.
Griffin: I agree. I’ll add wavelength sweeps for optical engines. Those can take a significant amount of time, depending on customer requirements.
Yamaguchi: I also agree, but we need to be mindful of correlating such performance with not only ‘known good die,’ but also ‘known good and reliable die.’ It’s the probability of surviving integration and service life, because defects that escape pre-assembly are largely integration-induced effects such as fiber/FAU coupling loss after attach, resonance drift versus laser tunability, thermal and packaging effects. In the end, overall transmitter and receiver performance are defined by standards, using metrics such as TDECQ (Transmitter and Dispersion Eye Closure Quaternary) and receiver sensitivity.
Leventhal: Going forward, the main issue is whether your data transmission is working correctly in both directions — electrical to optical, optical to electrical — and how are you going to root-cause problems when the system is not working? We will need to gather key information as early as possible to determine what causes data transmission issues.
Leave a Reply

articles.title: La voiture la plus vendue du monde va passer à l'électrique
articles.text:
Toyota s’apprête à faire un grand pas pour sa gamme de voitures électriques. Le constructeur japonais va donner à son best-seller, figurant régulièrement comme la voiture la plus vendue au monde annuellement, une version électrique. Voici ce que l’on peut attendre de la future Toyota Corolla électrique, qui pourrait ne pas être fabriquée au Japon.
Une Corolla électrique à l’horizon 2028
Selon les informations venant du média japonais Nikkei, Toyota aurait l’ambition de lancer cette Corolla électrique à l’horizon 2028 en s’appuyant sur la Chine. En effet, pour préparer cette berline électrique très importante pour le constructeur japonais, l’aide de la coentreprise FAW Toyota est à envisager. C’est déjà le cas pour le Toyota bZ3X commercialisé en Chine, qui représente une bonne part des ventes de voitures électriques dans le monde pour Toyota.
Cette berline électrique portant le nom de Corolla devrait être la première Toyota à utiliser la plateforme nommée « multipathway », mais celle-ci serait multiénergie.
Adapter la Corolla au monde entier
La Toyota Corolla est un modèle essentiel pour Toyota, car elle est distribuée dans le monde entier. Mais c’est aussi un exercice difficile de proposer un même véhicule sur tous les marchés du monde. Il y a bien sûr quelques adaptations pour les différents marchés, mais une Corolla vendue aux États-Unis, au Japon ou en Europe est, dans les grandes lignes, identique.
De ce fait, Toyota doit être prudent, car il est très difficile de concilier les besoins des marchés américain, japonais, chinois ou européen dans un même et unique véhicule. C’est pour cela que Toyota ne va pas proposer qu’une version électrique de la prochaine Corolla, mais bien un véhicule multiénergie pour s’adapter aux différents marchés.
On attend donc des motorisations électriques, mais aussi des hybrides et des essence sur la future génération de Corolla. De ce fait, elle pourrait être vendue uniquement en électrique en Chine, en électrique et hybride en Europe pour répondre à nos contraintes réglementaires, et avec toutes les énergies aux États-Unis. Ce qui devrait assurer une belle réussite encore à la prochaine génération de Corolla, car Toyota ne met pas tous ses œufs dans le même panier.

- Îlot photo vraiment très épais.
